Chapter 4 Energy principles and virtual work

4.3 Mathematics: change of variables

We now have the integral over a body and the divergence theorem for bodies that we can cut into pieces between two graphs, and in section 4.2.10 the integral also for every set with volume, without an order of integration. Three questions are still open.

  1. The volume of a small piece after loading. In chapter 2, section 2.10.5, we replaced the piece of a body near the point \(P\) after loading by the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors \(\mat F\) times the vectors of the fibres. The ratio of its volume to the volume of the piece before loading is the Jacobian \(J = \det\mat F\). On the hanging bar we checked only that the ratio of volumes for the parallelepiped spanned by the exact vectors of the fibres after loading approaches this number. For the true piece with curved edges we did not show it even there. The general statement needs the volume of a body with curved faces, which we now have (section 4.2.10), and a rule for how an integral changes when we describe the points of a body by new variables.
  2. A surface described in two ways. The cut \(y = 3\) mm between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round hanging bar is a side piece of the surface for the piece \(C\) and the bottom lid for the piece \(D\) (section 4.2.11). For this cut both descriptions gave the same iterated integral. When two descriptions of the same surface use different variables, however, we still have to show that they give the same surface integral.
  3. Bodies that we cannot cut into pieces between graphs. A ball and a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre, are such bodies, and we will need them in chapter 11. We have not yet proved the divergence theorem for them.

We answer all three questions with the same move. We describe a body or a surface as the image of a simple set, a box or a rectangle, under a rule that assigns a point to every point. We already know such a rule. The deformation assigns to every point \(P\) of a body before loading the point \(P + \vek u(P)\), where this part of the material is after loading, and the piece after loading is the image of the piece before. We will assemble a ball from a cube and six bodies that are images of boxes, and a surface will be the image of a rectangle. We then turn the integral over the image into an integral over the simple set, and in this translation the Jacobian of the rule appears, just as the Jacobian of the deformation appeared for the small piece.

From history

The first to gather the derivatives of coordinates with respect to other coordinates into a determinant with more than two rows was Cauchy, and in a question of exactly this kind, the volume of a piece that moves (MUIR, PDF p. 372). For the prize in mathematical analysis of 1815 he wrote about waves on the surface of a heavy fluid. A small element of fluid, at first a cuboid with edges \(\mathrm{d}a\), \(\mathrm{d}b\), \(\mathrm{d}c\) at a corner with coordinates \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), moves after a time \(t\) and the corner arrives at the point \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The three edges are then no longer parallel to the axes. Cauchy wrote their projections on the axes with the derivatives of the coordinates \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) with respect to \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and wrote the volume of the element as the determinant of these nine derivatives multiplied by \(\mathrm{d}a\,\mathrm{d}b\,\mathrm{d}c\). He wrote that the volumes before and after the motion must be equal, and obtained an equation between the derivatives (MUIR, PDF p. 373-374). The reason for this condition we see ourselves: the fluid does not compress in such a motion, so the element keeps its volume. This is the same ratio of volumes that we wrote in chapter 2 for a piece of a body after loading. The memoir was printed only in 1827 (MUIR, PDF p. 372).

In 1839 Eugène-Charles Catalan, in a memoir that won a prize of the academy in Brussels, treated the question of how a multiple integral changes when we introduce new variables. For two and three variables he referred to Lagrange and others (MUIR, PDF p. 382-384). In 1841 Jacobi gave the determinants of derivatives that appear when we introduce new variables in an integral a memoir of their own. He called them functional determinants (funkcionalne determinante) and devoted almost half of his 87-page account of determinants to them (MUIR, PDF p. 384). In the same memoir he also treated the notation for partial derivatives that we discussed in section 1.7.2 (MUIR, PDF p. 385). He pointed out that for a system of functions the functional determinant plays the role that the derivative plays for a function of one variable (MUIR, PDF p. 385). Indeed, the derivative tells how many times a small interval is stretched, and the determinant tells how many times a small volume is enlarged, as with Cauchy's element of fluid. This is why it is called the Jacobian determinant (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 125).

Back to the three questions about the volume of a piece, the surface and the bodies that we do not know how to cut up, and to the rule for how an integral changes when points are described by new variables, with which we solve them. The route is as follows. First we name rules that assign a point to a point and show how to differentiate a function that we evaluate at the image of a point (section 4.3.1). Then we show when a rule can be reversed, so that from the image we get the point it came from, and that the reverse rule is again continuously differentiable (section 4.3.2). Next come the volume of the image under a rule that is multiplication by a matrix (section 4.3.3) and the rule for the integral over an image (section 4.3.4). With it we answer the first question (section 4.3.5), with a description of a surface by two variables the second (section 4.3.6), and with the divergence theorem for bodies that are images of boxes the third (section 4.3.7).

4.3.1 The chain rule

The deformation is the first example of a rule whose input is a point and whose output is a point. In chapter 1 we wrote it with the displacement field: the material that was at the point \(P\) before loading is at the point \(P + \vek u(P)\) after loading. From the partial derivatives of the displacements we assembled the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) (definition 1.110), which tells how short fibres near \(P\) stretch and turn. In the questions at the start of the section we will meet other such rules, also rules whose input is a point of the plane and whose output is a point of space. Such a rule will send a rectangle to a curved surface. A rule that assigns to an element of one set an element of another we called a function in definition 1.4. When input and output are points, we also call it a map (preslikava), just as in section 1.16.2 we called multiplication by a matrix a linear map. LEBL1 uses the two words as synonyms (PDF p. 14).

Definition 4.42 Map and its matrix of partial derivatives (preslikava in njena matrika odvodov)

Let \(D\) be a set of points of space. A map \(\Phi\) on \(D\) is a rule that assigns to every point \(P\) of \(D\) exactly one point of space \(\Phi(P)\), the image of the point \(P\). In a chosen rectangular Cartesian coordinate system the image has the coordinates \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(P)\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(P)\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(P)\). The functions \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\), whose input is the point \(P\), given by three coordinates, and whose output is one number each, are the components of the map. The image of a set \(W \subseteq D\) is the set \(\Phi(W)\) of the images of all points of \(W\). In the same way a map on a set of points of the plane or on an interval is a rule that assigns to every point of the plane, given by two coordinates, or to every number of the interval exactly one point of space or exactly one point of the plane.

Let \(D\) be an open set (definition 1.90, in the plane definition 4.15) or an open interval. The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\) if all its components are continuously differentiable on \(D\). Then the matrix of partial derivatives, or Jacobian matrix (matrika odvodov), of the map \(\Phi\) at a point \(P\) of \(D\) is the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)\) with the elements

\[\big(\mat F_\Phi(P)\big)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) , \tag{4.23}\]

where \(i\) runs over the coordinates of the image and \(j\) over the coordinates of the input point. When the input point and the image have the same number of coordinates, \(\mat F_\Phi(P)\) is a square matrix, and the number \(J_\Phi(P) = \det\mat F_\Phi(P)\) is the Jacobian (Jacobijeva determinanta) of the map \(\Phi\) at the point \(P\).

Source: LEBL1 PDF p. 14, where a map (mapping) is another name for a function. LEBL2 Def. 8.3.1 (PDF p. 35) defines the derivative of a map, Prop. 8.3.9 (PDF pp. 39-40) shows that the matrix of partial derivatives represents it, and Def. 8.3.10 (PDF p. 42) defines the Jacobian and in a footnote the Jacobian matrix. KREYSZIG §10.3, (7) (PDF p. 456), for maps of the plane.

The definition says what goes in and what comes out. The input is a point, given by its coordinates, the output is a point, given by the components. The matrix of partial derivatives has as many rows as the image has coordinates and as many columns as the input point has coordinates. For a map from space to space it is of size \(3 \times 3\), for a map that assigns a point of space to a point of the plane it is \(3 \times 2\), and such a matrix has no determinant. The deformation is a map with the components

\[\begin{aligned} \Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) &= x + u_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z) , \\ \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) &= y + u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z) , \\ \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) &= z + u_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z) . \end{aligned}\]

The partial derivative of the coordinate \(x\) with respect to \(x\) is \(1\), with respect to \(y\) and to \(z\) it is \(0\), because the function \(t \mapsto t\) has derivative \(1\) and a constant function derivative \(0\) (lemma 1.81, item 4). The same holds for \(y\) and \(z\). Therefore

\[\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = I_{\mathrm{ij}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}} = I_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ij}} ,\]

where \(I_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is an element of the identity matrix, \(1\) for \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) and \(0\) otherwise. The matrix of partial derivatives of the deformation is thus the deformation gradient, \(\mat F_\Phi = \mat I + \mat H = \mat F\), and its Jacobian is the Jacobian \(J_\Phi = J\) of lemma 2.55. For the sheared cube, the steel cube with edge 10 mm whose bottom face is glued to a table and whose top face we shift by 10 µm in the direction of the axis \(x\), with the axis \(z\) up, we have by (1.16) \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\) and \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The map is \(\Phi(x, y, z) = (x + 0{,}001\,z,\ y,\ z)\), and

\[\mat F_\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad J_\Phi = 1 .\]

What does a column of the matrix of partial derivatives tell us? Column \(j\) has the elements \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). When the input point moves by a short step \(h\) along the axis \(j\), its image moves, by theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step applied to each component, by approximately \(h\) times column \(j\). A small square with sides \(h\) along the axes is therefore sent by the map to a figure that is almost the parallelogram spanned by \(h\) times the two columns, as with the deformation gradient the piece near \(P\) went almost into a parallelepiped (section 2.10.5). Let us look at this for the map of the plane

\[\Phi(s, t) = (s,\ t + s^2) .\]

Its input is a point of the plane with the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\), its output a point of the plane with the coordinates \(x = s\) and \(y = t + s^2\). It moves every vertical segment with constant \(s\) up by \(s^2\) and bends the horizontal segments into parabolas (figure 4.35). It sends the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) to the figure between the parabolas \(y = x^2\) and \(y = 1 + x^2\). The components are \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t) = s\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(s, t) = t + s^2\), so the matrix of partial derivatives and the Jacobian are

\[\mat F_\Phi(s, t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2s & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad J_\Phi(s, t) = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 2s = 1 .\]

At the point \(P\) with the coordinates \(s = 0{,}5\) and \(t = 0{,}25\) the columns of the matrix of partial derivatives are \((1, 1)\) and \((0, 1)\), and \(\Phi(P)\) has the coordinates \(x = 0{,}5\) and \(y = 0{,}5\). The square with side \(h = 0{,}25\) and corner \(P\) goes to a figure that the parallelogram spanned by \(h\) times the columns almost covers. The left side of the figure is the left side of the parallelogram itself. The bottom and top sides of the figure, however, curve upwards, so the right side of the figure lies somewhat higher than the right side of the parallelogram. The right end of the bottom side of the figure is the image of the point with \(s = 0{,}75\) and \(t = 0{,}25\), at the height \(y = 0{,}25 + 0{,}75^2 = 0{,}8125\), while the corresponding corner of the parallelogram is at the height \(0{,}5 + 0{,}25 \cdot 1 = 0{,}75\). The difference is the remainder of the theorem on the change of a field,

\[(0{,}5 + h)^2 - 0{,}5^2 - 2 \cdot 0{,}5 \cdot h = h^2 = 0{,}0625 ,\]

and for half the \(h\) it would be four times smaller, while the sides of the parallelogram would only be halved.

Now take a function that we evaluate at the image of a point. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with cross-section radius \(r = 5\) mm hangs under its own weight. It is held in an idealized way, so that only the centre \(O\) of its top face is fixed, the axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, and the displacement field is (1.18). How far from the axis of the bar is, after loading, the material that was at the point \(P\) before? The square of the distance of the point with the coordinates \((x, y, z)\) from the axis \(x\) is

\[f(x, y, z) = y^2 + z^2 .\]

The function \(f\) has a place in space as input and a number as output. The material from the point \(P\) is at the point \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\) after loading, so the square of its distance from the axis after loading is

\[g(P) = f\big(\Phi(P)\big) .\]

The function \(g\) has a point before loading as input and a number as output. We reach the number in two steps, first with the map \(\Phi\), then with the function \(f\) (figure 4.36). How does \(g\) change when we move the point \(P\) by a short step \(h\) along the axis \(x\), to the point \(Q = P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\)? The map sends the step to the step from \(\Phi(P)\) to \(\Phi(Q)\), which is approximately \(h\) times column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)\). By the theorem on the change of a field, the function \(f\) changes over this step by approximately the sum of the products of its partial derivatives at \(\Phi(P)\) with the components of the step. We therefore expect

\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}(P) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}(P) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P) .\]

Both changes are only approximate. We have to show that the two errors together stay small compared with the step \(h\).

Lemma 4.43 Chain rule (verižno pravilo)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space, an open set of points of the plane or an open interval, and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42) and has all its images in an open set \(E\) of points of space or of the plane. Let \(f\) be a function whose input is a point of \(E\) and whose output is a number, continuously differentiable on \(E\). Then the function \(g\) that assigns to a point \(P\) of \(D\) the number \(g(P) = f(\Phi(P))\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), and at every point \(P\) of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) , \tag{4.24}\]

where \(i\) runs over the coordinates of the points of \(E\) and \(j\) over the coordinates of the points of \(D\). When \(D\) is an interval, the left side is the derivative \(g'(P)\), and on the right the derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}'\) stands in place of \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Proof

We have to show that the difference quotient of the function \(g\) along the axis \(j\) converges to the right side of (4.24) and that the partial derivatives obtained in this way are continuous. We write the change of the function \(f\) with the theorem on the change of a field over a short step, and the step is given by the map \(\Phi\). We write the proof for \(D\) and \(E\) in space and say at the end what changes elsewhere.

1. The partial derivative.

  1. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\), \(Q = \Phi(P)\) its image and \(j\) one of the coordinates \(x\), \(y\), \(z\). The sets \(D\) and \(E\) are open, so there are numbers \(r_{\mathrm{D}} > 0\) and \(r_{\mathrm{E}} > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r_{\mathrm{D}}\) are in \(D\) and all points closer to \(Q\) than \(r_{\mathrm{E}}\) are in \(E\). At these points of \(E\) the partial derivatives of the function \(f\) exist, and they are continuous at \(Q\), so theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds for \(f\) at the point \(Q\).
  2. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r_{\mathrm{D}}\) the point \(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is at the distance \(|h|\) from \(P\), so it lies in \(D\). Write \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = \Phi(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\) and for every coordinate \(i\)
    \[d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) = \frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P)}{h} .\]
    This is the difference quotient of the component \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) along the axis \(j\), which by the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 converges to \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\) as \(h\) goes to \(0\). The components of the step from \(Q\) to \(Q_{\mathrm{h}}\) are \(h\,d_{\mathrm{x}}(h)\), \(h\,d_{\mathrm{y}}(h)\) and \(h\,d_{\mathrm{z}}(h)\).
  3. We bound the step from \(Q\) to \(Q_{\mathrm{h}}\) by \(|h|\). The definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(1\), applied to each of the three quotients \(d_{\mathrm{x}}(h)\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}(h)\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}(h)\), gives three bands. Let \(\delta_1\) be the smallest of these three bands and the number \(r_{\mathrm{D}}\). Then \(0 < \delta_1 \le r_{\mathrm{D}}\) and \(|d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) - \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)| < 1\) for all three \(i\) and for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\). For such \(h\), by the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), \(|d_{\mathrm{i}}(h)| < |\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)| + 1\). The distance of two points is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of the differences of their coordinates (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so
    \[|Q Q_{\mathrm{h}}| \le |h|\,\big(|d_{\mathrm{x}}(h)| + |d_{\mathrm{y}}(h)| + |d_{\mathrm{z}}(h)|\big) < C\,|h| , \qquad C = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Big( \Big|\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P)\Big| + 1 \Big) .\]
  4. Let \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\) and \(C\,|h| < r_{\mathrm{E}}\). By step 3, \(|QQ_{\mathrm{h}}| < r_{\mathrm{E}}\), and by (1.34) for the function \(f\) at the point \(Q\)
    \[g(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - g(P) = f(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - f(Q) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}(Q)\,h\,d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) + R(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) ,\]
    where \(R(Q_{\mathrm{h}})\) is the remainder. If \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = Q\), the left side and the sum are zero, so \(R(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) = 0\) too.
  5. We divide by \(h\) and obtain the difference quotient of the function \(g\) along the axis \(j\):
    \[\frac{g(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - g(P)}{h} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}(Q)\,d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) + \frac{R(Q_{\mathrm{h}})}{h} .\]
  6. We choose an error \(\eta > 0\). Write \(c_{\mathrm{i}} = \partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\) and \(M = |c_{\mathrm{x}}| + |c_{\mathrm{y}}| + |c_{\mathrm{z}}| + 1\). The definition of the limit with the error \(\eta/(2M)\), applied to each of the three quotients \(d_{\mathrm{x}}(h)\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}(h)\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}(h)\), gives three bands, and the smallest of them, \(\delta_2 > 0\), is such that \(|d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) - \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)| < \eta/(2M)\) for all three \(i\) and for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_2\). By the theorem on the change of a field with the error \(\eta/(2C)\) there is \(\delta_3 > 0\) such that \(|R(Q')| \le \tfrac{\eta}{2C}\,|QQ'|\) for every point \(Q'\) with \(0 < |QQ'| < \delta_3\).
  7. Let \(\delta\) be the smallest of the positive numbers \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\), \(r_{\mathrm{E}}/C\) and \(\delta_3/C\), and let \(0 < |h| < \delta\). By step 3, \(|QQ_{\mathrm{h}}| < C\,|h| < \delta_3\), so \(|R(Q_{\mathrm{h}})| \le \tfrac{\eta}{2C} \cdot C\,|h| = \tfrac{\eta}{2}\,|h|\), which holds also when \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = Q\). By step 5, by the triangle inequality for numbers and because the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values (lemma 1.6, items 1 and 2),
    \[\begin{aligned} \Big| \frac{g(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}) - g(P)}{h} - \sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{i}}\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) \Big| &\le \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |c_{\mathrm{i}}|\,\Big| d_{\mathrm{i}}(h) - \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) \Big| + \frac{|R(Q_{\mathrm{h}})|}{|h|} \\ &< M\,\frac{\eta}{2M} + \frac{\eta}{2} = \eta . \end{aligned}\]
  8. We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so by the definition of the limit the difference quotient converges to \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{i}}\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\). By the definition of the partial derivative this limit is \(\partial g/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), and (4.24) holds.

2. Continuity of the partial derivatives.

  1. The components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(D\), so by lemma 1.91 they are continuous at every point of \(D\).
  2. The partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on \(E\). By lemma 4.35 on the continuity of a composite function, with \(p = \Phi\), the function that assigns to a point \(P\) the number \(\partial f/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(\Phi(P))\) is continuous at every point of \(D\). The lemma speaks about a set \(M\) that is an interval or a set of points of the plane, but its proof with lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points works in the same way for a set of points of space.
  3. The partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous on \(D\). By corollary 1.69, item 1, the products in (4.24) and their sum are therefore continuous on \(D\). The function \(g\) thus has at every point of \(D\) all partial derivatives, which are continuous on \(D\), and it is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90).

3. The plane and the interval.

  1. If \(D\) or \(E\) lies in the plane, the steps are the same, only \(j\) or \(i\) runs over two coordinates. The theorem on the change of a field holds also for functions of two variables, with the same proof (section 1.15.3), and in step 3 the distance is at most the sum of two absolute values of differences of coordinates.
  2. If \(D\) is an interval, we take the number \(P + h\) in place of the point \(P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the difference quotients of step 2 converge to the derivatives \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}'(P)\) (definition 1.9). In the second part we use lemma 1.79, that a differentiable function is continuous, in place of lemma 1.91, and lemma 1.61 on continuity through sequences and corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions in place of lemma 1.68 and corollary 1.69.

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 8.3.7 (PDF p. 38) for differentiable maps, where the derivative of a composite map is the product of the derivatives, LEBL1 Prop. 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159) for functions of one variable. The proof with the theorem on the change of a field over a short step is not from the sources.

The proof split the change of the function \(g\) into two steps, as the figure does. The map \(\Phi\) sent a short step \(h\) along the axis \(j\) to a step with the components \(h\,d_{\mathrm{i}}(h)\), which is almost \(h\) times column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)\) and not longer than \(C\,|h|\). The theorem on the change of a field then wrote the change of the function \(f\) over this step with its partial derivatives at \(\Phi(P)\), up to a remainder that is small compared with the step in \(E\) and therefore also compared with \(h\). It was the bound \(C\,|h|\) of step 3 that carried the smallness of the remainder from the step in \(E\) to the step in \(D\). The chain rule contains lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment. The map \(t \mapsto P + t\,\vek d\) has the number \(t\) as input and the components \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,d_{\mathrm{z}}\), whose derivatives are \(d_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(d_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{z}}\), so (4.24) gives (1.71). In the chain rule the derivatives are linked like the links of a chain, from \(f\) through \(\Phi\) to the variable.

Let us test the rule on the hanging bar. The components of the map \(\Phi\) that we need are

\[\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = y - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y = \big(1 - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big)\,y , \qquad \Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = \big(1 - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big)\,z ,\]

and the function \(f(x, y, z) = y^2 + z^2\) has the partial derivatives \(0\), \(2y\) and \(2z\). Take the point \(P\) at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm from the axis in the plane \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\), as in section 1.7.2. Its image has the coordinates \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(P) = (1 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}) \cdot 0{,}004\ \text{m} = 0{,}0039999977\) m and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(P) = 0\). The partial derivative \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\) equals \(4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10}\) at \(P\), the element \(H_{\mathrm{yx}}\) of the displacement gradient of section 1.7.2. By (4.24)

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}(P) &= 0 \cdot \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) + 2 \cdot 0{,}0039999977\ \text{m} \cdot 4{,}6848 \cdot 10^{-10} + 2 \cdot 0 \cdot \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}(P) \\ &= 3{,}748 \cdot 10^{-12}\ \text{m} . \end{aligned}\]

Let us check without the rule. Since \(g(x, y, z) = \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = \big(1 - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big)^2\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the rule for the derivative of a product (lemma 1.81, item 3), applied to the square of the bracket, whose derivative with respect to \(x\) is \(0{,}6\,a\), gives

\[\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} = 2\,\big(1 - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\big) \cdot 0{,}6\,a \cdot (y^2 + z^2) ,\]

and at \(P\) this is \(2 \cdot (1 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}) \cdot 1{,}1712 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot 1{,}6 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^2 = 3{,}748 \cdot 10^{-12}\) m, the same. We checked both computations with SymPy. What does the number say? For points that were 4 mm from the axis, the square of the distance from the axis after loading grows with every metre of depth by about \(3{,}748 \cdot 10^{-12}\ \text{m}^2 = 3{,}748 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm}^2\). The bar thins by the fraction \(0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), which decreases with depth, because a cross section lower down carries less weight. Material lower down therefore comes less close to the axis (figure 4.36). Of the three terms of the chain rule only the middle one remained, because \(f\) does not depend on \(x\) and because \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(P) = 0\).

What if a second map follows the first? In section 1.16.3 we showed that two linear rules one after the other are a single rule, multiplication by the product of the matrices (figure 1.127). For maps that are not linear the same holds for the matrices of partial derivatives.

Corollary 4.44 Matrix of a composite map (matrika odvodov sestavljene preslikave)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space, an open set of points of the plane or an open interval, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) and has all its images in an open set \(E\) of points of space or of the plane, and \(\Psi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(E\) (definition 4.42). The composite map (sestavljena preslikava) \(\Psi\circ\Phi\), which assigns to a point \(P\) of \(D\) the point \(\Psi(\Phi(P))\), is continuously differentiable on \(D\), and at every point \(P\) of \(D\)

\[\mat F_{\Psi\circ\Phi}(P) = \mat F_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\mat F_\Phi(P) . \tag{4.25}\]

When all three matrices are square and of the same size, \(3 \times 3\) or \(2 \times 2\),

\[J_{\Psi\circ\Phi}(P) = J_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,J_\Phi(P) .\]
Proof

We have to show that the components of the composite map are continuously differentiable, that the elements of its matrix of partial derivatives are the elements of the matrix product, and that the determinants multiply.

  1. Component \(k\) of the map \(\Psi\circ\Phi\) is the function that assigns to a point \(P\) the number \(\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(\Phi(P))\). The function \(\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\), so by the chain rule (lemma 4.43) this component is continuously differentiable on \(D\) and
    \[\frac{\partial (\Psi\circ\Phi)_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \frac{\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) .\]
  2. On the left, by (4.23), is the element in row \(k\) and column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat F_{\Psi\circ\Phi}(P)\). On the right is row \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Psi(\Phi(P))\) times column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)\), which by definition 1.98 is the element in row \(k\) and column \(j\) of their product. This is (4.25).
  3. For \(3 \times 3\) matrices, by theorem 2.52 on the determinant of a product, the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants. For \(2 \times 2\) matrices this holds by the argument after that theorem, where we place the \(2 \times 2\) matrices in \(3 \times 3\) matrices.

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 8.3.7 (PDF p. 38) for the derivative of a composite map, PDF p. 42 for the Jacobian of a composite map. The proof component by component with the chain rule is not from the sources.

We read the notation \(\Psi\circ\Phi\) from right to left, like a matrix product: first \(\Phi\) acts, then \(\Psi\). This is also why in (4.25) the matrix of the map \(\Phi\) stands on the right, and why we take the matrix of the map \(\Psi\) at the image \(\Phi(P)\), where \(\Psi\) acts. Let us test this on the map of the plane \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\), followed by the turn of the plane with which we turned the plate in section 1.17.6, with the numbers \(0{,}6\) and \(0{,}8\) (figure 4.37):

\[\Psi(x, y) = (0{,}6\,x - 0{,}8\,y,\ 0{,}8\,x + 0{,}6\,y) , \qquad \mat F_\Psi = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By (4.25)

\[\mat F_{\Psi\circ\Phi}(s, t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2s & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 - 1{,}6\,s & -0{,}8 \\ 0{,}8 + 1{,}2\,s & 0{,}6 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Directly, \(\Psi(\Phi(s, t)) = \big(0{,}6\,s - 0{,}8\,(t + s^2),\ 0{,}8\,s + 0{,}6\,(t + s^2)\big)\), and the partial derivatives of the first component with respect to \(s\) and \(t\) are \(0{,}6 - 1{,}6\,s\) and \(-0{,}8\), those of the second \(0{,}8 + 1{,}2\,s\) and \(0{,}6\), the same matrix. The Jacobian is \((0{,}6 - 1{,}6\,s) \cdot 0{,}6 + 0{,}8 \cdot (0{,}8 + 1{,}2\,s) = 1\), which is \(J_\Psi \cdot J_\Phi = (0{,}36 + 0{,}64) \cdot 1\). For a deformation followed by a turn of the whole body the corollary says that the deformation gradient is multiplied from the left by the matrix of partial derivatives of the turn, while the Jacobian does not change, because this matrix has determinant \(1\).

4.3.2 The inverse map

We will turn an integral over an image into an integral over the original set. For this every point of the image must come from a single point of the original set, and the rule that assigns this point to it must again be continuously differentiable, so that we can use it in the reverse direction. For a deformation this is a question we often ask ourselves: where was the material that is now at a given point before loading? For the sheared cube with edge 10 mm, whose top face we shift by 10 µm in the direction of the axis \(x\), the map is \(\Phi(x, y, z) = (x + 0{,}001\,z,\ y,\ z)\). A point at the height \(z\) moves by \(0{,}001\,z\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), so it is brought back by the rule

\[\Psi(x, y, z) = (x - 0{,}001\,z,\ y,\ z) ,\]

which moves a point at the height \(z\) back by \(0{,}001\,z\). Indeed \(\Psi(\Phi(x, y, z)) = (x + 0{,}001\,z - 0{,}001\,z,\ y,\ z) = (x, y, z)\), and likewise \(\Phi(\Psi(x, y, z)) = (x, y, z)\). The corner \(C\) at the top of the front face has the coordinates \((10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) in micrometres, \(\Phi\) sends it to \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\), and \(\Psi\) brings it back (figure 4.38).

From history

The question whether equations linking two sets of variables allow us to express one set by the other is a question of the existence of a solution. The study of existence theorems began with Cauchy. For functions given implicitly, by an equation, he assumed that they can be written as infinite sums of powers (CAJORI, PDF p. 447). For systems of functions Jacobi showed that the functional determinant is zero when there is a relation between the functions (MUIR, PDF p. 389). Why? Take the functions \(u = x + y\) and \(v = 2x + 2y\), between which there is the relation \(v = 2u\). Their functional determinant is \(1 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 2 = 0\). The point \((u, v)\) always lies on the line \(v = 2u\), so a small square in the plane \((x, y)\) is mapped onto a segment of zero area, and the determinant is the ratio of the areas of the image and of the square (chapter 2). He also wrote a theorem similar to the relation \(\mathrm{d}x/\mathrm{d}y \cdot \mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}x = 1\) for a function of one variable (MUIR, PDF p. 396). The restriction to infinite sums of powers was removed by Ulisse Dini of Pisa, and simplifications were contributed by Rudolf Lipschitz of Bonn (CAJORI, PDF p. 447). The condition of a nonzero determinant that we will demand belongs to the same story.

Back to the question of when the rule \(\Phi\) can be reversed, as we did for the shifted cube with \(\Psi\). A rule that does the opposite of \(\Phi\) exists only if two different points do not have the same image. Otherwise the rule would not know to which of them to return the image.

Definition 4.45 One-to-one map and inverse map (injektivna preslikava in inverzna preslikava)

Let \(\Phi\) be a map on a set \(D\) (definition 4.42). The map \(\Phi\) is one-to-one (injektivna) on \(D\) if any two different points of \(D\) have different images: \(P \neq Q\) implies \(\Phi(P) \neq \Phi(Q)\). Let \(\Phi\) be one-to-one on \(D\). The inverse map (inverzna preslikava) of the map \(\Phi\) is the map \(\Psi\) on the image \(\Phi(D)\) that assigns to every point \(Q\) of \(\Phi(D)\) the point \(P\) of \(D\) for which \(\Phi(P) = Q\).

Source: LEBL1 Def. 0.3.17 (PDF p. 15) for a one-to-one function and PDF p. 16 for the inverse function, which the source defines for functions for which every element of the second set is the image of exactly one element of the first.

Why is the point \(P\) of the definition a single one? Since \(Q\) lies in the image \(\Phi(D)\), it is the image of at least one point of \(D\). If it were the image of two different points, these two points would have the same image, which the one-to-one property does not allow. The notation \(\Psi(Q)\) therefore means a single point, as the definition of a function 1.4 requires. By the definition

\[\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big) = P \quad \text{for every } P \in D , \qquad \Phi\big(\Psi(Q)\big) = Q \quad \text{for every } Q \in \Phi(D) .\]

The map \(\Psi\) undoes what \(\Phi\) does, and \(\Phi\) undoes what \(\Psi\) does. For a deformation the one-to-one property means that two different parts of the material are not at the same place after loading: the material does not penetrate itself. CM writes the inverse map, which takes a point after loading back to the point before it, and says that it cannot always be constructed from a known deformation (CM §3.2.1, PDF p. 112). From the fact that no short fibre shrinks to nothing it concludes only that \(J \neq 0\) and that the deformation gradient has an inverse matrix (CM, PDF pp. 119-120). That the deformation is one-to-one over the whole body, EP takes as an assumption: a continuous medium has no gaps and no overlaps, so the points of the body before loading and the points after it correspond one to one, and the inverse map exists, although in general it is not easy to construct (EP §2.3.1, p. 57). The overlap that the assumption excludes is exactly two points having the same image. Without this requirement the material would not have a uniquely determined place before loading. BATHE imposes the same requirement on the map that describes the shape of a finite element, which must not fold back upon itself (BATHE §5.3, PDF p. 363).

Is the inverse map continuously differentiable, and what is its matrix of partial derivatives? For the sheared cube

\[\mat F_\Psi = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By theorem 2.54 the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) with the columns \(\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek b = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek c = (0{,}001, 0, 1)\) and with determinant \(1\) has the inverse matrix with the rows \(\vek b\times\vek c = (1, 0, -0{,}001)\), \(\vek c\times\vek a = (0, 1, 0)\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b = (0, 0, 1)\). This is exactly \(\mat F_\Psi\). It is no accident. If \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable, then by corollary 4.44 on the matrix of a composite map \(\mat F_\Psi(\Phi(P))\,\mat F_\Phi(P)\) is the matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\Psi\circ\Phi\), which leaves every point in place and therefore has the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat I\). The matrix of partial derivatives of the inverse map must therefore be the inverse of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), and both Jacobians must be different from zero, because their product is \(\det\mat I = 1\).

For the sheared cube we wrote \(\Psi\) with a formula. For the hanging bar, however, we would have to solve three equations for a point after loading, one of them quadratic in \(x\), with terms that couple all three unknown coordinates. We need a theorem that tells from the properties of the map \(\Phi\) that \(\Psi\) exists and is continuously differentiable, without computing it. Let us prepare the tools. First a bound for the length of a matrix times a vector, with which we will bound how far a map moves two points apart.

Lemma 4.46 Bound for a matrix times a vector (ocena produkta matrike in vektorja)

Let \(g \ge 0\) be a number.

  1. If every element of a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) is at most \(g\) in absolute value, then \(|\mat A\vek v| \le 3g\,|\vek v|\) for every vector \(\vek v\).
  2. If every element of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\mat A\) is at most \(g\) in absolute value, then \(|\mat A\vek v| \le 2g\,|\vek v|\) for every vector \(\vek v\) with two components.
  3. If the matrix \(\mat A\) has one, two or three rows and one, two or three columns and every element of it is at most \(g\) in absolute value, then \(|\mat A\vek v| \le 3g\,|\vek v|\) for every column \(\vek v\) with as many components as \(\mat A\) has columns.
Proof

We have to show that every component of the product is small compared with \(|\vek v|\), and to assemble the components into a length. We bound every component with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

1. A \(3 \times 3\) matrix.

  1. Let \(\vek p_{\mathrm{i}} = (A_{\mathrm{ix}}, A_{\mathrm{iy}}, A_{\mathrm{iz}})\) be row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat A\), written as a vector. By (1.38) and (2.6) component \(i\) of the product is \((\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek p_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\vek v\).
  2. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (corollary 2.15) \(|(\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}}| \le |\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}|\,|\vek v|\).
  3. Every element of the row is at most \(g\) in absolute value, so by lemma 1.28 its square is at most \(g^2\), and \(|\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}|^2 = A_{\mathrm{ix}}^2 + A_{\mathrm{iy}}^2 + A_{\mathrm{iz}}^2 \le 3g^2\).
  4. By step 2 and lemma 1.28 \((\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}}^2 \le |\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}|^2\,|\vek v|^2\), and by step 3 this is at most \(3g^2\,|\vek v|^2\).
  5. We sum over \(i\): \(|\mat A\vek v|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}}^2 \le 9g^2\,|\vek v|^2\). The numbers \(|\mat A\vek v|\) and \(3g\,|\vek v|\) are nonnegative, so by lemma 1.28 \(|\mat A\vek v| \le 3g\,|\vek v|\).

2. A \(2 \times 2\) matrix.

  1. We write the rows and the vector with two components as vectors with third component \(0\), which does not change the scalar products and the lengths. The steps are the same, except that in step 3 \(|\vek p_{\mathrm{i}}|^2 \le 2g^2\), and in step 5 there are only two components and \(|\mat A\vek v|^2 \le 2 \cdot 2g^2\,|\vek v|^2 = 4g^2\,|\vek v|^2\).

3. Fewer rows or columns.

  1. We fill the matrix \(\mat A\) with zeros to a matrix of size \(3 \times 3\), and the column \(\vek v\) with zeros to three components. All elements of the filled matrix are at most \(g\) in absolute value. The product of the filled matrix with the filled column has the components of the vector \(\mat A\vek v\), filled with zeros, so the lengths of the product and of the column do not change. By item 1 the bound \(3g\) holds.

Source: LEBL2 PDF p. 26 bounds the norm of a matrix by the square root of the sum of the squares of its elements, also with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The bound with the largest element is not from the sources.

The bound is crude. The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), which we will meet soon, has the largest element \(g = 2\) in absolute value, so by item 2 it does not lengthen a vector more than \(4\) times. It sends the vector \((1, 0)\) to \((1, -2)\) with length \(\sqrt 5 = 2{,}236\), and NumPy tells us that it lengthens no vector more than \(2{,}414\) times. For our proofs it matters only that the bound exists and that we compute it from the elements.

With the lemma we bound how far apart a map sends two points. When the partial derivatives of the components are bounded, the images cannot move apart more than the bound times the distance.

Lemma 4.47 Bounded derivatives and distances (omejeni odvodi in razdalje)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42) and has points of space as images. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points for which the segment \(PQ\), the set of the points \(P + t\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\), lies in \(D\), and let \(M\) be a number for which \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le M\) at every point of the segment for all \(i\) and \(j\). Then

\[|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ| . \tag{4.26}\]

In particular this holds for any two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of a set \(C \subseteq D\) that contains, with any two of its points, also the segment between them, when \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le M\) at every point of \(C\). When \(D\) and the images are in the plane, the bound \(2M\) holds in place of \(3M\). When only \(D\) or only the images are in the plane, the bound \(3M\) holds. The same holds for a vector field \(\vek v\) that is continuously differentiable on \(D\), for example a displacement field: if \(|\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le M\) at every point of the segment for all \(i\) and \(j\), then \(|\vek v(Q) - \vek v(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\).

Proof

We have to show that every component of the image changes by at most the sum of the partial derivatives times the components of the step, and to assemble the components into a length. On every component we use the mean value theorem along the segment.

  1. Let \(\vek d = \overrightarrow{PQ}\), and for every component \(i\) let \(g_{\mathrm{i}}(t) = \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P + t\,\vek d)\) for every \(t\) for which \(P + t\,\vek d\) is in \(D\), among them every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\).
  2. By lemma 1.132 on the derivative along a segment, item 1, \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) is differentiable at every \(t\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\), with the derivative \(g_{\mathrm{i}}'(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P + t\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 1.79 \(g_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous at every such \(t\), so it is continuous on \([0, 1]\).
  3. By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a number \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) between \(0\) and \(1\) such that
    \[\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = g_{\mathrm{i}}(1) - g_{\mathrm{i}}(0) = g_{\mathrm{i}}'(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}) \cdot 1 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d)\,d_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
  4. Let \(\mat A\) be the matrix whose row \(i\) consists of the partial derivatives of the component \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the point \(P + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d\), that is \(A_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P + \xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek d)\). Every row is taken at its own point of the segment, so by assumption \(|A_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le M\). By step 3 and (1.38) the vector \(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)\) equals \(\mat A\vek d\).
  5. By lemma 4.46 on the bound for a matrix times a vector, item 1, \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| = |\mat A\vek d| \le 3M\,|\vek d| = 3M\,|PQ|\).
  6. If \(P\) and \(Q\) are points of the set \(C\), the segment \(PQ\) lies in \(C\) and so in \(D\), and on it \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le M\). By steps 1 to 5 (4.26) holds.
  7. In the plane the steps are the same, with two components in place of three. Lemma 1.132 holds for functions of two variables with the same proof, because the theorem on the change of a field also holds for functions of two variables (section 1.15.3). In step 5 we use item 2 of lemma 4.46 in place of item 1 when \(D\) and the images are in the plane, and item 3 when only one of them is in the plane.
  8. For a vector field \(\vek v\) steps 1 to 7 are the same, with the components \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) in place of \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\). Only the components and their partial derivatives appear in them, and the difference \(\vek v(Q) - \vek v(P)\) is the vector with the components \(v_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - v_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), just as \(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)\) is the vector with the components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 8.4.2 (PDF p. 46) for differentiable maps on a convex open set, with a bound for the norm of the derivative and with Lemma 8.4.1 on the mean value. The proof with the mean value theorem component by component and with the bound from the elements of the matrix is not from the sources.

For a function of one variable on an interval the mean value theorem alone gives the same: where the derivative is at most \(M\) in absolute value, the values differ by at most \(M\) times the distance. In space we get the factor \(3\), because in each of the three components three contributions add up, and the components are then assembled into a length.

The lemma also tells when a map does not send two different points to the same point. Take again the hanging bar of length \(L = 10\) m with cross-section radius \(r = 5\) mm, which hangs under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) down from the centre of the top face. Let \(D\) be the set of the points with \(0 < x < L\) and \(y^2 + z^2 < r^2\), the bar without its surface. Let us show in five steps that \(\Phi\) hardly shrinks distances on \(D\).

  1. The set \(D\) is open. For a point \(P\) of it let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the numbers \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(r - \sqrt{y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\). A point \(T\) with \(|PT| < \rho\) has \(|x_{\mathrm{T}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}| < \rho\), so \(0 < x_{\mathrm{T}} < L\). By the triangle inequality for vectors (corollary 2.16), applied to \((0, y_{\mathrm{T}}, z_{\mathrm{T}}) = (0, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}}) + (0, y_{\mathrm{T}} - y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{T}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\), \(\sqrt{y_{\mathrm{T}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{T}}^2} < \sqrt{y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2} + \rho \le r\).
  2. The set \(D\) contains, with any two of its points \(P\) and \(Q\), also the segment between them. The point \(T = P + t\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) with \(0 \le t \le 1\) has the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{T}} = (1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\). The coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{T}}\) lies between \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\). By the same inequality, applied to \((0, y_{\mathrm{T}}, z_{\mathrm{T}}) = (1 - t)\,(0, y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}}) + t\,(0, y_{\mathrm{Q}}, z_{\mathrm{Q}})\), \(\sqrt{y_{\mathrm{T}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{T}}^2} \le (1 - t)\sqrt{y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2} + t\sqrt{y_{\mathrm{Q}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{Q}}^2} < r\).
  3. The displacement field (1.18) is a vector field. The partial derivatives of its components are in the table of section 1.7.2: \(2a\,(L - x)\), \(\pm 0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\pm 0{,}6\,a\,z\), \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and zero. These are polynomials, continuous by corollary 1.69, so the field is continuously differentiable on \(D\). On \(D\) each is at most \(M = 2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) in absolute value, because \(0 < L - x < L\) and \(0{,}6\,a\,|y| < 0{,}6\,a\,r = 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-10}\), and likewise for \(z\).
  4. By step 2 and lemma 4.47, applied to the displacement field, therefore \(|\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\) for any two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of \(D\).
  5. The map \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\) has \(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P) = \overrightarrow{PQ} + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big)\). By the triangle inequality for vectors \(|PQ| \le |\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| + |\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)|\), so by step 4
    \[|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \ge (1 - 3M)\,|PQ| = (1 - 1{,}1712 \cdot 10^{-5})\,|PQ| .\]

Two different points of the bar therefore have different images, and \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on \(D\). No distance between two points shrinks by more than the fraction \(1{,}1712 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The largest shortening in the bar is across the bar at the top, the fraction \(0{,}6\,aL = 1{,}1712 \cdot 10^{-6}\), ten times less. The bound is crude, but it suffices.

After loading the body is the image of the body before loading. Is it again a closed and bounded set, so that the extreme value theorem and uniform continuity hold on it? It is, if the map is continuous.

Lemma 4.48 Image of a closed bounded set (slika zaprte omejene množice)

Let \(W\) be a closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.74) and \(\Phi\) a map on \(W\) (definition 4.42) whose components are continuous on \(W\) (definition 1.67). Then the image \(\Phi(W)\) is a closed and bounded set of points. The same holds when \(W\) is a set of points of the plane or a closed interval and when the images are points of the plane. Here we view a point of the plane with the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\) as the point \((s, t, 0)\) of space, and a number \(t\) as the point \((t, 0, 0)\).

Proof

We have to show that all images are at most some number away from the origin and that the limit of a convergent sequence of images lies again in the image. For the first we use the extreme value theorem, for the second the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem and the closedness of the set \(W\), as in the proof of theorem 4.6.

Boundedness.

  1. If \(W\) is empty, \(\Phi(W)\) is empty too, and the conditions of definition 1.74 require nothing. Let \(W\) be nonempty.
  2. The component \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous on the nonempty closed and bounded set \(W\), so by theorem 1.78, the extreme value theorem in space, it attains a largest value \(m_1\) and a smallest value \(m_2\). Let \(M_{\mathrm{x}}\) be the larger of the numbers \(|m_1|\) and \(|m_2|\). Then \(|\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(P)| \le M_{\mathrm{x}}\) for every \(P \in W\). In the same way we get \(M_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. By lemma 1.28 \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(P)^2 \le M_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\), so the distance of an image from the origin \(O\) is at most \(R = \sqrt{M_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + M_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + M_{\mathrm{z}}^2}\), by the same lemma. The set \(\Phi(W)\) is bounded.

Closedness.

  1. Let a sequence of points \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(\Phi(W)\) converge to a point \(Q\). For every \(n\) we choose a point \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in W\) with \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}}) = Q_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. The set \(W\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.77, the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in space, the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(P\). The set \(W\) is closed, so \(P\) lies in \(W\).
  3. The components are continuous at \(P\), so by lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\) for every \(i\). By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} = \Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) therefore converges to \(\Phi(P)\).
  4. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) is a subsequence of the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\). By lemma 1.66 the coordinates of the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the coordinates of the point \(Q\), by lemma 1.54 on the limit of a subsequence so do the coordinates of the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\), and by the same lemma on convergence coordinate by coordinate \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) converges to \(Q\).
  5. By steps 3 and 4 the coordinates of the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) converge to the coordinates of the points \(\Phi(P)\) and \(Q\). By lemma 1.41 on the uniqueness of the limit of a sequence the coordinates are equal, so \(Q = \Phi(P)\), and \(Q\) lies in \(\Phi(W)\). The set \(\Phi(W)\) is closed.

The plane and the interval.

  1. In the plane and on an interval the steps are the same, because we view points of the plane and numbers as points of space with one or two coordinates equal to zero.

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 7.5.5 (PDF p. 289): the continuous image of a compact set is compact, proved with subsequences as here, with Theorem 7.4.11 (PDF p. 282), that a set is compact exactly when every sequence in it has a subsequence with a limit in it, and with the Heine-Borel theorem 7.4.14 (PDF p. 284), that closed and bounded sets are compact. The proof without the notion of compactness and the bound from the extreme value theorem are not from the sources.

The hanging bar before loading is closed and bounded (section 1.13.4), and the components of its deformation are polynomials and hence continuous (corollary 1.69). By the lemma the bar after loading is therefore closed and bounded too.

Now let us turn to the inverse map. For a map that is not linear there is no single matrix to invert. Near a point \(P_0\), however, we can compare it with its linear part, the rule that sends the point \(P\) to \(\Phi(P_0) + \mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\), where \(\mat F_0 = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\). When \(\mat F_0\) has an inverse matrix, the linear part cannot shrink distances too much. When the partial derivatives near \(P_0\) are close to those at \(P_0\), the map differs little from its linear part, and it does not shrink distances too much either. For \(2 \times 2\) matrices we still need a formula for the inverse matrix, which theorem 2.54 gives only for \(3 \times 3\) matrices.

Lemma 4.49 Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix (inverzna matrika 2 × 2)

A \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\mat A\) with \(\det\mat A = A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} \neq 0\) has the inverse matrix

\[\mat A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det\mat A} \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{yy}} & -A_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ -A_{\mathrm{yx}} & A_{\mathrm{xx}} \end{bmatrix} . \tag{4.27}\]
Proof

We have to show that the product in both orders is the identity matrix (definition 1.107). Let \(\mat B\) be the matrix in brackets.

  1. By definition 1.98
    \[\mat B\mat A = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xx}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} & A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} \\ -A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xx}} + A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} & -A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} + A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} \end{bmatrix} = \det\mat A\;\mat I .\]
  2. Likewise
    \[\mat A\mat B = \begin{bmatrix} A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} & -A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{xx}} \\ A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} & -A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} + A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xx}} \end{bmatrix} = \det\mat A\;\mat I .\]
  3. We divide both equalities by \(\det\mat A \neq 0\). The matrix \(\mat B/\det\mat A\) satisfies (1.43).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.8, (4*) (PDF p. 330). The proof by multiplication is not from the sources.

For the matrix \(\mat F_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) of the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\) at the point \(P_0\) with the coordinates \(s = 1\) and \(t = 0\) we have \(\det\mat F_0 = 1\) and \(\mat F_0^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the matrix we mentioned after lemma 4.46.

Lemma 4.50 Lower bound for stretching (spodnja meja raztezanja)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42) and has points of space as images, and \(P_0\) a point of \(D\) at which the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat F_0 = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\) has determinant \(\det\mat F_0 \neq 0\) and therefore, by theorem 2.54, an inverse matrix. Let \(m > 0\) be a number for which \(|\mat F_0^{-1}\vek w| \le m\,|\vek w|\) for every vector \(\vek w\). Then there is a number \(r > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r\), the set of the points closer to \(P_0\) than \(r\), lies in \(D\), and

\[|\Phi(P) - \Phi(Q)| \ge \frac{|PQ|}{2m} \tag{4.28}\]

for any two points \(P\) and \(Q\) of this ball. The same holds in the plane, for a map that assigns points of the plane to the points of an open set of the plane, with a disc in place of the ball and with lemma 4.49 in place of theorem 2.54.

Proof

We have to show that near \(P_0\) the map differs little from its linear part and that the linear part shrinks distances by at most the factor \(m\). We bound the deviation with the lemma on bounded derivatives, and the linear part with the matrix \(\mat F_0^{-1}\).

  1. The set \(D\) is open, so there is \(r_1 > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P_0\) than \(r_1\) are in \(D\). Every partial derivative \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuous at \(P_0\), so by definition 1.67 with the error \(1/(6m)\) there is a band \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} > 0\). We choose the error \(1/(6m)\) so that in step 4 the factor \(3\) of lemma 4.47 gives \(3 \cdot \tfrac{1}{6m} = \tfrac{1}{2m}\), half the factor \(\tfrac1m\) of step 6. Let \(r\) be the smallest of the number \(r_1\) and the nine bands \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\). For every point \(T\) with \(|P_0 T| < r\), \(T\) is then in \(D\) and
    \[\Big| \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(T) - (\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}} \Big| < \frac{1}{6m} \quad \text{for all } i \text{ and } j .\]
  2. Let \(G\) be the map on \(D\) with the components \(G_{\mathrm{i}}(T) = \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(T) - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\big(x_{\mathrm{j}}(T) - x_{\mathrm{j}}(P_0)\big)\), where \(x_{\mathrm{j}}(T)\) is coordinate \(j\) of the point \(T\). For every \(i\) the subtracted term is the sum of a constant number and multiples of the coordinates, so by lemma 1.81, items 1, 2 and 4, applied to the function of the variable \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the other coordinates fixed, its partial derivative with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By items 1 and 2 of the same lemma
    \[\frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(T) = \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(T) - (\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}} .\]
    These partial derivatives are differences of continuous functions and constant numbers, so by corollary 1.69, item 1, they are continuous on \(D\), and \(G\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\).
  3. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of the ball with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r\). The segment \(PQ\) lies in the ball. For \(0 \le t \le 1\) the point \(T = P + t\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) is such that \(\overrightarrow{P_0 T} = (1 - t)\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P} + t\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q}\), and by the triangle inequality for vectors (corollary 2.16) \(|P_0 T| \le (1 - t)\,|P_0 P| + t\,|P_0 Q| < r\).
  4. By steps 1 to 3, on the segment \(PQ\) every partial derivative of the components of the map \(G\) is less than \(1/(6m)\) in absolute value. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances
    \[|G(Q) - G(P)| \le 3 \cdot \frac{1}{6m}\,|PQ| = \frac{|PQ|}{2m} .\]
  5. By the definition of the map \(G\) the vector \(G(Q) - G(P)\) equals \(\big(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)\big) - \mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\), because the constant terms cancel.
  6. The linear part does not shrink distances by more than the factor \(m\). By lemma 1.99, item 1, and lemma 1.106 \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \mat F_0^{-1}\big(\mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\big)\), so by assumption \(|PQ| \le m\,|\mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ}|\), that is \(|\mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ}| \ge |PQ|/m\).
  7. By step 5 \(\mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \big(\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)\big) - \big(G(Q) - G(P)\big)\), and by the triangle inequality for vectors \(|\mat F_0\,\overrightarrow{PQ}| \le |\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| + |G(Q) - G(P)|\). By steps 4 and 6 therefore
    \[|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \ge \frac{|PQ|}{m} - \frac{|PQ|}{2m} = \frac{|PQ|}{2m} .\]
  8. In the plane the steps are the same, with four bands in step 1. Lemma 4.47 gives in step 4 the bound \(2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{6m}\,|PQ| = \tfrac{|PQ|}{3m}\), which is smaller than \(\tfrac{|PQ|}{2m}\), so step 7 gives the same inequality.

Source: LEBL2, in the proof of Thm. 8.5.1 (PDF pp. 51-53), requires on a ball around the point that the derivative differs from the derivative at the centre by less than \(1/(2\|A^{-1}\|)\), and from this obtains \(|h| \le 2\|A^{-1}\|\,|k|\), where \(h\) and \(k\) are steps in the original set and in the image. Our bound with the elements of the matrix and the proof with lemma 4.47 are not from the sources.

The lemma says two things. The first is the lower bound: near \(P_0\) the map shrinks no distance by more than the factor \(2m\). The second follows from the first: two different points of the ball have different images, because the distance of the images is at least \(|PQ|/(2m) > 0\). A map with \(\det\mat F_0 \neq 0\) is therefore always one-to-one near \(P_0\). Let us test it on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\) at the point \(P_0\) with the coordinates \(s = 1\) and \(t = 0\) (figure 4.39). The matrix \(\mat F_0^{-1}\) has the largest element \(2\), so by lemma 4.46 on the bound for a matrix times a vector, item 2, \(m = 4\) will do, and the lemma gives the bound \(|PQ|/8\). The radius from step 1 of the proof: of the elements of the matrix of partial derivatives only \(2s\) varies, and the condition \(|2s - 2| < 1/24\) holds for \(|s - 1| < 1/48\), so \(r = 1/48\) will do. NumPy shows that in this disc the smallest ratio \(|\Phi(P) - \Phi(Q)|/|PQ|\) is about \(0{,}408\), which is more than the bound \(0{,}125\). Distances in the direction that the linear part shrinks most shrink to about \(0{,}41\) times their length.

Now the idea of the theorem. Let \(Q_0 = \Phi(P_0)\) and let \(Q\) be a point near \(Q_0\). We look for a point \(P\) near \(P_0\) with \(\Phi(P) = Q\). Instead of solving the equation, we look for the point whose image is closest to \(Q\). The function

\[f(P) = |\Phi(P) - Q|^2\]

is continuous, so on a closed ball around \(P_0\) it attains a smallest value (theorem 1.78). The lower bound for stretching keeps the images of the points on the surface of the ball far from \(Q_0\) and therefore far from \(Q\), farther than \(Q_0\) itself. The smallest value is therefore not on the surface but inside the ball, and there the partial derivatives of the function \(f\) are zero, as the derivative is zero at an interior extremum (lemma 1.82). By the chain rule this means \(\mat F_\Phi^\T\,(\Phi(P) - Q) = \vek 0\), and since the determinant is not zero, \(\Phi(P) = Q\). Figure 4.40 shows the idea for the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\).

Theorem 4.51 Inverse function theorem (izrek o inverzni preslikavi)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42), has points of space as images, is one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45) and has at every point \(P\) of \(D\) the Jacobian \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\). Let \(\Psi\) be its inverse map on \(E = \Phi(D)\). Then:

  1. Openness. For every open set \(U \subseteq D\) the image \(\Phi(U)\) is an open set. In particular \(E\) is open.
  2. Differentiability. The map \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\).
  3. Matrix of partial derivatives. For every point \(P\) of \(D\)
    \[\mat F_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big) = \mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1} , \qquad J_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big) = \frac{1}{J_\Phi(P)} . \tag{4.29}\]

The same holds in the plane, for a map that assigns points of the plane to the points of an open set of the plane.

Proof

We have to show all three items. For the first we find the point whose image is closest to the given point and show that the image is exactly this point. For the second and the third we write the change of the map \(\Psi\) with the theorem on the change of a field for \(\Phi\) and invert it with the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1}\), while the lower bound for stretching bounds the step in \(D\) by the step in \(E\).

1. Openness.

  1. Let \(U \subseteq D\) be an open set, \(Q_0\) a point of \(\Phi(U)\) and \(P_0\) a point of \(U\) with \(\Phi(P_0) = Q_0\). We have to show that there is \(\rho > 0\) such that every point closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho\) is in \(\Phi(U)\).
  2. Let \(\mat F_0 = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\). Since \(\det\mat F_0 = J_\Phi(P_0) \neq 0\), \(\mat F_0\) has an inverse matrix by theorem 2.54. Let \(g\) be the largest absolute value of its elements. Then \(g > 0\), because otherwise \(\mat F_0^{-1}\mat F_0\) would be the zero matrix, not \(\mat I\). By lemma 4.46 \(|\mat F_0^{-1}\vek w| \le m\,|\vek w|\) for every \(\vek w\), with \(m = 3g\). By lemma 4.50 there is \(r_0 > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r_0\) lies in \(D\) and (4.28) holds in it.
  3. The set \(U\) is open, so there is \(r_{\mathrm{U}} > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P_0\) than \(r_{\mathrm{U}}\) are in \(U\). Let \(r\) be half the smaller of the numbers \(r_0\) and \(r_{\mathrm{U}}\), and \(K\) the closed ball, the set of the points \(P\) with \(|P_0 P| \le r\). All points of \(K\) lie in \(U\) and in the ball of step 2. The set \(K\) is closed by lemma 1.75, because \(|P_0 P| \le r\) exactly when \(|P_0 P|^2 \le r^2\) (lemma 1.28), and \(|P_0 P|^2\) is a polynomial in the coordinates of the point \(P\). It is bounded, because by the triangle inequality for vectors (corollary 2.16) \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le |\overrightarrow{OP_0}| + r\). It is nonempty, because it contains \(P_0\).
  4. Let \(\rho = r/(4m)\), so that the bound \(r/(2m)\) of step 6 equals \(2\rho\), and let \(Q\) be a point with \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho\). Let \(f(P) = |\Phi(P) - Q|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\big)^2\) for every \(P\) of \(D\), where \(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\) is coordinate \(i\) of the point \(Q\). The components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuous (lemma 1.91), so by corollary 1.69, item 1, \(f\) is continuous on \(K\). By theorem 1.78, the extreme value theorem in space, there is a point \(P_* \in K\) at which \(f\) attains its smallest value on \(K\).
  5. At the centre \(f(P_0) = |Q_0 - Q|^2 < \rho^2\).
  6. Let \(P\) be a point with \(|P_0 P| = r\), on the surface of the ball \(K\). The points \(P\) and \(P_0\) lie in the ball of step 2, so by (4.28) \(|\Phi(P) - Q_0| \ge r/(2m) = 2\rho\). By the triangle inequality for vectors \(|\Phi(P) - Q_0| \le |\Phi(P) - Q| + |Q - Q_0|\), so \(|\Phi(P) - Q| \ge 2\rho - |Q - Q_0| > \rho\), and \(f(P) > \rho^2 > f(P_0)\).
  7. By steps 4 to 6 the point \(P_*\) is not on the surface of the ball, because \(f(P_*) \le f(P_0)\). Hence \(|P_0 P_*| < r\). Let \(\varepsilon_* = r - |P_0 P_*| > 0\).
  8. Let \(j\) be one of the coordinates. For \(|h| < \varepsilon_*\) the point \(P_* + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is, by the triangle inequality for vectors, at most \(|P_0 P_*| + |h| < r\) away from \(P_0\), so it lies in \(K\). The function \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(h) = f(P_* + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\) is therefore defined on the open interval \((-\varepsilon_*, \varepsilon_*)\) and attains its smallest value on it at \(h = 0\), because \(P_*\) is the point of the smallest value on \(K\).
  9. The function \(f\) is composed of the map \(\Phi\) and the polynomial that assigns to a point \(Y\) the number \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} (x_{\mathrm{i}}(Y) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q))^2\) and has the partial derivatives \(2\,(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Y) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q))\). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\) and
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_*) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} 2\,\big(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P_*) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_*) .\]
    By the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 this is the derivative \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'(0)\).
  10. By lemma 1.82 on the derivative at an interior extremum \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'(0) = 0\). Let \(\vek w = \Phi(P_*) - Q\) and \(\mat F_* = \mat F_\Phi(P_*)\). Since \((\mat F_*^\T)_{\mathrm{ji}} = (\mat F_*)_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.100), step 9 for \(j = x, y, z\) says \(\mat F_*^\T\,\vek w = \vek 0\).
  11. By lemma 2.51, item 6, \(\det\mat F_*^\T = \det\mat F_* = J_\Phi(P_*) \neq 0\), because \(P_*\) lies in \(D\). By theorem 2.54 \(\mat F_*^\T\) has an inverse matrix, so by lemma 1.99, item 1, and lemma 1.106 \(\vek w = (\mat F_*^\T)^{-1}(\mat F_*^\T\,\vek w) = (\mat F_*^\T)^{-1}\vek 0 = \vek 0\). Hence \(\Phi(P_*) = Q\).
  12. The point \(P_*\) lies in \(K\) and so in \(U\), hence \(Q\) lies in \(\Phi(U)\). This holds for every point \(Q\) closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho\), and \(Q_0\) was an arbitrary point of \(\Phi(U)\), so \(\Phi(U)\) is open. For \(U = D\) we get that \(E\) is open.

2. Continuity of the map \(\Psi\).

  1. Let \(Q_0\) be a point of \(E\), \(P_0 = \Psi(Q_0)\), and \(\mat F_0\), \(m\) and \(r_0\) as in step 2 of the first part. The ball \(B_0\) with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r_0\) is an open set. For a point \(P\) of it, all points closer to \(P\) than \(r_0 - |P_0 P|\) are, by the triangle inequality for vectors, closer to \(P_0\) than \(r_0\). By the first part \(\Phi(B_0)\) is open and contains \(Q_0\), so there is \(\rho_0 > 0\) such that all points closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho_0\) are in \(\Phi(B_0)\).
  2. Let \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho_0\). Then \(Q = \Phi(P)\) for some point \(P\) of \(B_0\), and since \(\Phi\) is one-to-one, \(\Psi(Q) = P\). The points \(P\) and \(P_0\) lie in \(B_0\), so by (4.28)
    \[|\Psi(Q) - \Psi(Q_0)| = |P_0 P| \le 2m\,|\Phi(P) - \Phi(P_0)| = 2m\,|Q_0 Q| .\]
  3. No component of a vector is longer than the vector (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so \(|\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0)| \le 2m\,|Q_0 Q|\). For the error \(\eta > 0\) a band smaller than the numbers \(\rho_0\) and \(\eta/(2m)\) will do. The components of the map \(\Psi\) are continuous at \(Q_0\) (definition 1.67).

3. The partial derivatives of the map \(\Psi\).

  1. Let \(\mat A = \mat F_0^{-1}\). For \(Q\) with \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho_0\) let \(P = \Psi(Q)\) and \(\vek\Delta = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, applied to every component \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the point \(P_0\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P_0) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{j}} + R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), written with vectors
    \[\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q} = \mat F_0\,\vek\Delta + \vek R , \qquad \vek R = (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]
  2. We multiply the equality by \(\mat A\). By lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix, lemma 1.99, item 1, and lemma 1.106 \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q} = \vek\Delta + \mat A\vek R\). Since \(\vek\Delta = \Psi(Q) - \Psi(Q_0)\), for every component \(k\)
    \[\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} A_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\big(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\big) + R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) , \qquad \vek R' = -\mat A\vek R .\]
  3. The remainder \(R'_{\mathrm{k}}\) is small compared with \(|Q_0 Q|\). We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\eta' = \eta/(12m^2)\). Then the factors \(3m\) and \(2m\) of step 4 together with \(\eta'\) give \(\eta/2\). By the theorem on the change of a field there is for every \(i\) a band \(\delta_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)| \le \eta'\,|P_0 P|\) for \(0 < |P_0 P| < \delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). Let \(\delta'\) be the smallest of the three bands. Let \(0 < |Q_0 Q|\), with \(|Q_0 Q|\) smaller than \(\rho_0\) and than \(\delta'/(2m)\). Then \(P \neq P_0\), because \(\Phi(P) = Q \neq Q_0 = \Phi(P_0)\), and by step 2 of the second part \(|P_0 P| \le 2m\,|Q_0 Q| < \delta'\). Hence \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)| \le \eta'\,|P_0 P|\) for every \(i\).
  4. The distance is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of the components (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so \(|\vek R| \le 3\eta'\,|P_0 P|\). By the assumption on the number \(m\) of step 2 of the first part and by step 2 of the second part
    \[|R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)| \le |\vek R'| = |\mat A\vek R| \le m\,|\vek R| \le 3m\,\eta'\,|P_0 P| \le 6m^2\,\eta'\,|Q_0 Q| = \tfrac{\eta}{2}\,|Q_0 Q| .\]
  5. Let \(i\) be one of the coordinates and \(h\) a number with \(0 < |h| < \min(\rho_0, \delta'/(2m))\). For \(Q = Q_0 + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(x_{\mathrm{l}}(Q) - x_{\mathrm{l}}(Q_0)\) equals \(h\) for \(\ix{l} = \ix{i}\) and \(0\) otherwise, and \(|Q_0 Q| = |h|\). By step 2
    \[\frac{\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0 + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0)}{h} = A_{\mathrm{ki}} + \frac{R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)}{h} ,\]
    and by step 4 \(|R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)/h| \le \eta/2 < \eta\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so by the definition of the limit 1.5 and of the partial derivative 1.25 \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\) exists and equals \(A_{\mathrm{ki}}\). Hence \(\mat F_\Psi(Q_0) = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)^{-1}\), which is the first equality of (4.29).

4. Continuity of the partial derivatives and the Jacobian.

  1. By step 5 of the third part, at every point \(Q\) of \(E\) the partial derivative \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\) is the element \((k, i)\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(\Psi(Q))^{-1}\). By theorem 2.54 this element is a component of the vector product of two columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(\Psi(Q))\), divided by its determinant. The numerator \(p_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is the difference of two products of two elements of the matrix each, the denominator \(d\) the sum of six products of three elements each with signs ((2.51)).
  2. Let a sequence of points \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(E\) converge to \(Q_0\), and let \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = \Psi(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\). By step 3 of the second part and lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points the coordinates of the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the coordinates of the point \(P_0\), and by lemma 1.66 \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) converges to \(P_0\). The partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous at \(P_0\), so by the same lemma on sequences the elements of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to the elements of the matrix \(\mat F_0\).
  3. By lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences, items 1 to 3, the numerators \(p_{\mathrm{ki}}\) at the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) therefore converge to the numerator at \(P_0\), and the determinants \(d_{\mathrm{n}} = J_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) to \(d = J_\Phi(P_0) \neq 0\).
  4. The reciprocals of the determinants converge to \(1/d\). By the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.38 with the error \(|d|/2\) there is a place \(N_1\) such that \(|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < |d|/2\) for \(n \ge N_1\), and by the triangle inequality for numbers then \(|d_{\mathrm{n}}| > |d|/2\). For \(n \ge N_1\) therefore
    \[\Big| \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{n}}} - \frac{1}{d} \Big| = \frac{|d - d_{\mathrm{n}}|}{|d_{\mathrm{n}}|\,|d|} \le \frac{2}{d^2}\,|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| .\]
    For an error \(\eta > 0\) there is by the same definition a place \(N_2\) such that \(|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\,d^2/2\) for \(n \ge N_2\). For \(n\) not smaller than \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) therefore \(|1/d_{\mathrm{n}} - 1/d| < \eta\), and \(1/d_{\mathrm{n}}\) converges to \(1/d\).
  5. By lemma 1.60, item 3, the product of the numerator and the reciprocal of the determinant, \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\), converges to \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\). We chose the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) arbitrarily, so by lemma 1.68, second direction, the partial derivative is continuous at \(Q_0\). The set \(E\) is open by the first part, so \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\) (definition 4.42).
  6. By theorem 2.52 on the determinant of a product and lemma 2.51, item 5, \(\det\big(\mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1}\big)\det\mat F_\Phi(P) = \det\mat I = 1\), so \(J_\Psi(\Phi(P)) = 1/J_\Phi(P)\), which is the second equality of (4.29).

5. The plane.

  1. In the plane the steps are the same, with sums over two coordinates and with \(2 \times 2\) matrices. Lemma 4.46, item 2, gives \(m = 2g\), lemmas 4.50 and 4.47 hold in the plane, the theorem on the change of a field holds for functions of two variables, and in place of theorem 2.54 we use lemma 4.49, by which the elements of the inverse matrix are again elements divided by the determinant. For \(2 \times 2\) matrices \(\det\mat A^\T = A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} = \det\mat A\), and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants by the argument after theorem 2.52.

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 8.5.1 (PDF pp. 51-54), where the theorem is proved with contractions for a neighbourhood of a point with invertible derivative, with the equality \(g'(y) = (f'(x))^{-1}\), and Cor. 8.5.2 (PDF p. 54), that the image of every open set is open.
