The proof of items 2 and 3 follows the idea of the source (PDF p. 53), the proof of item 1 with the smallest value is not from the sources.

The proof showed where each assumption is needed. Continuous differentiability and \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) gave the lower bound for stretching, which in the first part kept the images of the points on the surface of the ball far from \(Q_0\), and in the second and third parts bounded the step in \(D\) by the step in \(E\). The first part did not need the one-to-one property: the image of an open set is open also for a continuously differentiable map with \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) at every point that is not one-to-one. We needed it only for \(\Psi\) to be defined at all. The moves that will come back are finding the smallest value on a closed ball, the zero derivative at an interior extremum, and writing a change with a remainder that is small compared with the step.

What if we drop the one-to-one property? The map of the plane

\[\Phi(s, t) = (s^2 - t^2,\ 2st)\]

has the matrix of partial derivatives with the columns \((2s, 2t)\) and \((-2t, 2s)\) and the Jacobian \(4s^2 + 4t^2\), which is not zero at any point except the origin. On the plane without the origin, which is an open set, \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) therefore. But the map is not one-to-one, because \(\Phi(-s, -t) = \Phi(s, t)\): the points \(P\) and \(-P\), symmetric with respect to the origin, have the same image (figure 4.41). There is therefore no inverse map on the whole image. By lemma 4.50 on the lower bound for stretching, however, \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on a small disc around every point, and on this disc, which is an open set, the theorem holds. On a small disc around every point \(\Phi\) therefore has an inverse map, but not on the whole plane without the origin. For a deformation this would mean that two parts of the material come to the same place, although every small piece by itself deforms admissibly, with \(J > 0\). This is why for a deformation we require the one-to-one property for the whole body, not only for every piece. The example is from LEBL2 (Example 8.5.4, PDF p. 54).

Why do we need \(J_\Phi \neq 0\)? The function \(\Phi(t) = t^3\) is one-to-one on the number line. The difference \(t'^3 - t^3 = (t' - t)(t'^2 + t' t + t^2)\) has the second factor equal to \((t' + t/2)^2 + \tfrac34\,t^2\), which is positive unless both numbers are zero, so \(t'^3 = t^3\) implies \(t' = t\). Its derivative \(3t^2\), however, is zero at \(t = 0\). The inverse function \(\Psi\) assigns to the cube \(h^3\) the number \(h\). Between the points \(0\) and \(h^3\) its difference quotient has the value

\[\frac{\Psi(h^3) - \Psi(0)}{h^3 - 0} = \frac{h}{h^3} = \frac{1}{h^2} ,\]

which grows beyond all bounds as \(h\) goes to zero, so \(\Psi\) has no derivative at \(0\) (LEBL2, PDF p. 54). The function \(\Phi\) squeezes a short piece of the line near \(0\) almost into a point, and the reverse rule must therefore stretch it beyond all bounds.

Let us test the theorem on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\). It is one-to-one on the whole plane. From \((s, t + s^2) = (s', t' + s'^2)\) follows \(s = s'\) and then \(t = t'\). The Jacobian is \(1\) everywhere. The inverse map is

\[\Psi(x, y) = (x,\ y - x^2) ,\]

because \(\Psi(\Phi(s, t)) = (s, t + s^2 - s^2) = (s, t)\). Its matrix of partial derivatives at the point \(\Phi(s, t)\), where \(x = s\), is

\[\mat F_\Psi\big(\Phi(s, t)\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2s & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by lemma 4.49, with the elements \(1\), \(0\), \(2s\) and \(1\) and the determinant \(1\), \(\mat F_\Phi(s, t)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2s & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the same matrix, as (4.29) says. Also \(J_\Psi = 1 = 1/J_\Phi\).

Now the hanging bar, for which we do not know \(\Psi\). We have shown that \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on the set \(D\) of the interior points of the bar. The Jacobian is positive on \(D\). All nine partial derivatives of the displacements are at most \(g = 2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) in absolute value, so by lemma 2.55 on the change of volume, item 2, \(J\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 + 2a\,(L - x) - 2 \cdot 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 1 + 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3 < 10^{-10}\), and \(J > 1 - 10^{-10} > 0\). The theorem therefore tells us that the image \(E = \Phi(D)\) is an open set, that the inverse map \(\Psi\), which assigns to a point after loading its place before loading, is continuously differentiable on \(E\), and that its matrix of partial derivatives at the point \(\Phi(P)\) is the matrix \(\mat F(P)^{-1}\). For the point \(P\) at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm from the axis in the plane \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\), by theorem 2.54, computed with SymPy,

\[\mat F(P)^{-1} - \mat I = \begin{bmatrix} -1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6} & 4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ -4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 5{,}856003 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5{,}856003 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us check with a difference quotient. We found the point \(Q\) whose image is \(h\) lower than the image of the point \(P\), \(\Phi(Q) = \Phi(P) + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), numerically, by solving the three equations with a program to 40 decimal places. The quotient \((\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}(\Phi(P) + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) - \Psi_{\mathrm{x}}(\Phi(P)))/h - 1\) is \(-1{,}951801 \cdot 10^{-6}\) for \(h = 1\) mm and \(-1{,}951977 \cdot 10^{-6}\) for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm. The differences from the element \(-1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6}\) above are \(1{,}95 \cdot 10^{-10}\) and \(1{,}95 \cdot 10^{-11}\), ten times smaller for a ten times shorter step. The inverse matrix is almost \(\mat I - \mat H\), the identity matrix minus the displacement gradient: the element \(-H_{\mathrm{xx}} = -1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) differs from the element above by \(3{,}8 \cdot 10^{-12}\), which is \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\). This agrees with intuition: the displacement back is almost the opposite displacement, and for the sheared cube \(\mat I - \mat H\) was even exactly the inverse matrix.

With the inverse map and the chain rule we have everything we need about maps. The next step is the volume of an image, first under a map that is multiplication by a matrix.

4.3.3 Volume under a linear map

In section 2.10.2 we saw that a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) maps the unit cube onto the parallelepiped spanned by its columns, and that this parallelepiped has the volume \(|\det\mat A|\) (lemma 2.47). There we took the volume of a parallelepiped from school, as the area of the base times the height. Now we have an exact notion of volume for every set with volume (definition 4.27): the volume is the limit of the total volume of those cells of a grid that lie in the set. Two questions therefore arise. Does this notion give the same number for a parallelepiped as school does? And does a matrix with a nonzero determinant multiply the volume of every set with volume, for instance of the cross section of the round bar, by the same number \(|\det\mat A|\)?

We need the answer in section 4.3.4, where we will turn an integral over the image of a set into an integral over the set itself. There we will replace a map near each point by its linear part, just as in theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step we replaced the difference of displacements by the product of the displacement gradient and the step. A small cube then goes almost onto a parallelepiped, and we will compare its volume after the map with the volume of this parallelepiped. So we must know the volume of the image under a linear map exactly, as the volume of a set with volume.

The route is this. First we show that every matrix with a nonzero determinant is a product of matrices of three simple kinds. Then we show that the image of such a set has a volume too, and we do it at once for every continuously differentiable one-to-one map with a nonzero Jacobian, because we will need this in the next section as well. Finally we compute the volume of the image under a linear map: directly for the simple matrices, and through the product for the others.

In section 1.16.3 we met the matrices \(\mat D\) and \(\mat G\). The first doubles the component \(x\) of a vector, the second adds the component \(z\) to the component \(x\). Each of them does a single simple thing to a vector. There are three kinds of such simple things.

Definition 4.52 Elementary matrix (elementarna matrika)

Let \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) be two different indices among \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). An elementary matrix (elementarna matrika) of size \(3 \times 3\) is a matrix of one of three kinds:

  1. swap of the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\): the matrix obtained from the identity matrix \(\mat I\) (definition 1.105) by swapping its rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\),
  2. multiplication of the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) by a number \(c \neq 0\): the matrix obtained from \(\mat I\) by replacing the element \(1\) in the place \(ii\) by \(c\),
  3. addition of \(k\) times the coordinate \(\ix{j}\) to the coordinate \(\ix{i}\), where \(k\) is any number: the matrix obtained from \(\mat I\) by replacing the element \(0\) in the place \(ij\) by \(k\).

An elementary matrix of size \(2 \times 2\) is a matrix of the same three kinds, with the indices \(x\) and \(y\).

Source: LEBL2 §8.2 (PDF pp. 30-31), for \(n \times n\) matrices.

The names say what the matrix does to a vector. For \(\ix{i} = x\) and \(\ix{j} = z\) the matrices of the three kinds are

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} c & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by (1.38) they map the vector \((v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) to the vectors \((v_{\mathrm{z}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{x}})\), \((c\,v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \((v_{\mathrm{x}} + k\,v_{\mathrm{z}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\). The matrix \(\mat D\) of section 1.16.3 is therefore an elementary matrix of the second kind with \(c = 2\), the matrix \(\mat G\) an elementary matrix of the third kind with \(k = 1\), and the deformation gradient of the sheared cube, which has the number \(0{,}001\) in the place \(xz\), is also an elementary matrix of the third kind. Geometrically the second kind stretches or compresses a body along one axis, and for \(c < 0\) also mirrors it, the third kind shears it like a deck of cards, and the first mirrors it in the plane in which the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) are equal. The next lemma says that these three kinds are enough for every matrix with a nonzero determinant.

Lemma 4.53 Factorization into elementary matrices (razcep na preproste matrike)

Let \(\mat E\) be an elementary matrix of size \(3 \times 3\) (definition 4.52), with the indices \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\).

  1. For every matrix \(\mat M\) with three rows, \(\mat E\mat M\) is the matrix obtained from \(\mat M\) by the same operation on the rows: for a swap we swap the rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), for a multiplication we multiply the row \(\ix{i}\) by \(c\), for an addition we add \(k\) times the row \(\ix{j}\) to the row \(\ix{i}\). In particular, for a vector \(\vek v\) written as a column, \(\mat E\vek v\) is the vector obtained from \(\vek v\) by swapping the components \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\), multiplying the component \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) by \(c\), or adding \(k\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) to the component \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\), respectively.
  2. The determinant of a swap is \(-1\), the determinant of a multiplication of a coordinate by \(c\) is \(c\), the determinant of an addition is \(1\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat E\) has an inverse matrix, which is an elementary matrix of the same kind with the same indices: a swap, a multiplication by \(1/c\), or an addition of \((-k)\) times, respectively.
  4. Every \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) with \(\det\mat A \neq 0\) is a product of finitely many elementary matrices, \(\mat A = \mat E_1\,\mat E_2 \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\).

The same holds for matrices of size \(2 \times 2\).

Proof

We must show four items. The first three follow from the definition of the matrix product. We prove the fourth by elimination: step by step we turn the matrix \(\mat A\) into the identity matrix by multiplying it by elementary matrices from the left.

1. Action on the rows.

  1. By definition 1.98 the element in row \(\ix{l}\) and column \(\ix{q}\) of the matrix \(\mat E\mat M\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{m}} E_{\mathrm{lm}} M_{\mathrm{mq}}\). Row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is therefore the sum of the rows of \(\mat M\) multiplied by the elements of row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\): row \(\ix{m}\) of \(\mat M\) is multiplied by \(E_{\mathrm{lm}}\).
  2. A row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\) that equals row \(\ix{l}\) of the identity matrix has a single nonzero element, \(1\) in column \(\ix{l}\). By step 1 row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is therefore row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat M\). So it is, for a swap, with all rows except \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), and for the other two kinds with all rows except \(\ix{i}\).
  3. Swap. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, with the element \(1\) in column \(\ix{j}\), so by step 1 row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat M\). In the same way row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\).
  4. Multiplication. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has a single nonzero element, \(c\) in column \(\ix{i}\), so row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\) multiplied by \(c\).
  5. Addition. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has the nonzero elements \(1\) in column \(\ix{i}\) and \(k\) in column \(\ix{j}\), so row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is the sum of row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\) and \(k\) times its row \(\ix{j}\).
  6. A vector \(\vek v\) written as a column is a matrix with one column whose rows are its components. Steps 2 to 5 give for it the claim about the vector \(\mat E\vek v\).

2. Determinants.

  1. Swap. The identity matrix is symmetric, so swapping its rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) gives the same matrix as swapping its columns \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\): in both cases we get the matrix with ones in the places \(ij\) and \(ji\), with ones on the diagonal in the other rows and with zeros elsewhere. By items 4 and 5 of lemma 2.51 on the properties of the determinant, \(\det\mat E = -\det\mat I = -1\).
  2. Multiplication. Column \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is \(c\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), the other columns are columns of the identity matrix. By linearity in column \(\ix{i}\) (item 2 of the same lemma) and item 5, \(\det\mat E = c\det\mat I = c\).
  3. Addition. The element \(k\) in the place \(ij\) lies in column \(\ix{j}\), which is therefore \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} + k\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), while the other columns are columns of the identity matrix. By linearity in column \(\ix{j}\), \(\det\mat E\) is the sum of the number \(\det\mat I = 1\) and \(k\) times the determinant of the matrix that has the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) in column \(\ix{j}\). This matrix has equal columns \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), so by item 3 of the same lemma its determinant is zero. Therefore \(\det\mat E = 1\).

3. Inverse matrix.

  1. Let \(\mat E'\) be the elementary matrix of the same kind with the same indices, a swap, a multiplication by \(1/c\), or an addition of \((-k)\) times, respectively. By the first item we get \(\mat E'\mat E\) by doing the operation of \(\mat E'\) on the rows of \(\mat E\).
  2. Swap. The matrix \(\mat E\) is the identity matrix with the rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) swapped. When we swap them back, we get \(\mat I\).
  3. Multiplication. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has the element \(c\) on the diagonal. When we multiply it by \(1/c\), we get row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix, and the other rows already are rows of the identity matrix.
  4. Addition. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is the sum of row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix and \(k\) times row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, while row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat E\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, because \(\ix{j} \neq \ix{i}\). When we add \((-k)\) times row \(\ix{j}\) to row \(\ix{i}\), we get row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix.
  5. In all three cases therefore \(\mat E'\mat E = \mat I\). The matrix \(\mat E\) is the elementary matrix of the same kind for \(\mat E'\), with the reciprocal of the number \(1/c\) or with the opposite number of \(-k\), so by steps 2 to 4 with the roles exchanged also \(\mat E\mat E' = \mat I\). By definition 1.107, \(\mat E'\) is the inverse matrix of \(\mat E\).

4. Factorization.

  1. We will multiply the matrix \(\mat A\) by elementary matrices from the left, one after another. We denote the current matrix after each step by \(\mat B\). It has the form \(\mat E_{\mathrm{s}} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A\), so by theorem 2.52 on the determinant of a product and the second item, \(\det\mat B = \det\mat E_{\mathrm{s}} \cdots \det\mat E_1\,\det\mat A\), a product of nonzero numbers, which is not zero. What multiplication by an elementary matrix does to the rows of \(\mat B\) is said by the first item.
  2. Column \(x\). Column \(x\) of \(\mat B\) is not the zero vector. If it were, then by linearity in the first column (item 2 of lemma 2.51), used with the number \(0\), the determinant would be \(\det\mat B = \det(0 \cdot \vek 0, \vek b, \vek c) = 0 \cdot \det(\vek 0, \vek b, \vek c) = 0\), where \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) are the other two columns. So some element \(B_{\mathrm{lx}}\) is not zero. If \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), we multiply by the swap of the coordinates \(x\) and \(\ix{l}\), and then \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} \neq 0\).
  3. We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(x\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Then \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\).
  4. We multiply by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{yx}})\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(y\) and then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{zx}})\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(z\). The rows \(y\) and \(z\) get \(-B_{\mathrm{yx}}\) times and \(-B_{\mathrm{zx}}\) times the row \(x\), which has the element \(1\) in column \(x\), so then \(B_{\mathrm{yx}} = B_{\mathrm{zx}} = 0\). Column \(x\) is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  5. Column \(y\). The elements \(B_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{zy}}\) are not both zero. If they were, column \(y\) would be \(B_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by linearity in the second column and item 3 of lemma 2.51 we would have \(\det\mat B = B_{\mathrm{xy}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek c) = 0\). If \(B_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), we multiply by the swap of the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The rows \(y\) and \(z\) have zeros in column \(x\), so column \(x\) remains \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and then \(B_{\mathrm{yy}} \neq 0\).
  6. We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(y\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{yy}}\), then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{xy}})\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(x\) and by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{zy}})\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(z\). Row \(y\) has a zero in column \(x\), so column \(x\) remains \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), while column \(y\) becomes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), as in steps 3 and 4.
  7. Column \(z\). We have \(B_{\mathrm{zz}} \neq 0\). Otherwise column \(z\) would be \(B_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and by linearity in the third column and item 3 of the same lemma we would have \(\det\mat B = B_{\mathrm{xz}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0\). We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(z\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{zz}}\), then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{xz}})\) times the coordinate \(z\) to the coordinate \(x\) and by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{yz}})\) times the coordinate \(z\) to the coordinate \(y\). Row \(z\) has zeros in the columns \(x\) and \(y\), so these two columns remain, while column \(z\) becomes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Now \(\mat B = \mat I\).
  8. We have obtained elementary matrices \(\mat E_1, \dots, \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) with \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A = \mat I\). By the third item \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\). We multiply both sides by it from the left. By item 2 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product we may group the factors as we like, and \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat I\), so we get \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-1} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A = \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\). In the same way we remove \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-1}\), then \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-2}\), and finally \(\mat E_1\). We get \(\mat A = \mat E_1^{-1}\,\mat E_2^{-1} \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\), by the third item a product of elementary matrices.
  9. For matrices of size \(2 \times 2\) the steps are the same, with the columns \(x\) and \(y\), with two rows and with the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, for which the same properties hold. The determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix is namely the determinant of the \(3 \times 3\) matrix that has the \(2 \times 2\) matrix in the rows and columns \(x\) and \(y\), the number \(1\) at the place \(zz\) and zeros elsewhere in the row and the column \(z\) (section 2.10.2), and row operations on the \(2 \times 2\) matrix are the same operations on the bigger matrix.

Source: LEBL2 §8.2 (PDF pp. 30-31): the kinds of elementary matrices, their determinants and Prop. 8.2.11, whose proof the source leaves to the reader. KREYSZIG §7.3 (PDF pp. 298-303) for elimination in systems of linear equations. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof is the elimination that KREYSZIG uses to solve systems of linear equations (Gauss elimination, Gaussovo izločanje, KREYSZIG §7.3, PDF p. 298). The nonzero determinant made sure that the procedure never gets stuck: in every column we found a nonzero element by which we divided. Let us try it on the turned plate of section 2.10.5. A thin square plate in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) turns as a whole about the axis \(z\) with the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), and in the plane of the plate its deformation gradient is the \(2 \times 2\) matrix

\[\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The elimination has four steps.

  1. The element \(R_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}6\) is not zero. We multiply the row \(x\) by \(1/0{,}6 = 5/3\) and get the rows \((1, -\tfrac43)\) and \((0{,}8,\ 0{,}6)\).
  2. We add \((-0{,}8)\) times the row \(x\) to the row \(y\). We get \((0,\ 0{,}6 + 0{,}8 \cdot \tfrac43) = (0, \tfrac53)\).
  3. We multiply the row \(y\) by \(\tfrac35\) and get \((0, 1)\).
  4. We add \(\tfrac43\) times the row \(y\) to the row \(x\) and get \((1, 0)\).

The inverse matrices of these four steps, in the reverse order, give the factorization, which we checked with SymPy:

\[\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac53 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tfrac43 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

As a rule that assigns a vector to a vector, the rightmost factor acts first (figure 4.42). We first shear the square by adding \(-\tfrac43\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(x\), then stretch it along the axis \(y\) to \(\tfrac53\) times its height, then shear it by adding \(0{,}8\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(y\), and finally compress it along the axis \(x\) to \(0{,}6\) times its width. The areas are, in turn, \(1\), \(1\), \(\tfrac53\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\), and the determinants of the factors give \(0{,}6 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac53 \cdot 1 = 1 = \det\mat R\), as theorem 2.52 on the determinant of a product demands for \(2 \times 2\) matrices. A rotation, which stretches nothing, is thus made of two shears and two stretches that cancel. For the matrix \(\mat A\) of figure 2.57, with the columns \((1, 1, 2)\), \((2, 0, 0)\), \((1, 3, 0)\) and with the determinant \(12\), the elimination has eight steps, if we leave out the multiplication of a row by the number \(1\), which does not change the matrix. Two are multiplications of rows by \(-\tfrac12\) and by \(-\tfrac16\), six are additions. The inverse matrices of the multiplications have the determinants \(-2\) and \(-6\), those of the additions the determinant \(1\), and \((-2) \cdot (-6) = 12\).

Now to the volume of the image. Before we compute it, we must make sure that the image has a volume at all when the set we map has one. A set with volume is closed and bounded, and its boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27). Does its image have the same properties? The answer holds for every map that is continuously differentiable and one-to-one and has a nonzero Jacobian at every point, as described by theorem 4.51 on the inverse map, so we prove it at once for such maps. The idea has two parts. Every boundary point of the image is the image of a boundary point, because the map takes interior points to interior points and back. A set of zero volume stays such, because a map with bounded partial derivatives takes a small cube to a set that a cube with an edge proportional to the edge of the first covers. First the interior points.

Lemma 4.54 Interior and boundary points of an image (notranje in robne točke slike)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\). Let \(Y\) be a set of points in \(D\).

  1. A point \(P \in Y\) is an interior point of the set \(Y\) if and only if \(\Phi(P)\) is an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\).
  2. If \(Y\) is closed and bounded (definition 1.74), every boundary point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\) (definition 4.23) is the image of some boundary point of the set \(Y\).
  3. If \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are sets of points in \(D\) and no interior point of either of them lies in the other, then also no interior point of either of the sets \(\Phi(Y_1)\) and \(\Phi(Y_2)\) lies in the other.

The same holds in the plane.

Proof

We must show three items. We get the first from theorem 4.51 on the inverse map, which says that \(\Phi\) and its inverse map \(\Psi\) take open sets to open sets. The other two follow from the first.

1. Interior points.

  1. Let \(P\) be an interior point of the set \(Y\). Then there is \(r > 0\) such that the ball \(B\) with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\), the set of points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) (section 1.12.6), lies in \(Y\).
  2. The ball \(B\) is open. For a point \(S \in B\) we have \(r - |PS| > 0\), and for every point \(T\) with \(|ST| < r - |PS|\) corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 2, gives \(|PT| \le |PS| + |ST| < r\), so \(T\) lies in \(B\).
  3. The ball \(B\) lies in \(Y \subseteq D\). By theorem 4.51, item 1, \(\Phi(B)\) is an open set. It contains \(\Phi(P)\) and lies in \(\Phi(Y)\), so all points close enough to \(\Phi(P)\) are in \(\Phi(Y)\). The point \(\Phi(P)\) is an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\).
  4. Conversely, let \(\Phi(P)\) be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\), and let \(B'\) be a ball with centre \(\Phi(P)\) that lies in \(\Phi(Y)\). By step 2 it is open.
  5. Let \(E = \Phi(D)\) and let \(\Psi\) be the inverse map (definition 4.45), for which \(\Psi(\Phi(Q)) = Q\) for every \(Q \in D\) and \(\Phi(\Psi(T)) = T\) for every \(T \in E\). By theorem 4.51, \(E\) is open, \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\) and \(J_\Psi(\Phi(Q)) = 1/J_\Phi(Q) \neq 0\). The map \(\Psi\) is one-to-one on \(E\): from \(\Psi(T_1) = \Psi(T_2)\) it follows that \(T_1 = \Phi(\Psi(T_1)) = \Phi(\Psi(T_2)) = T_2\).
  6. Theorem 4.51, item 1, applied to \(\Psi\) and the open set \(B' \subseteq \Phi(Y) \subseteq E\), says that \(\Psi(B')\) is an open set. It contains \(\Psi(\Phi(P)) = P\). Each of its points is \(\Psi(T)\) for some \(T \in B' \subseteq \Phi(Y)\), so \(T = \Phi(Q)\) with \(Q \in Y\), and \(\Psi(T) = Q\) lies in \(Y\). Around \(P\) there is therefore a ball that lies in \(\Psi(B') \subseteq Y\), and \(P\) is an interior point of the set \(Y\).

2. Boundary points.

  1. The map \(\Phi\) is continuous on \(Y\) (lemma 1.91 for each component), so by lemma 4.48 the set \(\Phi(Y)\) is closed and bounded.
  2. Let \(T\) be a boundary point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\). By lemma 4.24, item 1, it lies in \(\Phi(Y)\), so \(T = \Phi(P)\) for some point \(P \in Y\).
  3. If \(P\) were an interior point of the set \(Y\), then by the first item \(T\) would be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\). Then some ball around \(T\) would lie in \(\Phi(Y)\) and would contain no point outside \(\Phi(Y)\), which contradicts \(T\) being a boundary point.
  4. The point \(P\) is therefore not an interior point of the set \(Y\). By lemma 4.24, item 2, it is therefore a boundary point of the set \(Y\), and \(T = \Phi(P)\).

3. Overlapping.

  1. Let \(T\) be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y_1)\) that lies in \(\Phi(Y_2)\). Then \(T = \Phi(P_1)\) with \(P_1 \in Y_1\) and \(T = \Phi(P_2)\) with \(P_2 \in Y_2\).
  2. The map \(\Phi\) is one-to-one, so \(P_1 = P_2\). This point lies in \(Y_2\), and by the first item it is an interior point of the set \(Y_1\). This contradicts the assumption.
  3. With the roles of the sets \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) exchanged we show that also no interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y_2)\) lies in \(\Phi(Y_1)\).
  4. In the plane the steps are the same, with discs instead of balls and with the inverse function theorem in the plane.

Source: LEBL2 proves item 2 in the proof of Prop. 10.5.9 (PDF pp. 126-127), with sequences and the inverse function theorem, and Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134) uses it where it needs that the image of a set with volume is again such a set. Items 1 and 3 and the proof with open images are not from the source.

The lemma says that a map that has an inverse map with the same properties keeps the difference between the inside and the boundary. An interior point stays interior, because a small ball around it goes to an open set, and a boundary point cannot become interior, because the inverse map would then return it to the inside. Without the one-to-one property the third item fails. A map that takes two separate discs to the same set, such as the one we met in section 4.3.2 (figure 4.41), turns two sets without common points into two sets that overlap.

For the second part of the idea we need bounds for the partial derivatives that hold also a little outside the set, since the cubes that cover the boundary reach beyond it.

Lemma 4.55 Bounded stretching near a closed bounded set (omejeno raztezanje ob zaprti omejeni množici)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42), and \(K\) a nonempty closed and bounded set of points in \(D\). Then there are numbers \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) with the following properties.

  1. The set \(K_\rho\) of all points at a distance of at most \(\rho\) from some point of the set \(K\) is closed and bounded and lies in \(D\).
  2. For every point \(Q \in K_\rho\) and all indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\), \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q)| \le M\).
  3. For every point \(P \in K\) and every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\), \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\).

The same holds in the plane, with \(2M\) instead of \(3M\).

Proof

We must show three items. We get the radius \(\rho\) from lemma 4.38 on the neighbourhood of a closed bounded set, the bound \(M\) from the extreme value theorem, and item 3 from the bound for stretching along a segment.

  1. By lemma 4.38 there is \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that every point at a distance less than \(\delta_0\) from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\). Let \(\rho = \delta_0/2\). The points of the set \(K_\rho\) are at a distance of at most \(\rho < \delta_0\) from some point of \(K\), so they lie in \(D\).
  2. Boundedness. The set \(K\) is bounded, so there is \(R\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every \(P \in K\). For \(Q \in K_\rho\) and a point \(P \in K\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\), corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 2, gives \(|\overrightarrow{OQ}| \le |\overrightarrow{OP}| + |PQ| \le R + \rho\).
  3. Closedness. Let a sequence of points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) of \(K_\rho\) converge to a point \(Q\), and let \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) be a point with \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| \le \rho\). The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.77 the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(P\). The set \(K\) is closed, so \(P \in K\).
  4. By the same item of the same corollary, used twice,
    \[|PQ| \le |P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q| \le |P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + \rho + |Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q| .\]
    The sequences \(|P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}|\) and \(|Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q|\) converge to \(0\), the first by step 3, the second by lemma 1.54 on the limit of a subsequence. By lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences, item 1, the right side converges to \(\rho\), and by lemma 1.48, that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 1, with the constant sequence \(|PQ|\) on the left, \(|PQ| \le \rho\). The point \(Q\) lies in \(K_\rho\), which is therefore closed.
  5. The bound \(M\). Each of the nine partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuous on \(D\), so on \(K_\rho\). By theorem 1.78, the extreme value theorem in space, it attains on \(K_\rho\) a greatest value \(M_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and a least value \(m_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le |M_{\mathrm{ij}}| + |m_{\mathrm{ij}}|\) on \(K_\rho\). Let \(M\) be \(1\) more than the largest of these nine numbers. Then \(M > 0\) and item 2 holds.
  6. Item 3. Let \(P \in K\) and \(|PQ| \le \rho\). The points of the segment from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(P + t\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) with \(t \in [0, 1]\), and they are at the distance \(t\,|PQ| \le \rho\) from \(P\), so they lie in \(K_\rho\), where all partial derivatives are at most \(M\) in absolute value. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\).
  7. In the plane the steps are the same, with discs instead of balls, with lemma 4.38 in the plane, whose proof is the same, and with lemma 4.47 in the plane, which gives \(2M\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 135) uses the same idea with the Lebesgue covering lemma and with a bound for the derivative.

To cover the boundary we need cubes, not just boxes. A box with the edges \(1\) mm, \(1\) mm and \(0{,}001\) mm goes, under a map that increases distances at most three times, to a set that perhaps only a cube with an edge of a few millimetres covers. The volume of such a cube is several thousand times the volume of the box, which is \(0{,}001\) mm³. For a cube with the edge \(h\), however, the image lies in a cube with an edge proportional to \(h\), and the two volumes differ only by a constant factor. We get cubes from a grid in which all pieces of the partitions are equally long. Lemma 4.29, item 1, says that the cells of such a grid that contain a point of a set of zero volume cover this set, for a fine enough grid, with an arbitrarily small total volume.

Now let us show that the image has a volume too.

Lemma 4.56 Image of a set with volume (slika množice s prostornino)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42).

  1. If \(Z\) is a set of zero volume (definition 4.25) that lies in some closed and bounded set \(K \subseteq D\), then \(\Phi(Z)\) is also a set of zero volume.
  2. If moreover \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on \(D\) and \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\), then for every set with volume \(W \subseteq D\) (definition 4.27) also \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.

The same holds in the plane, with area instead of volume.

Proof

We must show both items. In the first we replace every cube of the cover by a cube around the image of one of its points. In the second we use the first on the boundary of the set \(W\).

1. Set of zero volume.

  1. If \(Z\) is empty, so is \(\Phi(Z)\). Let it be nonempty. By lemma 4.55 for the set \(K\) there are \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) such that \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\) for every \(P \in K\) and every \(Q\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\).
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\eta' = \eta/(648\sqrt3\,M^3)\). By lemma 4.29, item 1, there is \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta\) the cells that contain a point of the set \(Z\) have a total volume less than \(\eta'\). The set \(K\) is bounded, so it lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) for some \(R > 0\). By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(h = 2R/n\) is less than \(\delta\) and than \(\rho/\sqrt3\). We divide every edge of the cube \([-R, R]^3\) into \(n\) equal pieces. The cells of this grid are cubes with the edge \(h\). We keep the cells that contain a point of the set \(Z\). They cover \(Z\), because every point of the set \(Z\) lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) and so in some cell, and they have a total volume less than \(\eta'\).
  3. For every kept cube \(C\) we choose a point \(P_{\mathrm{C}} \in Z \cap C\). For every point \(Q \in Z \cap C\) the coordinates of the points \(Q\) and \(P_{\mathrm{C}}\) differ by at most \(h\), so by (1.10) and lemma 1.28 \(|P_{\mathrm{C}} Q| \le \sqrt{3h^2} = \sqrt3\,h \le \rho\). Since \(P_{\mathrm{C}} \in Z \subseteq K\), step 1 gives \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})| \le 3\sqrt3\,M h\).
  4. No difference of coordinates is larger than the distance, so every coordinate of the point \(\Phi(Q)\) differs from the same coordinate of the point \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) by at most \(3\sqrt3\,M h\). The point \(\Phi(Q)\) therefore lies in the cube \(C'\) with centre \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) and edge \(6\sqrt3\,M h\), with the volume \((6\sqrt3\,M)^3 h^3 = 648\sqrt3\,M^3\,h^3\).
  5. Every point of the set \(\Phi(Z)\) is \(\Phi(Q)\) for some \(Q \in Z\), which lies in some kept cube \(C\), and so by step 4 in the cube \(C'\). The cubes \(C'\) therefore cover \(\Phi(Z)\). Their total volume is \(648\sqrt3\,M^3\) times the total volume of the cubes \(C\), which is less than \(648\sqrt3\,M^3\,\eta' = \eta\).
  6. We chose the error \(\eta\) freely, so by definition 4.25 \(\Phi(Z)\) is a set of zero volume.

2. Set with volume.

  1. The set \(W\) is closed and bounded, and \(\Phi\) is continuous on it (lemma 1.91 for each component). By lemma 4.48, \(\Phi(W)\) is closed and bounded.
  2. The set \(W\) is closed, so by lemma 4.24, item 1, its boundary lies in \(W\). The boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27).
  3. By the first item with \(K = W\) and with \(Z\) the boundary of the set \(W\), the set of the images of the boundary points has zero volume.
  4. By lemma 4.54, item 2, every boundary point of the set \(\Phi(W)\) is the image of a boundary point of the set \(W\). The boundary of the set \(\Phi(W)\) therefore lies in the set of step 3, and by lemma 4.26, item 1, it has zero volume.
  5. By steps 1 and 4, \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.
  6. In the plane the steps are the same, with squares instead of cubes and with the bound \(2M\) of lemma 4.55: a square with the edge \(h\) goes into a square with the edge \(4\sqrt2\,M h\) and the area \(32\,M^2 h^2\).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 10.3.10 (PDF p. 114) for item 1 and Prop. 10.5.9 (PDF pp. 126-127) for item 2, which Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134) uses to know that \(g(S)\) is Jordan measurable. The proof is not from the source.

Now we need one more tool for computing with the volumes of images. When we add up over the cells of a grid, no interior point of the image of one cell lies in the image of another, so the integrals over the images add up. That a smaller set has a smaller volume is said by lemma 4.32, item 2.

Lemma 4.57 Integral over the images of cells (integral po slikah celic)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every \(P \in D\), and let \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\) be different cells of one grid (section 4.2.3), all lying in \(D\). Then \(Y = \Phi(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(Y\),

\[\int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

In particular \(V_{\mathrm{Y}} = V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_1)} + \dots + V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k})}\). The same holds in the plane, with rectangles instead of boxes.

Proof

We must show that the images of the cells do not overlap in interior points, and then use the additivity of the integral over sets with volume.

  1. An interior point of a cell lies strictly between the planes that bound the cell in each direction. Let the cell be \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{n}-1}, z_{\mathrm{n}}]\) and \(P\) a point of it with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). Every ball around \(P\) with radius \(r\) contains the point \(P - \tfrac{r}{2}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), whose coordinate \(x\) is less than \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and which is therefore not in the cell. Such a point \(P\) is therefore not interior. The same holds for \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and for the other two coordinates.
  2. An interior point \(P\) of a cell \(C\) lies in no other cell \(C'\). The cell \(C'\) differs from \(C\) in at least one index, for instance in the index for \(x\), and has the interval \([x_{\mathrm{l}-1}, x_{\mathrm{l}}]\) with \(l \neq i\). The partition points increase, so for \(l < i\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{l}} \le x_{\mathrm{i}-1} < x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and for \(l > i\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{l}-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}} > x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and by step 1 \(P\) does not lie in \(C'\).
  3. Every cell is a box, so it is a set with volume (lemma 4.32, item 6), and it lies in \(D\). By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) is a set with volume.
  4. Let \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{m}}\) be different cells. By step 2 no interior point of either of them lies in the other. By lemma 4.54, item 3, therefore no interior point of either of the sets \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) and \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{m}})\) lies in the other.
  5. By lemma 4.32, item 4, \(Y\) is therefore a set with volume, and the integral of every function continuous on \(Y\) is the sum of the integrals over \(\Phi(C_1), \dots, \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  6. For \(f = 1\) we get the sum of volumes. In the plane the steps are the same, with rectangles and discs.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 137) uses that the images of rectangles overlap only in the images of their boundaries, which have measure zero.

Now we can compute the volume of the image under a linear map. For a matrix \(\mat A\) and points \(P_0\) and \(Q_0\) let us take the map that assigns to a point \(P\) the point

\[\Lambda(P) = Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P} ,\]

where we write the vector \(\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) as a column. It sends the point \(P_0\) to \(Q_0\) and multiplies the vector between two points by the matrix \(\mat A\): by the linearity of the product with a matrix (lemma 1.97), \(\overrightarrow{\Lambda(P)\Lambda(Q)} = \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q} - \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P} = \mat A\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\). We already know such maps. The sheared cube deformed by \(\Phi(P) = P + (0{,}001\,z_{\mathrm{P}}, 0, 0)\), which is \(\Lambda\) with \(P_0 = Q_0 = O\) and with the matrix \(\mat F\) that has the number \(0{,}001\) in the place \(xz\). The plate turned with the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\) moved by a \(\Lambda\) whose matrix is \(\mat R\). For these two the deformation gradient was the same at all points, because the displacement field was linear. Mathematics, however, keeps the name linear map for maps that send the zero vector to the zero vector (section 1.16.2), so a \(\Lambda\) that does not send the origin to the origin is not linear in this narrower sense. Where it matters, we will say so.

How will we compute the volume of the image? For an elementary matrix the image of a box is again a box, or a box tilted by a shear (figure 4.43). We compute the volume of the tilted box with a single iterated integral, because it is a body between the graphs of two linear functions. Then we fill a set with volume with the cells of a grid, which are boxes, and for other matrices we use the factorization of lemma 4.53.

Theorem 4.58 Volume under a linear map (prostornina pri linearni preslikavi)

Let \(\mat A\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with \(\det\mat A \neq 0\), let \(P_0\) and \(Q_0\) be points, and let the map \(\Lambda\) assign to a point \(P\) the point \(\Lambda(P) = Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). If \(W\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), then \(\Lambda(W)\) is also a set with volume, and

\[V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}} . \tag{4.30}\]

The same holds in the plane, for a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, with area instead of volume.

Proof

We must show that \(\Lambda(W)\) has a volume and that it is \(|\det\mat A|\) times the volume of the set \(W\). We compute the volume first for elementary matrices and shifts on boxes, then for every set with volume, and finally for every matrix with the factorization.

1. The map \(\Lambda\) has the properties of the inverse function theorem.

  1. Let \(P\) have the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\), the point \(P_0\) the coordinates \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(Q_0\) the coordinates \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(q_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(q_{\mathrm{z}}\). By (1.38) the components of the map are \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = q_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(x_{\mathrm{j}} - p_{\mathrm{j}})\), polynomials of degree one. Their partial derivatives are the constant numbers \(\partial\Lambda_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which are continuous. The map \(\Lambda\) is therefore continuously differentiable in the whole space, with the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat F_\Lambda = \mat A\) and with the Jacobian \(J_\Lambda = \det\mat A \neq 0\) (definition 4.42).
  2. The map \(\Lambda\) is one-to-one. If \(\Lambda(P) = \Lambda(Q)\), then \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{\Lambda(P)\Lambda(Q)} = \vek 0\), and since \(\det\mat A \neq 0\), lemma 2.53 on a zero determinant gives \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \vek 0\), so \(P = Q\).
  3. The whole space is an open set. By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Lambda(W)\) is therefore a set with volume.

2. Basic maps on a box.

  1. The basic maps are of two kinds. For an elementary matrix \(\mat E\) (definition 4.52), \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P) = O + \mat E\,\overrightarrow{OP}\), the point whose coordinates are \(\mat E\) times the coordinates of the point \(P\). Its factor is \(|\det\mat E|\). For a vector \(\vek w\), the shift is \(T_{\vek{w}}(P) = P + \vek w\). Its factor is \(1\). Both kinds have the form \(\Lambda\) of the theorem, the first with \(P_0 = Q_0 = O\), the second with the matrix \(\mat I\), \(P_0 = O\) and \(Q_0 = O + \vek w\), so the first part holds for them.
  2. Let \(K = [a_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{x}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{z}}, b_{\mathrm{z}}]\) be a box. Its volume as a set with volume is the school one, \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = (b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}})(b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}})(b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}})\), by lemma 4.32, item 6.
  3. Shift. The image \(T_{\vek{w}}(K)\) is the box \([a_{\mathrm{x}} + w_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{x}} + w_{\mathrm{x}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{y}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{z}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}, b_{\mathrm{z}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}]\) with the same lengths of the edges, so it has the volume \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  4. Swap of the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\). By lemma 4.53, item 1, the point \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) of the point \(P\) swapped. The image of the box is therefore the box with the intervals in the directions \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) swapped, with the same product of the lengths of the edges. The volume is \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = |{-1}|\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\) (lemma 4.53, item 2).
  5. Multiplication of the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) by \(c\). The point \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) equal to \(c\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the other two stay. When \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) runs over \([a_{\mathrm{i}}, b_{\mathrm{i}}]\), \(c\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\) runs over the interval \([c\,a_{\mathrm{i}}, c\,b_{\mathrm{i}}]\) for \(c > 0\), or \([c\,b_{\mathrm{i}}, c\,a_{\mathrm{i}}]\) for \(c < 0\), whose length is \(|c|\,(b_{\mathrm{i}} - a_{\mathrm{i}})\). The image of the box is therefore a box with the volume \(|c|\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  6. Addition of \(k\) times the coordinate \(\ix{j}\) to the coordinate \(\ix{i}\). Let \(\ix{l}\) be the third index. The point \(Q = \Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinates \(y_{\mathrm{j}} = x_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{l}} = x_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{i}} = x_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The point \(Q\) lies in the image of the box if and only if \(a_{\mathrm{j}} \le y_{\mathrm{j}} \le b_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{l}} \le y_{\mathrm{l}} \le b_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}} \le y_{\mathrm{i}} \le b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\). The image is therefore the body between the graphs of the functions \(a_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\) over the rectangle \([a_{\mathrm{j}}, b_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{l}}, b_{\mathrm{l}}]\), in which the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) runs between the graphs (definition 4.15). The functions are polynomials, continuously differentiable in the whole plane, and the first is smaller than the second. By theorem 4.33 the volume equals the iterated integral whose inner integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_\mathrm{i} + \mathrm{k}\,\mathrm{y}_\mathrm{j}}^{b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}} 1\,\mathrm{d}y_{\mathrm{i}} = b_{\mathrm{i}} - a_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the middle and outer integrals multiply this constant number by \(b_{\mathrm{j}} - a_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{l}} - a_{\mathrm{l}}\). The volume is \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

3. Basic maps on a set with volume.

  1. Let \(\Lambda'\) be a basic map with the factor \(\gamma\). Its inverse map \(\Lambda''\) is basic with the factor \(1/\gamma\): for \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}\) it is \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}^{-1}}\), because \(O + \mat E^{-1}\mat E\,\overrightarrow{OP} = P\), where \(\mat E^{-1}\) is elementary (lemma 4.53, item 3) with the determinant \(1/\det\mat E\) (theorem 2.52, because \(\det\mat E\,\det\mat E^{-1} = \det\mat I = 1\)), and for \(T_{\vek{w}}\) it is \(T_{-\vek{w}}\).
  2. Let \(W\) be a set with volume and \(\eta > 0\). By definition 4.30 with the function \(1\) there is a band \(\delta\) such that for every grid of a box containing \(W\) with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta\) the total volume \(S\) of the cells that lie in \(W\) is larger than \(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta\). We take such a grid.
  3. Let \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the cells that lie in \(W\). By the second part, \(\Lambda'(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) has the volume \(\gamma\,V_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l}}\). By the first part, \(\Lambda'\) has the properties of lemma 4.57 with \(D\) the whole space, so \(Y = \Lambda'(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Lambda'(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with the volume \(\gamma\,(V_{\mathrm{C}_1} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k}}) = \gamma\,S\).
  4. The cells \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) lie in \(W\), so \(Y\) lies in \(\Lambda'(W)\), which by the first part is a set with volume. By lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,S > \gamma\,(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta)\). If no cell lies in \(W\), then \(S = 0\), and the inequality holds because a volume is not negative (lemma 4.32, item 2, with the functions \(0 \le 1\)).
  5. Therefore \(\gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}} - V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} < \gamma\,\eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). By lemma 1.34, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  6. We use steps 2 to 5 for the inverse map \(\Lambda''\) with the factor \(1/\gamma\) and for the set with volume \(\Lambda'(W)\). Since \(\Lambda''(\Lambda'(W)) = W\), we get \(V_{\mathrm{W}} \ge V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})}/\gamma\). Together with step 5, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} = \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).

4. Any matrix.

  1. By lemma 4.53, item 4, \(\mat A = \mat E_1 \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) with elementary matrices \(\mat E_{\mathrm{l}}\). By item 1 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, used \((m - 1)\) times, \(\mat A\vek v = \mat E_1\big(\mat E_2(\cdots(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\vek v))\big)\), so \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) is the map \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}_\mathrm{m}}\) followed by \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}_{\mathrm{m}-1}}, \dots, \Lambda_{\mat{E}_1}\).
  2. By the third part, used \(m\) times, every intermediate image is a set with volume, and \(V_{\Lambda_{\mat{A}}(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat E_1| \cdots |\det\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. By theorem 2.52, used \((m - 1)\) times, \(\det\mat E_1 \cdots \det\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} = \det\mat A\), and the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values. Therefore \(V_{\Lambda_{\mat{A}}(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  4. The map \(\Lambda\) is the shift \(T_{-\overrightarrow{OP_0}}\) followed by \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) and the shift \(T_{\overrightarrow{OQ_0}}\). The shift \(T_{-\overrightarrow{OP_0}}\) sends \(P\) to the point \(O + \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\), \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) sends this point to \(O + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\), and the second shift to \(Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). The shifts keep the volume (third part with the factor \(1\)), so \(V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  5. In the plane the steps are the same, with \(2 \times 2\) matrices, rectangles and areas. We use lemma 2.53 and theorem 2.52 on \(3 \times 3\) matrices into which we put the \(2 \times 2\) matrices with \(1\) at the place \(zz\), as in section 2.10.2. In step 6 of the second part the image of a rectangle is a region between the graphs of two linear functions, whose area theorem 4.33 in the plane gives.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 10.7.1 (PDF p. 134) for rectangles, whose proof the source leaves to the reader (Exercise 10.7.1, PDF p. 137) with the hint that the proof for elementary matrices is enough. The proof is not from the source.

The proof used the same idea twice. Since for the volume we only have an inequality from the cells that lie in the set, we only got \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\). The reverse inequality came from the same inequality for the inverse map. We will take the same route in section 4.3.4. The second idea is the factorization: for elementary matrices the image of a box is again a box or a tilted box, whose volume we compute with a single integral.

Let us now answer the two questions from the beginning of the section. The parallelepiped spanned from a point \(P\) by the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) with \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) \neq 0\) is the image of the unit cube \([0, 1]^3\) under \(\Lambda(Q) = P + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{OQ}\), where the matrix \(\mat A\) has the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\). The point \((s, t, w)\) of the cube goes to \(P + s\,\vek a + t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c\), as in section 2.10.2. By the theorem the parallelepiped is a set with volume, and its volume is \(|\det\mat A| \cdot 1 = |\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|\), exactly the school volume of lemma 2.47. The two volumes therefore agree, and what we took from school in chapter 2 now holds as a theorem. A flattened parallelepiped with determinant zero is not covered by the theorem, and we will not need it.

The second test is a set with a curved boundary. Let us take the cross section of the round hanging bar, a disc with the radius \(5\) mm and the area \(78{,}54\) mm², and the \(2 \times 2\) matrix with the columns \((3, 1)\) and \((1, 2)\) and the determinant \(5\) of figure 2.58. The image of the disc is an ellipse, which should have the area \(5 \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 392{,}70\ \text{mm}^2\) (figure 4.44). Let us check with the definition of area: with NumPy we added up, for grids with square cells of edge \(h\) whose division points are the multiples of \(h\), the areas of the cells that lie in the ellipse.

\(h\) in mm \(1\) \(0{,}5\) \(0{,}25\) \(0{,}1\) \(0{,}05\)
area of the cells in the ellipse in mm² \(348{,}0\) \(368{,}5\) \(379{,}9\) \(387{,}2\) \(390{,}0\)

The sums approach \(392{,}70\) mm², as the theorem says. Why so slowly? The cells in the ellipse do not cover a narrow band along the boundary of the ellipse. A point of the ellipse that is farther from the boundary than the diagonal of a cell, \(h\sqrt2\), lies in a cell that is entirely in the ellipse, so the band is narrower than \(h\sqrt2\). For half the \(h\) the band is half as wide, and the missing area roughly halves: for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm \(5{,}5\) mm² is missing, for \(h = 0{,}05\) mm \(2{,}7\) mm².

For the sheared cube the matrix is elementary, with determinant \(1\), and the theorem says that the volume of the cube after the shear is exactly \(1000\) mm³, as we found for small pieces in section 2.10.5. For the turned plate the determinant of the matrix \(\mat R\) is \(1\), and every shape on the plate has the same area after the rotation as before it, whatever its form.

4.3.4 Change of variables in an integral

Now we can write down the rule we need. Let \(\Phi\) be a map that is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on an open set \(D\) and has a nonzero Jacobian at every point, and let \(W\) be a set with volume in \(D\). What is the volume of the set \(\Phi(W)\), and how do we integrate a function over it if we know how to integrate over \(W\)? For the deformation of a body, \(W\) is a part of the body before loading, \(\Phi(W)\) the same part after it, and the question is what its volume after loading is.

The idea is old. We cut the set \(W\) with a grid into small cubes with the edge \(h\). Near a point \(P_0\) of a cube, theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, applied to each component, gives \(\Phi(P) \approx \Phi(P_0) + \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). On the cube \(\Phi\) therefore behaves almost like the map \(\Lambda\) of theorem 4.58 with the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P_0)\), which sends the cube to a parallelepiped with the volume \(|J_\Phi(P_0)|\,h^3\). The integral of a function \(f\) over \(\Phi(W)\) is therefore roughly the sum of the numbers \(f(\Phi(P_0))\,|J_\Phi(P_0)|\,h^3\) over the cubes, and this is a sum that approaches the integral of the function \(f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\) over \(W\).

The proof must handle two things that the idea passes over. First, the cubes at the boundary of the set \(W\) do not lie entirely in \(W\). These are the boundary cells, and their total volume is small by lemma 4.29. Second, the image of a cube is not a parallelepiped. It lies, however, in a slightly enlarged parallelepiped, because the partial derivatives change only a little on a small cube (figure 4.45). This gives only an inequality: the integral over \(\Phi(W)\) is not larger than the integral over \(W\). We get the reverse inequality from the same inequality for the inverse map \(\Psi\), just as for theorem 4.58 we got the reverse inequality with the inverse map. This is the route of LEBL2 (Theorem 10.7.2, PDF pp. 134-137).

Theorem 4.59 Change of variables theorem (izrek o zamenjavi spremenljivk)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\). Let \(W \subseteq D\) be a set with volume (definition 4.27). Then \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(\Phi(W)\),

\[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\big|J_\Phi(P)\big|\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.31}\]

In particular \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds in the plane, for a map that has a point of the plane as input and as output, with a set with area \(W\), with areas and with \(\mathrm{d}A\) instead of \(\mathrm{d}V\).

Proof

We must show that \(\Phi(W)\) has a volume and that both inequalities between the sides of (4.31) hold. First we bound the volume of the image of a small cube, then we prove the inequality \(\le\) for nonnegative functions, the reverse inequality with the inverse map, and finally we pass to any function.

1. The set \(\Phi(W)\) and the integral on the right.

  1. By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.
  2. The function \(J_\Phi\) is a sum of products of partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\Phi\) ((2.51)), which are continuous on \(D\), so by corollary 1.69, item 1, it is continuous on \(D\). Also \(|J_\Phi|\) is continuous. By lemma 1.6 on the triangle inequality, item 1, we have \(|a| \le |a - b| + |b|\) and \(|b| \le |b - a| + |a|\), so \(\big||a| - |b|\big| \le |a - b|\) for any two numbers \(a\) and \(b\). The function \(P \mapsto f(\Phi(P))\) is continuous on \(W\) by lemma 4.35. The integrand on the right is a product of continuous functions and is continuous on \(W\), so the integral on the right exists (theorem 4.31).
  3. If \(W\) is empty, so is \(\Phi(W)\), and both sides are zero, because no cell lies in the empty set. Let \(W\) be nonempty.

2. Constants.

  1. By lemma 4.55 for \(K = W\) there are \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) such that the set \(W_\rho\) of points at a distance of at most \(\rho\) from some point of \(W\) is closed, bounded and in \(D\), and that on it all partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are at most \(M\) in absolute value.
  2. The function \(|J_\Phi|\) is continuous and positive on \(W_\rho\). By theorem 1.78, the extreme value theorem in space, it attains on \(W_\rho\) a least value \(m_{\mathrm{J}} > 0\) and a greatest value \(M_{\mathrm{J}}\).
  3. By theorem 2.54 the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)\) for \(Q \in W_\rho\) has an inverse matrix whose rows are vector products of the columns divided by \(J_\Phi(Q)\). Every element of a vector product is a difference of two products of two elements of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)\), so it is at most \(2M^2\) in absolute value. Every element of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)^{-1}\) is therefore at most \(N = 2M^2/m_{\mathrm{J}}\) in absolute value.
  4. By theorem 4.6, applied to each of the nine partial derivatives on \(W_\rho\), for every \(\omega > 0\) there is \(\delta_\omega > 0\) such that \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q) - \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q')| < \omega\) for all \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and for any two points \(Q, Q' \in W_\rho\) with \(|QQ'| < \delta_\omega\). For \(\delta_\omega\) we take the smallest of the nine bands.

3. The image of a small cube.

Let \(\omega > 0\) and \(\kappa = 9\sqrt3\,N\omega\). Let \(C\) be a cube with edges parallel to the axes, of length \(h\), where \(\sqrt3\,h\) is less than \(\rho\) and than \(\delta_\omega\), that contains some point of the set \(W\), and let \(P_0\) be any point of the cube \(C\). Let us show that \(C\) lies in \(D\) and that

\[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C})} \le |J_\Phi(P_0)|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3\,h^3 .\]
  1. Two points of the cube differ by at most \(h\) in each coordinate, so by (1.10) they are at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h\). Every point of the cube is therefore at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h < \rho\) from the point of the set \(W\) in the cube and lies in \(W_\rho \subseteq D\). The cube is a set with volume (lemma 4.32, item 6), so by lemma 4.56 also \(\Phi(C)\) is a set with volume.
  2. Let \(\mat A = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\) and \(\mat B = \mat A^{-1}\), whose elements are at most \(N\) in absolute value. Let \(\Lambda(Q) = \Phi(P_0) + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q}\), the map of theorem 4.58, and \(G(P) = P_0 + \mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)}\) for \(P \in D\). Then
    \[\Lambda\big(G(P)\big) = \Phi(P_0) + \mat A\mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)} = \Phi(P) ,\]
    because \(\overrightarrow{P_0 G(P)} = \mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)}\) and \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\). Therefore \(\Phi(C) = \Lambda(G(C))\).
  3. The components of the map \(G\) are \(G_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{P}_0, \mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\big(\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}(P) - \Phi_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0)\big)\), where \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0, \mathrm{i}}\) is the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) of the point \(P_0\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81, items 1 and 2), applied to a partial derivative as to a derivative with respect to one variable, \(\partial G_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), and these derivatives are continuous on \(D\).
  4. Let \(H(P) = \overrightarrow{P\,G(P)}\), a vector field with the components \(H_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = G_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - x_{\mathrm{i}}\). Since \(\sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P_0) = (\mat B\mat A)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\),
    \[\frac{\partial H_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) - \delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) - \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_0)\Big) .\]
  5. For \(P \in C\) the points \(P\) and \(P_0\) are in \(W_\rho\) and at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h < \delta_\omega\), so every bracket in step 4 is less than \(\omega\) in absolute value, and \(|\partial H_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)| \le 3N\omega\).
  6. The cube contains the segment between any two of its points, because the coordinates of the points of the segment lie between the coordinates of the endpoints. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, applied to the map \(P \mapsto O + H(P)\), whose components are \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\), on the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P \in C\), \(|H(P) - H(P_0)| \le 9N\omega\,|P_0 P| \le 9\sqrt3\,N\omega\,h = \kappa h\). Since \(G(P_0) = P_0\), we have \(H(P_0) = \vek 0\), so \(|\overrightarrow{P\,G(P)}| \le \kappa h\).
  7. Every coordinate of the point \(G(P)\) therefore differs from the same coordinate of the point \(P\) by at most \(\kappa h\). Let \(\tilde C\) be the cube obtained from \(C\) by extending each of its intervals by \(\kappa h\) on both sides. Its edge is \((1 + 2\kappa)\,h\), and \(G(C) \subseteq \tilde C\).
  8. By step 2, \(\Phi(C) = \Lambda(G(C)) \subseteq \Lambda(\tilde C)\). By theorem 4.58, \(\Lambda(\tilde C)\) is a set with the volume \(|\det\mat A|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3 h^3 = |J_\Phi(P_0)|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3 h^3\), and by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C})}\) is at most that.

4. The inequality \(\le\) for a nonnegative function.

Let \(f \ge 0\) be continuous on \(\Phi(W)\) and \(g(P) = f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\) for \(P \in W\). Let us show that \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\).

  1. The set \(\Phi(W)\) is closed, bounded and nonempty, so by theorem 1.78 \(f\) attains on it a greatest value \(\mu\).
  2. We choose \(\eta\) with \(0 < \eta \le 1\) and take \(\omega = \eta/(9\sqrt3\,N)\), so that \(\kappa = \eta\). By definition 4.30 for \(g\) on \(W\) there is a band \(\delta_1\), and by lemma 4.29, item 3, a band \(\delta_2\) such that for every grid of a box containing \(W\) with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta_2\) the total volume of the boundary cells is less than \(\eta\).
  3. The set \(W\) is bounded, so it lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) for some \(R > 0\). By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(h = 2R/n\) is less than \(\delta_1\) and than \(\delta_2\) and that \(\sqrt3\,h\) is less than \(\rho\) and than \(\delta_\omega\). We divide every edge of the cube \([-R, R]^3\) into \(n\) equal pieces. The cells of this grid are cubes with the edge \(h\).
  4. We denote the cells that lie in \(W\) by \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\), and the boundary cells, which contain a point of the set \(W\) and a point outside it, by \(C'_1, \dots, C'_{\mathrm{k}'}\). Every point of the set \(W\) lies in some cell, which therefore contains a point of the set \(W\) and is of one of these two kinds. So \(W\) lies in the union \(U\) of all these cells. By the first step of the third part they all lie in \(D\).
  5. The function \(P \mapsto f(\Phi(P))\) is continuous on \(C_{\mathrm{l}} \subseteq W\), so by theorem 1.78 it attains its greatest value on \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) at some point \(P_{\mathrm{l}} \in C_{\mathrm{l}}\). This is also the greatest value of the function \(f\) on \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\). The sum \(S = \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} g(P_{\mathrm{l}})\,h^3\) is a sum of definition 4.30, so \(S < \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + \eta\).
  6. By lemma 4.57, \(\Phi(U)\) is a set with the volume \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{U})} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} + \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}'_\mathrm{l})}\), and the set \(Y = \Phi(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with the volume \(V_{\mathrm{Y}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})}\), over which the integral of the function \(f\) is the sum of the integrals over \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\). If no cell lies in \(W\), \(Y\) is empty, and \(V_{\mathrm{Y}}\), the integral over \(Y\) and the sum \(S\) are zero.
  7. The set \(\Phi(W)\) lies in \(\Phi(U)\), so by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} \le V_{\Phi(\mathrm{U})}\), and
    \[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}} \le \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k'} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}'_\mathrm{l})} .\]
  8. The cells \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) lie in \(W\), so \(Y\) lies in \(\Phi(W)\). The function \(\mu - f\) is continuous and nowhere negative on \(\Phi(W)\), so by the same item of the same lemma \(\int_{\mathrm{Y}} (\mu - f)\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} (\mu - f)\,\mathrm{d}V\). By linearity (lemma 4.32, item 1), with \(\int \mu\,\mathrm{d}V = \mu\) times the volume, we rearrange this into
    \[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \mu\,\big(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}}\big) + \int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  9. The first term. By step 7 and the third part with the point \(P_0\) in the cell \(C'_{\mathrm{l}}\),
    \[\mu\,\big(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}}\big) \le \mu\,M_{\mathrm{J}}\,(1 + 2\eta)^3 \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k'} h^3 \le \mu\,M_{\mathrm{J}}\,(1 + 2\eta)^3\,\eta ,\]
    because the total volume of the boundary cells is less than \(\eta\).
  10. The second term. On \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) we have \(f \le f(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}}))\), so by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le f(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}}))\,V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})}\). By the third part with \(P_0 = P_{\mathrm{l}}\), \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} \le |J_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}})|\,(1 + 2\eta)^3 h^3\). By step 6 and step 5 therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le (1 + 2\eta)^3 \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} g(P_{\mathrm{l}})\,h^3 = (1 + 2\eta)^3 S < (1 + 2\eta)^3\Big(\int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + \eta\Big) .\]
  11. Let \(I = \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\), which is not negative (lemma 4.32, item 2), and \(c = 1 + \mu M_{\mathrm{J}}\). From steps 8 to 10, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V < (1 + 2\eta)^3\,(I + c\,\eta)\). Since \(\eta \le 1\), \((1 + 2\eta)^3 = 1 + 6\eta + 12\eta^2 + 8\eta^3 \le 1 + 26\eta\), and
    \[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - I < (1 + 26\eta)(I + c\,\eta) - I = \eta\,\big(26 I + c + 26\,c\,\eta\big) \le \eta\,(26 I + 27 c) .\]
  12. This holds for every \(\eta \le 1\), so the difference \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - I\) is less than every positive number: for a given number \(\varepsilon' > 0\) we take \(\eta\) smaller than \(1\) and than \(\varepsilon'/(26 I + 27 c)\). By lemma 1.34, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le I\).

5. The reverse inequality.

  1. Let \(E = \Phi(D)\) and \(\Psi\) the inverse map. By theorem 4.51, \(E\) is open, \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\), and \(J_\Psi(\Phi(P)) = 1/J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\). As in step 5 of the proof of lemma 4.54, \(\Psi\) is one-to-one on \(E\). The set \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume in \(E\), and \(\Psi(\Phi(W)) = W\).
  2. The function \(g\) of the fourth part is continuous and nowhere negative on \(W = \Psi(\Phi(W))\). The fourth part, applied to the map \(\Psi\), the set \(\Phi(W)\) and the function \(g\), gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} g\big(\Psi(Q)\big)\,\big|J_\Psi(Q)\big|\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  3. For \(Q = \Phi(P)\) we have \(g(\Psi(Q))\,|J_\Psi(Q)| = f(Q)\,|J_\Phi(P)| \cdot 1/|J_\Phi(P)| = f(Q)\). The right side is therefore \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). Together with the fourth part, (4.31) holds for every continuous function \(f \ge 0\).

6. Any continuous function.

  1. By theorem 1.78, \(f\) has a least value \(m\) on \(\Phi(W)\). The function \(f - m\) is continuous and nowhere negative, so by the fifth part (4.31) holds for \(f - m\), and for the constant function \(1\) we get \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. By the linearity of the integral on both sides, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - m\,V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\,\mathrm{d}V - m\int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\). The subtracted terms are equal by step 1, so (4.31) holds.
  3. In the plane the steps are the same, with squares instead of cubes, with \(\sqrt2\) instead of \(\sqrt3\), with areas and with the power \(2\) instead of \(3\). In the second part \(N = M/m_{\mathrm{J}}\), because by lemma 4.49 the elements of the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix are elements of the matrix or their opposites, divided by the determinant, the partial derivatives of the field \(H\) are at most \(2N\omega\) in absolute value, lemma 4.47 in the plane gives \(|H(P) - H(P_0)| \le 4N\omega\,|P_0 P|\), and \(\kappa = 4\sqrt2\,N\omega\).

Source: LEBL2 Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF pp. 134-137), with the integral from lower and upper sums and with a function \(f\) that is only integrable. KREYSZIG §10.3, (6) and (7) (PDF pp. 455-456), in the plane, without proof. The proof follows LEBL2: the image of a small rectangle in an enlarged rectangle, the inequality for \(g\), and the reverse inequality with the inverse map. The work with boundary cells instead of extending the function \(f\) by zero is not from the source.

The proof showed where the absolute value of the Jacobian comes from. On a small cube the map behaves almost like its linear part, and by theorem 4.58 this multiplies volume by \(|J_\Phi|\). Everything else was careful counting of errors: the uniform continuity of the partial derivatives gave an enlarged parallelepiped that is the same for all cubes, the lemma on boundary cells bounded the part at the boundary, and the inverse map gave the reverse inequality. For a linear map \(\Lambda\) the value \(|J_\Lambda| = |\det\mat A|\) is constant, and (4.31) with the function \(1\) gives \(V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\), theorem 4.58.

Let us test the theorem in the plane on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s,\ t + s^2)\) of section 4.3.2, on the square \(W = [0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and with the function \(f(x, y) = y\) (figure 4.35). The matrix of partial derivatives has the rows \((1, 0)\) and \((2s, 1)\), so \(J_\Phi = 1\). The image of the square is the region between the graphs of the functions \(x^2\) and \(x^2 + 1\) over the interval \([0, 1]\). The vertical segments of the square only move up by \(s^2\), so the area does not change. The left side of (4.31) is, by theorem 4.33, the iterated integral

\[\int_0^1 \int_{\mathrm{x}^2}^{x^2 + 1} y\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^1 \frac{(x^2 + 1)^2 - x^4}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^1 \Big(x^2 + \frac12\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac56 ,\]

and the right side is

\[\int_0^1 \int_0^1 (t + s^2) \cdot 1\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_0^1 \Big(\frac12 + s^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac56 .\]

We checked both with SymPy. The function \(f(x, y) = y\) is the height of a point, and the integral is the area times the mean height. Every vertical segment of the square rises by \(s^2\), so the mean height grows from \(\tfrac12\) by the mean of the number \(s^2\) on \([0, 1]\), which is \(\tfrac13\).

We will first use the theorem in the next two subsections. In the first we answer with it the question of chapter 2 of how the volume of a piece of a body near a point changes. In the second we use its plane version to show that the surface integral does not depend on how we describe the surface, when a suitable map joins the two descriptions. Then in section 4.3.7 we prove with it the divergence theorem for bodies that we get when we bend a box continuously.

4.3.5 The volume of a small piece after loading

In chapter 2, section 2.10.5, we drew three short fibres with the vectors \(h\,\vek a\), \(h\,\vek b\) and \(h\,\vek c\) from a point \(P\) of a body and showed that the ratio of the volume of the parallelepiped of the vectors \(\mat F(h\,\vek a)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek b)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek c)\) to the volume of the piece before loading is exactly the Jacobian \(J = \det\mat F\) at the point \(P\). The true piece after loading, however, is not this parallelepiped, because its edges curve slightly. On the hanging bar we saw with numbers that the ratio of volumes approaches \(J\) for ever shorter fibres, but we did not prove a general statement, because it needs the volume of a body with curved faces and the rule for a change of variables. Now we have both.

Let us set up the model. Before loading the body is a set of points contained in an open set \(D\) on which the displacement field \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable (definition 1.90). A point \(P\) goes after loading to the point \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\), and we call the map \(\Phi\) the deformation. Its components are \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), with the indices \(\ix{i}\) running over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) as in section 1.18.4, so \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\).
