The matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\Phi\) is the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) (definition 1.110), and its Jacobian is \(J = \det\mat F\) of lemma 2.55 on the change of volume. We assume two things. The deformation is one-to-one: two different points of the material are not at the same point after loading, which means that the material does not pass through itself. And \(J > 0\) at every point of \(D\). Why this is physically justified is said by corollary 2.58 on the positive Jacobian: for gradual loading in which the material nowhere collapses to nothing, \(J\) is positive.

Corollary 4.60 Volume of a small piece after loading (prostornina majhnega koščka po obremenitvi)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, the displacement field \(\vek u\) continuously differentiable on \(D\), the deformation \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\) one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45), and \(J(P) = \det\big(\mat I + \mat H(P)\big) > 0\) for every point \(P \in D\).

  1. For every set with volume \(W \subseteq D\), \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume and
    \[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.32}\]
  2. Let \(P \in D\). For every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(r > 0\) such that for every set with volume \(W\) with \(V_{\mathrm{W}} > 0\) all of whose points are closer to \(P\) than \(r\),
    \[\Big| \frac{V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}}{V_{\mathrm{W}}} - J(P) \Big| < \eta .\]
  3. In particular, for the cube \(K_{\mathrm{h}}\) with centre \(P\) and edge \(h\), with edges parallel to the axes, for every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{h})}/h^3 - J(P)| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\).
Proof

We must show three items. The first is the change of variables theorem with the function \(1\), the other two follow from the continuity of the function \(J\) at \(P\).

  1. The components of the deformation \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\) have the partial derivatives \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), which are continuous on \(D\). The map \(\Phi\) is therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat F_\Phi = \mat I + \mat H\) and with the Jacobian \(J_\Phi = J\) (definition 4.42).
  2. By assumption \(\Phi\) is one-to-one and \(J_\Phi = J > 0\). By theorem 4.59, the change of variables theorem, with the function \(f = 1\), \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume and \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J|\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V\). This is item 1.
  3. The function \(J\) is a sum of products of continuous partial derivatives ((2.51)), and by corollary 1.69, item 1, it is continuous at \(P\). For \(\eta > 0\) there is therefore \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|J(Q) - J(P)| < \eta/2\) for every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\). Since \(D\) is open, there is \(r_0 > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r_0\) are in \(D\). Let \(r\) be smaller than the numbers \(\delta\) and \(r_0\).
  4. Let \(W\) be a set with volume with \(V_{\mathrm{W}} > 0\) all of whose points are closer to \(P\) than \(r\). Then \(W\) lies in \(D\), and on \(W\) we have \(J(P) - \eta/2 < J < J(P) + \eta/2\). By lemma 4.32, items 1 and 2,
    \[\Big(J(P) - \frac\eta2\Big)\,V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V \le \Big(J(P) + \frac\eta2\Big)\,V_{\mathrm{W}} .\]
  5. By item 1 the middle term is \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}\). We divide by the positive number \(V_{\mathrm{W}}\) and get \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}/V_{\mathrm{W}} - J(P)| \le \eta/2 < \eta\). This is item 2.
  6. The cube \(K_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a set with the volume \(h^3 > 0\) (lemma 4.32, item 6). Its points differ from \(P\) in each coordinate by at most \(h/2\), so they are at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h/2\) from \(P\). Let \(\delta = r\) of step 3. For \(0 < h < \delta\) we have \(\sqrt3\,h/2 < h < r\), and by item 2, \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{h})}/h^3 - J(P)| < \eta\). This is item 3.

Source: CM (3.3.18)-(3.3.20) (PDF pp. 125-126), where \(\mathrm{d}v = J\,\mathrm{d}V\) is written for a parallelepiped of the vectors \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf X\), and CM (5.2.34), (5.2.35) (PDF p. 220), where the integral of the density over the body after loading is written, with \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = J\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf X\), as an integral over the body before loading. BOWER §2.1.4 (PDF pp. 46-47): \(\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}V_0 = \det\mathbf F = J\). The proof is not from the sources.

The corollary says what in chapter 2 we saw only on an example, now for every piece and every continuously differentiable displacement field with a one-to-one deformation and a positive Jacobian. Which pieces? Every set with volume that lies close enough to the point \(P\): a cube with centre \(P\), a cube with a corner at \(P\), and also the parallelepiped spanned from \(P\) by the fibres \(h\,\vek a\), \(h\,\vek b\) and \(h\,\vek c\), which by theorem 4.58 is a set with the volume \(h^3\,|\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)|\). The same holds for a ball around \(P\), once we have shown in section 4.3.7 that it is a set with volume. When the piece shrinks to the point \(P\), the ratio of the volumes after and before loading approaches \(J(P)\), whatever the shape of the piece. The first item says even more: the volume of every part of the body after loading is the integral of the Jacobian over this part before loading. The Jacobian is the density with which volumes add up.

Let us test this on the hanging bar of section 2.10.5. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with the radius of the cross section \(r = 5\) mm hangs under its own weight and is held in an idealized way: only the centre \(O\) of the top face is fixed, and the face is pulled up evenly by a force that carries the weight (section 1.7.1). The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down. The displacement field (1.18) is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Let us first check the assumptions of the corollary. For \(D\) we take the open box \((-1\ \text{m}, 11\ \text{m}) \times (-1\ \text{m}, 1\ \text{m}) \times (-1\ \text{m}, 1\ \text{m})\), which contains the bar. The components of the field are polynomials, so they are continuously differentiable. The partial derivatives are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,z\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,z\), and the others are zero. In \(D\) we have \(|L - x| < 11\) m and \(|y|, |z| < 1\) m, so all of them are less than \(g = 2a \cdot 11\ \text{m} = 4{,}294 \cdot 10^{-6}\) in absolute value.

  1. The deformation is one-to-one on \(D\). The box \(D\) contains the segment between any two of its points. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, applied to the map \(P \mapsto O + \vek u(P)\), whose components are \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(|\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)| \le 3g\,|PQ|\). Since \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)} - \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big)\), corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors gives \(|PQ| \le |\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)| + 3g\,|PQ|\), so \(|\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)| \ge (1 - 3g)\,|PQ|\). For \(P \neq Q\) this is positive, so \(\Phi(P) \neq \Phi(Q)\).
  2. \(J > 0\) on \(D\). By lemma 2.55, item 2, \(J\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), and the sum of the diagonal elements is at most \(3g\) in absolute value. Therefore \(J \ge 1 - 3g - 6g^2 - 6g^3 = 0{,}9999871\dots > 0\).

Now let us take the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\), where \(J(P) - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and the cube with a corner at \(P\) and edges of length \(h\) along the axes, as spanned by the fibres in section 2.10.5. We computed its volume after loading by (4.32) with SymPy, as the integral of the polynomial \(J\) over the cube. The table gives the ratios of the volumes after and before loading, reduced by \(1\), exactly and by the estimates of chapter 2:

\(h = 1\) mm \(h = 0{,}1\) mm
exact ratio \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K})}/h^3\), reduced by \(1\) \(7{,}80720 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(7{,}80790 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
difference from \(J(P) - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(-7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-11}\) \(-7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\)
parallelepiped of the fibres after loading, reduced by \(1\) \(7{,}80603 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(7{,}80779 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
difference from \(J(P) - 1\) \(-1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-10}\) \(-1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-11}\)

The exact ratio approaches \(J(P)\), as item 2 of the corollary says, and the difference becomes ten times smaller with a ten times smaller edge (figure 4.46). Where does this difference come from? By (4.32) the ratio is the mean of the function \(J\) over the cube. Its main part is \(J - 1 \approx 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\), the divergence of the field, which we computed in section 4.2.5, and it decreases with depth. The cube with a corner at \(P\) lies below \(P\), between the depths \(5\) m and \(5\ \text{m} + h\), so the mean equals the value at the depth \(5\ \text{m} + h/2\), which is \(0{,}8\,a\,h/2\) less than the value at \(P\). For \(h = 1\) mm this is \(0{,}8 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}0005 = 7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-11}\), exactly the difference in the table. For the cube with centre \(P\) and edge \(1\) mm SymPy gave a difference of only \(-4 \cdot 10^{-21}\), because \(J\) is almost a linear function, and the mean of a linear function over a cube is its value at the centre. The parallelepiped of the fibres of chapter 2 is a different set: it is not the image of the cube but the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors of the fibres after loading. Its difference is different, but it also goes to zero.

Finally the whole bar. It is cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), so it is a set with volume (corollary 4.34, item 2). Its volume before loading is \(L A = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3\), with the area of the cross section \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) of section 4.2.8. The volume after loading is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} J\,\mathrm{d}V\) by (4.32), so by linearity the change of volume is the integral of the function \(J - 1\) over the bar. SymPy gave

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} (J - 1)\,\mathrm{d}V = 0{,}6132369\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

In section 4.2.12 we computed the change of volume of the bar with the divergence theorem as the flux of the displacements through the surface and got \(0{,}6132\ \text{mm}^3\), with SymPy to more digits \(0{,}6132389\ \text{mm}^3\), which is the integral of the divergence \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). That computation was an approximation for small displacements: the flux \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) is only approximately the volume swept by a patch. The difference between the two numbers is \(0{,}6132369\ \text{mm}^3 - 0{,}6132389\ \text{mm}^3 = -2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm}^3\). By (2.56), \(J - 1\) differs from the divergence by the second bracket and the term \(\det\mat H\), the terms with products of two and three partial derivatives, so \(-2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm}^3\) is the integral of these terms. These are of the size \(a^2 L^2 \approx 4 \cdot 10^{-12}\), so the difference is smaller than the change itself by a factor of the order \(10^{-6}\). The exact change of volume is \(J - 1\) integrated over the body, and the divergence is its main part for small displacements.

4.3.6 Surfaces described by two parameters

In section 4.2.11 we integrated over the pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs. We described each piece with the two variables given by the description of the body: the top lid by the points \((x, y, h(x, y))\), the side piece in the plane \(x = a\) by the points \((a, y, z)\). The question remained whether the surface integral does not depend on how we describe the same surface. The part of the plane \(y = 3\) mm between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round bar is a side piece for the piece \(C\) and the bottom lid for the piece \(D\). In section 4.2.12 we checked the agreement of the two descriptions of this cut directly, because they gave the same iterated integral. In section 4.3.7, however, we will need surfaces that are not graphs over a rectangle, the surfaces of curved bodies, and there such a direct comparison will not be possible.

So we describe a surface more generally. A point of the surface is fixed by two numbers \(s\) and \(t\), which we call parameters (parametra), as the numbers \(x\) and \(y\) fix a point of a lid. The pair \((s, t)\) is a point of the plane of parameters, and the map \(\vek r\) assigns to it the position vector \(\vek r(s, t)\) of a point of the surface, the vector from the origin \(O\) to it, with the components \(r_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t)\), \(r_{\mathrm{y}}(s, t)\) and \(r_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t)\). We get the area of a small patch as for a lid (figure 4.47). A small rectangle of the plane of parameters with the sides \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta t\) goes to a patch that is almost a parallelogram spanned by the vectors \(\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\,\Delta s\) and \(\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t}\,\Delta t\), where \(\partial\vek r/\partial s\) is the vector of the partial derivatives of the components with respect to \(s\). By section 2.8.1 the area of the parallelogram is the length of the vector product of the sides, \(|\vek N|\,\Delta s\,\Delta t\) with \(\vek N = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t}\), and this vector is perpendicular to both sides, so to the patch.

Definition 4.61 Surface described by two parameters (ploskev, opisana s parametroma)

Let \(M\) be a set with area (definition 4.27) in the plane whose points we write with the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\), and \(U\) an open set of this plane that contains \(M\). Let \(\vek r\) be a map that has as input a point \((s, t)\) of \(U\) and as output the vector \(\vek r(s, t) = \big(r_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t), r_{\mathrm{y}}(s, t), r_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t)\big)\), and that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(U\). At every point of the set \(M\) let

\[\vek N = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t} \neq \vek 0 . \tag{4.33}\]

The set \(S\) of the points with the position vectors \(\vek r(s, t)\), \((s, t) \in M\), is a surface described by two parameters (ploskev, opisana s parametroma), the map \(\vek r\) on \(M\) is its description, and \(\vek N\) its normal vector (normalni vektor). For a function \(f\) that is continuous on \(S\), the surface integral (ploskovni integral) over \(S\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{M}} f\big(\vek r(s, t)\big)\,\big|\vek N(s, t)\big|\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.34}\]

where \(f(\vek r(s, t))\) means the value of the function \(f\) at the point with the position vector \(\vek r(s, t)\). For a vector field \(\vek v\) that is continuous on \(S\), the flux (pretok) through \(S\) in the direction of the vector \(\vek N\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{M}} \vek v\big(\vek r(s, t)\big)\cdot\vek N(s, t)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.35}\]

Source: KREYSZIG §10.5, (2), (4) (PDF pp. 466-467) for the description of a surface and the normal vector, §10.6, (3) (PDF p. 469) for the flux and (6), (8) (PDF p. 474) for the surface integral of a function and the area of a surface. KREYSZIG does not demand that the map be one-to-one and integrates only over a rectangle or a region of the plane.

The definition says what goes in. The set \(M\) is a part of the plane of parameters, and the map \(\vek r\) sends it onto the surface. Why do we demand that the map be one-to-one? So that the map covers no part of the surface twice. The map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s^2, t, 0)\) on the rectangle \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\) sends the points \((s, t)\) and \((-s, t)\) to the same point, and covers the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) in the plane \(z = 0\) twice. The integral (4.34) would then count every point twice. Why \(\vek N \neq \vek 0\)? So that the surface has at every point a normal \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\), as a lid has in definition 4.36. The flux (4.35) is the integral of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) by (4.34), since \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N| = \vek v\cdot\vek N\), as we saw for a lid in lemma 4.37. The direction of the vector \(\vek N\) depends on the order of the parameters. When we exchange \(s\) and \(t\), the vector \(\vek N\) turns around by item 1 of lemma 2.31, and the flux changes sign.

Let us state exactly that the integrals exist.

Lemma 4.62 Existence of the surface integral (obstoj ploskovnega integrala)

Let \(S\) be a surface with the description \(\vek r\) on the set \(M\) (definition 4.61), \(f\) a function continuous on \(S\), and \(\vek v\) a field continuous on \(S\). Then the functions under the integrals in (4.34) and (4.35) are continuous on \(M\), and both integrals exist.

Proof

We must show that the integrands are continuous and use the theorem on the existence of the integral.

  1. The components of the map \(\vek r\) are continuously differentiable on \(U\), so they are continuous (lemma 1.91 in the plane). By lemma 4.35 the function \((s, t) \mapsto f(\vek r(s, t))\) is continuous on \(M\), and so are the components of the field \(\vek v\) at the points of the surface.
  2. The components of the vector \(\vek N\) are differences of products of the partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\vek r\), which are continuous, so by corollary 1.69, item 1, they are continuous.
  3. The length \(|\vek N|\) is continuous. By corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 3, \(\big||\vek N(s, t)| - |\vek N(s_1, t_1)|\big| \le |\vek N(s, t) - \vek N(s_1, t_1)|\). The length of a vector is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of its components (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.66), and by step 2 these are arbitrarily small when the point \((s_1, t_1)\) is close enough to the point \((s, t)\).
  4. The integrands are products and sums of continuous functions and are continuous on \(M\). The set \(M\) has an area, so by theorem 4.31 the integrals exist.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources.

The pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs are special cases. Let the body lie between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). We describe the top lid with the parameters \(s = x\) and \(t = y\), with the map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, h(s, t))\) on \(M = R\). Its partial derivatives are \(\partial\vek r/\partial s = (1, 0, \partial h/\partial x)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (0, 1, \partial h/\partial y)\), and by definition 2.30

\[\vek N = \Big( 0 \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \cdot 1,\ \ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ \ 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0 \Big) = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}} ,\]

the vector of definition 4.36. For the other five pieces we must choose the parameters in the right order, so that \(\vek N\) points out of the body, as the next lemma says.

Lemma 4.63 Pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs as surfaces described by two parameters (kosi površine telesa med grafoma kot ploskve s parametroma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). Each of the six pieces of its surface (definition 4.36) is a surface described by two parameters (definition 4.61), with the description:

  1. the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, h(s, t))\) on \(M = [a, b] \times [c, d]\), with \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\),
  2. the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (t, s, g(t, s))\) on \(M = [c, d] \times [a, b]\), with \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\),
  3. the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (b, s, t)\) on the set \(M\) of the points with \(c \le s \le d\) and \(g(b, s) \le t \le h(b, s)\), with \(\vek N = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (a, t, s)\) on the set of the points with \(c \le t \le d\) and \(g(a, t) \le s \le h(a, t)\), with \(\vek N = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\),
  4. the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (t, d, s)\) on the set of the points with \(a \le t \le b\) and \(g(t, d) \le s \le h(t, d)\), with \(\vek N = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, c, t)\) on the set of the points with \(a \le s \le b\) and \(g(s, c) \le t \le h(s, c)\), with \(\vek N = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

For a body in which the coordinate \(y\) runs between the graphs and whose rectangle lies in the plane of the variables \(z\) and \(x\), we read the first coordinate in these descriptions and in the vectors \(\vek N\) as \(z\), the second as \(x\) and the third as \(y\). For a body in which \(x\) runs between the graphs and whose rectangle lies in the plane of the variables \(y\) and \(z\), we read them as \(y\), \(z\) and \(x\).

The surface integral (4.34) of every function continuous on a piece equals the integral over this piece as the definition of the integral over the surface of a body between graphs gives it, and the flux (4.35) equals the flux through the piece with the outward normal of the body.

Proof

We must show that the descriptions really are descriptions by the definition, that the vectors \(\vek N\) are as the lemma says, and that the integrals agree.

  1. All the maps are defined on open sets of the plane. For the lids it is the open set \(U\) of definition 4.15, or the set of the points \((s, t)\) for which \((t, s) \in U\), which is open because swapping the coordinates keeps distances. For the side pieces it is the whole plane, where the components are polynomials of degree one. The components are continuously differentiable.
  2. The maps are one-to-one, because the parameters can be read off the point \(\vek r(s, t)\) as two of its coordinates: for the top lid as \(x\) and \(y\), for the bottom one as \(y\) and \(x\), for \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) as \(y\) and \(z\), and similarly for the other pieces.
  3. The vectors \(\vek N\). For the top lid \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), as we computed before the lemma. For the bottom one \(\partial\vek r/\partial s = (0, 1, \partial g/\partial y)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (1, 0, \partial g/\partial x)\), and by definition 2.30 \(\vek N = \big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y},\ -1\big) = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). For the side pieces the two partial derivatives are unit vectors of the axes, and by items 1 and 6 of lemma 2.31, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). None of these vectors is the zero vector.
  4. The sets \(M\). The rectangles have an area by lemma 4.32, item 6. For the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(M\) is the region between the graphs of the functions \(s \mapsto g(b, s)\) and \(s \mapsto h(b, s)\) over the interval \([c, d]\). These functions are continuously differentiable on an open interval that contains \([c, d]\). By lemma 4.38, whose proof works the same way in the plane, there is \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that the points \((b, s)\) with \(c - \delta_0 < s < d + \delta_0\) lie in \(U\), where \(g\) and \(h\) have continuous partial derivatives with respect to \(y\). By theorem 4.33 in the plane, \(M\) has an area, and the integral of a continuous function over \(M\) is the iterated integral, first over \(t\) from \(g(b, s)\) to \(h(b, s)\) and then over \(s\) from \(c\) to \(d\). For the other side pieces it is the same.
  5. The integrals. For the lids the integral over the rectangle \(M\) is, by lemma 4.32, item 6, the iterated integral of definition 4.8, for the top lid \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d f(s, t, h(s, t))\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s\), which is (4.18). For the bottom lid theorem 4.9 on the order of integration gives the same iterated integral, only with the names of the variables exchanged. For the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) we have \(|\vek N| = 1\), and by step 4 the integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{s})}^{h(b, s)} f(b, s, t)\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s\), the integral of definition 4.36 with \(y = s\) and \(z = t\). For the other side pieces it is the same.
  6. The fluxes. By step 3 the vectors \(\vek N\) are the vectors of definition 4.36, which point out of the body, so \(\vek v\cdot\vek N = (\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N|\) with the outward unit normal \(\vek n\), and by step 5 the flux (4.35) is the integral of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) over the piece of definition 4.36.
  7. Renamed coordinates. When \(y\) runs between the graphs, a point or a vector with the components \((n_1, n_2, n_3)\) in the names of the lemma has the components \((n_2, n_3, n_1)\) along the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). For vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) the vector product of the vectors \((a_2, a_3, a_1)\) and \((b_2, b_3, b_1)\) has, by definition 2.30, the components \((a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3,\ a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1,\ a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\), which are the second, third and first components of the vector \(\vek a\times\vek b\). The vector product is therefore renamed in the same way as both factors, steps 1 to 6 hold with the renamed coordinates, and the vectors \(\vek N\) are the vectors of definition 4.36 with renamed coordinates, which point out of the body. When \(x\) runs between the graphs it is the same, with the same shift of the components once more.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6 (PDF p. 470), where for a surface \(z = h(x, y)\) he gets \(\vek N = (-h_{\mathrm{x}}, -h_{\mathrm{y}}, 1)\). The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

Now the answer to the question from the beginning. Let a surface \(S\) have two descriptions, \(\vek r_1\) on \(M_1\) and \(\vek r_2\) on \(M_2\), and let there be a map \(\tau\) of the plane of parameters between them that assigns to a point \((s, t)\) of \(M_2\) the point \(\tau(s, t)\) of \(M_1\) that describes the same point of the surface: \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(\tau(s, t))\). We denote the components of the map \(\tau\) by \(\tau_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{t}}\), because they are the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\) in the plane of parameters of the first description. By the chain rule the vectors of partial derivatives of the second description, \(\partial\vek r_2/\partial s\) and \(\partial\vek r_2/\partial t\), are expressed by the vectors of partial derivatives of the first, and the vector product gives the first normal vector multiplied by the Jacobian of the map \(\tau\). This is exactly the factor that the change of variables theorem in the plane brings into the integral.

Corollary 4.64 The surface integral does not depend on the description (ploskovni integral ni odvisen od opisa)

Let \(\vek r_1\) be a description of a surface \(S\) on the set \(M_1\) with the open set \(U_1 \supseteq M_1\) (definition 4.61), with the normal vector \(\vek N_1\). Let \(M_2\) be a set with area in the plane, \(U_2 \supseteq M_2\) an open set and \(\tau\) a map that has as input a point \((s, t)\) of \(U_2\) and as output the point \(\tau(s, t) = \big(\tau_{\mathrm{s}}(s, t), \tau_{\mathrm{t}}(s, t)\big)\) of \(U_1\), that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(U_2\), with \(J_\tau \neq 0\) on \(U_2\), and let \(\tau(M_2) = M_1\). Let \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(\tau(s, t))\) for \((s, t) \in U_2\). Then:

  1. \(\vek r_2\) on \(M_2\) is a description of the same surface \(S\), and its normal vector is
    \[\vek N_2(s, t) = J_\tau(s, t)\,\vek N_1\big(\tau(s, t)\big) . \tag{4.36}\]
  2. For every function \(f\) continuous on \(S\) the surface integrals (4.34) with the two descriptions are equal.
  3. For every field \(\vek v\) continuous on \(S\) the fluxes (4.35) with the two descriptions are equal if \(J_\tau > 0\) on \(M_2\), and opposite if \(J_\tau < 0\) on \(M_2\).
Proof

We must show that the normal vector gets multiplied by \(J_\tau\), and then use the change of variables theorem in the plane.

  1. The map \(\vek r_2\) is continuously differentiable on \(U_2\) by lemma 4.43 on the chain rule, applied to each component of the map \(\vek r_1\) composed with \(\tau\). It is one-to-one, because each of the maps \(\tau\) and \(\vek r_1\) is one-to-one: from \(\vek r_1(\tau(P)) = \vek r_1(\tau(Q))\) it follows that \(\tau(P) = \tau(Q)\) and then \(P = Q\). Since \(\tau(M_2) = M_1\), the set of the points with the position vectors \(\vek r_2(s, t)\), \((s, t) \in M_2\), is \(S\).
  2. Let \((s, t) \in U_2\) and \(\vek p = \frac{\partial\vek r_1}{\partial s}(\tau(s, t))\), \(\vek q = \frac{\partial\vek r_1}{\partial t}(\tau(s, t))\). By lemma 4.43 on the chain rule
    \[\frac{\partial\vek r_2}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial s}\,\vek p + \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial s}\,\vek q , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek r_2}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial t}\,\vek p + \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial t}\,\vek q ,\]
    with the derivatives of the components of the map \(\tau\) at the point \((s, t)\).
  3. We expand the vector product by items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.31. We get four terms, with \(\vek p\times\vek p\), \(\vek p\times\vek q\), \(\vek q\times\vek p\) and \(\vek q\times\vek q\). By item 1 of the same lemma the first and the last are zero, and \(\vek q\times\vek p = -\vek p\times\vek q\). Therefore
    \[\vek N_2 = \Big( \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial s}\,\frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial t} - \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial s}\,\frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial t} \Big)\,\vek p\times\vek q = J_\tau\,\vek N_1(\tau(s, t)) ,\]
    because the bracket is the determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\tau\) (definition 4.42, definition 2.50 for \(2 \times 2\) matrices). This is (4.36). Since \(J_\tau\) and \(\vek N_1(\tau(s, t))\) are nonzero for \((s, t) \in M_2\), we have \(\vek N_2 \neq \vek 0\), and \(\vek r_2\) meets all the requirements of a description. So the first item of the corollary holds.
  4. By (4.36), \(|\vek N_2| = |J_\tau|\,|\vek N_1 \circ \tau|\), so the integrand of the second description is \(f(\vek r_2)\,|\vek N_2| = \big(f(\vek r_1)\,|\vek N_1|\big)(\tau(s, t))\,|J_\tau(s, t)|\).
  5. The function \(F = f(\vek r_1)\,|\vek N_1|\) is continuous on \(M_1 = \tau(M_2)\) by lemma 4.62. By theorem 4.59, the change of variables theorem in the plane, with the map \(\tau\), the open set \(U_2\) and the set with area \(M_2\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{M}_1} F\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{M}_2} F\big(\tau(s, t)\big)\,\big|J_\tau(s, t)\big|\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
    The left side is the surface integral with the first description, the right side by step 4 the one with the second. This is item 2.
  6. The flux. By (4.36), \(\vek v(\vek r_2)\cdot\vek N_2 = J_\tau\,\big(\vek v(\vek r_1)\cdot\vek N_1\big)(\tau)\). For \(J_\tau > 0\) on \(M_2\) we have \(J_\tau = |J_\tau|\), and as in step 5 the fluxes are equal. For \(J_\tau < 0\) we have \(J_\tau = -|J_\tau|\), and by the linearity of the integral (lemma 4.32, item 1) the flux with the second description is opposite to the flux with the first. This is item 3.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, Theorem 1 (PDF p. 472): replacing the vector \(\vek N\) by \(-\vek N\) multiplies the flux by \(-1\). KREYSZIG does not prove the independence of the description for surfaces. The proof with the change of variables theorem is not from the source.

For the flux only the direction of the normal vector counts. The flux through a surface is the sum of \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\), and two descriptions with \(J_\tau > 0\) give the same direction of the normal, two with \(J_\tau < 0\) opposite ones. The surface integral of a function, however, does not know the direction, because it has only \(|\vek N|\).

Let us test the corollary on the cut \(y = 3\) mm between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round hanging bar (section 4.2.6, figure 4.48, left). We write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres. For the piece \(C\) the cut is the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) with \(d = 3\), and by lemma 4.63 we describe it by \(\vek r_1(s, t) = (t, 3, s)\) on \(M_1 = [-4, 4] \times [0, L]\), where \(s\) is the coordinate \(z\) and \(t\) the coordinate \(x\), with \(\vek N_1 = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). For the piece \(D\), in which \(y\) runs between the graphs, the cut is the bottom lid, the graph of the constant function \(3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). By lemma 4.63, item 2, with the first coordinate \(z\), the second \(x\) and the third \(y\), we describe it by \(\vek r_2(s, t) = (s, 3, t)\) on \(M_2 = [0, L] \times [-4, 4]\), with \(\vek N_2 = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). We have \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(t, s)\), so \(\tau(s, t) = (t, s)\), with the matrix of partial derivatives with the rows \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) and with \(J_\tau = -1\). By the corollary the surface integrals are equal, both are the area \(8\ \text{mm} \cdot L\), while the fluxes are opposite. This is exactly the condition on the pairs of corollary 4.40.

The second test is curved. On the mantle of the bar let us take the strip between the points \((y, z) = (3, 4)\) and \((4, 3)\) of the cross section, along the whole length of the bar (figure 4.48, right). The strip lies on the top lid of the piece \(D\), which is the graph \(y = q(z)\) with \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\), for \(z\) between \(3\) and \(4\). But we can also describe it as the graph \(z = q(y)\) for \(y\) between \(3\) and \(4\), like the top lid of the piece \(C\), only over another interval.

  1. The first description, as for the piece \(D\): \(\vek r_1(s, t) = (t, q(s), s)\) on \(M_1 = [3, 4] \times [0, L]\), with \(s = z\) and \(t = x\). By lemma 4.16, \(q'(s) = -s/q(s)\), so \(\partial\vek r_1/\partial s = (0, q'(s), 1)\), \(\partial\vek r_1/\partial t = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek N_1 = \big(0,\ 1,\ s/q(s)\big)\).
  2. The second description, as for the piece \(C\): \(\vek r_2(s, t) = (s, t, q(t))\) on \(M_2 = [0, L] \times [3, 4]\), with \(s = x\) and \(t = y\), and \(\vek N_2 = \big(0,\ t/q(t),\ 1\big)\).
  3. For \(t\) between \(0\) and \(5\) we have \(q(q(t)) = \sqrt{25 - (25 - t^2)} = t\), so \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(q(t), s)\) and \(\tau(s, t) = (q(t), s)\). The matrix of partial derivatives has the rows \((0, q'(t))\) and \((1, 0)\), so \(J_\tau = -q'(t) = t/q(t)\), for \(t\) between \(3\) and \(4\) between \(\tfrac34\) and \(\tfrac43\), positive. The map \(\tau\) is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on the open set of the points with \(0 < t < 5\), because \(q\) decreases on \((0, 5)\).
  4. Let us check (4.36): \(J_\tau\,\vek N_1(\tau(s, t)) = \frac{t}{q(t)}\,\big(0,\ 1,\ q(t)/t\big) = \big(0,\ t/q(t),\ 1\big) = \vek N_2\).

The area of the strip is, with both descriptions, \(L \cdot 1{,}41897\) mm, where \(1{,}41897\) mm is the length of the circular arc between the two points, computed by SymPy. The flux of the displacement field of the hanging bar is \(-0{,}041547\ \text{mm}^3\) with both descriptions, approximately the volume that the strip sweeps inwards as the bar gets thinner. The integrands differ. In the first description the point of the surface is \((t, q(s), s)\), so \(x = t\) and \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_1 = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - t)\,\big(q(s) + s^2/q(s)\big) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - t) \cdot 25/q(s)\), because \(q(s)^2 + s^2 = 25\). In the second the point is \((s, t, q(t))\), so \(x = s\) and \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_2 = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - s) \cdot 25/q(t)\). We integrate the first integrand over \(M_1\), the second over \(M_2\), and the integrals are equal, as the change of variables theorem says. Since \(J_\tau > 0\), both descriptions give the normal that points out of the bar.

With this we have answered the question from the beginning of the subsection: when two descriptions of the same surface are joined by a map \(\tau\) with the assumptions of the corollary, the surface integral does not depend on the description, and the flux depends only on the side to which the normal vector points. That any two descriptions of the same surface have such a map we do not prove in the book. We do not need it, because in every case we meet we write the map \(\tau\) down explicitly, as in the two tests. In section 4.3.7 we will use surfaces described by two parameters to describe the surface of bodies that are images of boxes, and prove the divergence theorem for them.

4.3.7 Curved boxes and the divergence theorem

So far we have proved the divergence theorem for a box and a body made of boxes (theorem 4.14), for a body between two graphs (theorem 4.39) and for a body cut into pieces between graphs (corollary 4.40). We cut the round bar into three pieces, because it is curved only in its cross section and straight along its axis. A ball is curved in all directions. Each of its pieces that reaches the surface would need a graph over a rectangle as its lid, and the pieces would have to meet in whole pieces of their surfaces. We will not look for such a cut. We will, however, need a ball and a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre, in chapter 11, and in chapter 15 bodies that the finite element method cuts into small six-faced pieces with curved faces. For them we need the divergence theorem in a form that does not rely on graphs.

The idea is simple. We know the box. If we bend and stretch a box continuously, without tearing it or folding it over itself, we get a body with curved faces. For instance, the deformation \(P \mapsto P + \vek u(P)\) of chapter 1 maps a box of material before loading into the body that this material occupies after loading. We will build the ball from a cube in the middle and six bent boxes, one over each face of the cube (figure 4.51). For a bent box we get the divergence theorem from the theorem for a box. A change of variables carries the integral over the bent box to the box, there we use theorem 4.14, and the faces of the box are mapped onto the curved faces of the body.

The route is this. First we say exactly what a bent box is, define the vectors of its faces and show that they point out of the body. Then we prove an identity for the second derivatives of the map, with it the divergence theorem for a bent box, and a corollary for a body made of such boxes and of bodies between graphs. At the end we cut a ball of radius 10 mm, a thick spherical shell and a ring into such pieces and test the theorem with numbers.

Definition 4.65 Curved box (ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box, \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(K\), and \(\Phi\) a map on \(D\) (definition 4.42) whose input is a point \(P = (x, y, z)\) of \(D\) and whose output is the point \(\Phi(P) = \big(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(P), \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(P), \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(P)\big)\). Let:

  1. the components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of the first and second order (definition 1.124), continuous at every point of \(D\),
  2. \(\Phi\) be one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45): it maps two different points of \(D\) to two different points,
  3. the Jacobian \(J_\Phi = \det\mat F_\Phi\) be positive at every point of \(D\).

The set \(V = \Phi(K)\), the image of the box \(K\), is a curved box (ukrivljen kvader). The columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), the vectors \(\partial\Phi/\partial x\), \(\partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) of the partial derivatives of the components, are multiplied two at a time by the vector product:

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z} , \qquad \vek N_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x} , \qquad \vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y} . \tag{4.37}\]

The surface (površina) \(S\) of the curved box has six faces, which are the images of the faces of the box \(K\):

  • the faces \(z = b_3\) and \(z = a_3\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) and \(\Phi(x, y, a_3)\) with \((x, y) \in [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\), with the face vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, a_3)\),
  • the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(b_1, y, z)\) and \(\Phi(a_1, y, z)\) with \((y, z) \in [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), with the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(b_1, y, z)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(a_1, y, z)\),
  • the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(x, b_2, z)\) and \(\Phi(x, a_2, z)\) with \((x, z) \in [a_1, b_1] \times [a_3, b_3]\), with the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}(x, b_2, z)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}(x, a_2, z)\).

On a face with the vector \(\vek N\) the outward unit normal is \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\). The flux (pretok) of a field \(\vek v\) through the face \(z = b_3\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1}\int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2} \vek v\big(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\big)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{4.38}\]

and through the other faces likewise, with the face vector and the iterated integral over the rectangle on which the face is described (definition 4.8). The integral of a function \(f\) over a face is the same iterated integral of the function \(f(\Phi)\,|\vek N|\). The flux through the surface \(S\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\), is the sum of the fluxes through the six faces.

Source: The definition is not from the sources. KREYSZIG §10.6, (2) (PDF p. 469) describes a surface by two parameters and its normal as the vector product of the derivatives with respect to the parameters. COOK §6.5 (PDF p. 231) describes six-faced isoparametric finite elements as images of a cube whose faces are the images of the faces of the cube.

The definition says what goes in. The box \(K\) and the map \(\Phi\) are given, and the curved box \(V\) is the set of points to which \(\Phi\) maps the points of the box (figure 4.49). This is the exact form of the bent box from the start of the section. Each of the three conditions has its task. The second derivatives will be needed in the proof of the divergence theorem, where we will differentiate the face vectors, which are built from the first derivatives. The one-to-one property, the condition that \(\Phi\) maps two different points to two different points, ensures that the box does not overlap itself when it is bent, and the change of variables theorem 4.59 needs it. A positive Jacobian says that no small cube in \(K\) is flattened, which the change of variables theorem also needs, and that none is mirrored, which will make the face vectors point out of the body. For the deformation of a body the last two conditions are physical. Material does not penetrate itself, and the Jacobian is the ratio of the volumes of a small piece after and before loading, which is positive (corollary 2.58).

The face vectors are vector products of columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), just as the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) in section 4.2.11 was the vector product of the sides of a patch on a lid. On the face \(z = b_3\) the point \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) moves by about \(\Delta x\,\partial\Phi/\partial x\) for a small step \(\Delta x\) and by about \(\Delta y\,\partial\Phi/\partial y\) for a step \(\Delta y\), as the theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step says, applied to each component. A small patch of the face is therefore nearly a parallelogram with the sides \(\Delta x\,\partial\Phi/\partial x\) and \(\Delta y\,\partial\Phi/\partial y\), and the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\) is perpendicular to it and as long as the area of the parallelogram. The columns are \(\partial\Phi/\partial x = \mat F_\Phi\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = \mat F_\Phi\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), so by Nanson's formula (2.79) \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-\T}(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-\T}\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The face vector is therefore the vector of Nanson's formula for the face of the box with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Where does the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) point? We take its scalar product with the third column. By the definition of the determinant 2.50 and the cyclic exchange of the columns (lemma 2.51, item 1)

\[\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}\Big) = \det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\Big) = J_\Phi > 0 .\]

The vector \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) says where the point \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) moves when \(z\) is increased a little. The points \(\Phi(x, y, b_3 + h)\) with a small \(h > 0\) do not lie in \(V\), because the point \((x, y, b_3 + h)\) is not in \(K\) and \(\Phi\) does not map two different points to the same point. The vector \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) therefore points from the face out of the body, and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) points to the same side of the face, because their scalar product is positive. The same holds on the other faces, on the face \(z = a_3\) for instance with the vectors \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(-\partial\Phi/\partial z\). With a negative Jacobian all face vectors would point into the body.

Each face is a surface described by two parameters (definition 4.61). The face \(z = b_3\) is described by the function \(\vek r(x, y) = \Phi(x, y, b_3)\) on the rectangle \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\), which has an area. The function is continuously differentiable on the set of the points \((x, y)\) of the plane for which \((x, y, b_3)\) is in \(D\). This set is open, because \(D\) is open, and it contains the rectangle. On it \(\vek r\) does not map two different points to the same point, and its normal vector \(\partial\vek r/\partial x\times\partial\vek r/\partial y = \vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) is not the zero vector, because its scalar product with \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) is positive. The integral over a rectangle is the iterated integral (lemma 4.32, item 6), so (4.38) is the flux of definition 4.61. For the face \(z = a_3\) we take the parameters in the reverse order, \(\vek r(y, x) = \Phi(x, y, a_3)\), so that \(\partial\vek r/\partial y\times\partial\vek r/\partial x = -\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) by item 1 of lemma 2.31. For the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) the parameters are \((y, z)\) and \((z, y)\), for the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) they are \((z, x)\) and \((x, z)\).

Let us try the definition on bodies we already know. For the map \(\Phi(P) = P\) we have \(\mat F_\Phi = \mat I\) with the columns \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and by item 6 of lemma 2.31 \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The curved box is then the box \(K\) itself, the face vectors are the outward normals of figure 4.16, and the flux is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces of a body made of boxes (definition 4.11, item 3).

The second is the body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) for which \(g < h\) at every point of \(R\) and \(g\) and \(h\) have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order on an open set \(U\). The set \(U'\) of the points of \(U\) at which \(h > g\) is open, because the continuity of the function \(h - g\) at such a point, written with an error equal to half the value of \(h - g\) there, gives a disc in which \(h - g > 0\). It contains \(R\). On the open set \(D\) of the points \((x, y, z)\) with \((x, y) \in U'\) let

\[\Phi(x, y, z) = \Big(x,\ y,\ g(x, y) + z\,\big(h(x, y) - g(x, y)\big)\Big) , \qquad K = [a, b] \times [c, d] \times [0, 1] .\]

At \(z = 0\) the point \(\Phi(x, y, z)\) lies on the bottom lid, at \(z = 1\) on the top lid, and in between \(z\) divides the vertical segment between the lids evenly. The first two rows of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) are \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\), and the third has \(h - g\) in its last place, so by (2.51) \(J_\Phi = h - g > 0\). Two points with the same image have the same \(x\) and \(y\), and \(g + z\,(h - g) = g + z'\,(h - g)\) gives \(z = z'\), because \(h - g \neq 0\). On the face \(z = 1\) we have \(\partial\Phi/\partial x = (1, 0, \partial h/\partial x)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = (0, 1, \partial h/\partial y)\), so \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = (-\partial h/\partial x, -\partial h/\partial y, 1) = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), the vector of the top lid of definition 4.36. On the face \(z = 0\) likewise \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). On the face \(x = b\) we have \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = (0, 1, \cdot)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z = (0, 0, h - g)\), so \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = (h - g, 0, 0)\), and the flux is

\[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_0^1 v_{\mathrm{x}}\big(b, y, g + z\,(h - g)\big)\,(h - g)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y ,\]

where \(g\) and \(h\) are taken at the point \((b, y)\). The inner integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{g}}^h v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, w)\,\mathrm{d}w\). Indeed, the function \(G(w) = \int_{\mathrm{g}}^w v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, \omega)\,\mathrm{d}\omega\) has by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 2, the derivative \(v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, w)\), and the function \(z \mapsto G\big(g + z\,(h - g)\big)\) has the derivative \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\big(b, y, g + z\,(h - g)\big)\,(h - g)\), because its difference quotient with the step \(k\) is \((h - g)\) times the difference quotient of the function \(G\) with the step \(k\,(h - g)\) (definition 1.9), so by item 1 of the same theorem the integral of this derivative from \(0\) to \(1\) is \(G(h) - G(g)\). The flux through the face \(x = b\) is therefore the flux through the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) of definition 4.36, and the same holds for the other side faces. A body between two graphs with \(g < h\) and continuous second derivatives is a curved box with the same surface and the same fluxes.

How do we show that the divergence theorem holds for a curved box too? By the change of variables theorem 4.59 the integral of the divergence of a field \(\vek v\) over \(V\) equals the integral of the function \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\) over the box \(K\), where \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) is short for the divergence (definition 4.13). We would like to use the theorem for a box on some field \(\vek G\) on \(K\). Which one? On the face \(z = b_3\) of the box the theorem for a box integrates the component \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\), and we want to obtain the flux (4.38). The natural choice is therefore \(G_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\), and likewise \(G_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\). Is the divergence of this field really \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\)? The product rule splits it into two parts. In the first the components of the field \(\vek v(\Phi)\) are differentiated, and the chain rule and the inverse matrix will turn it into \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\). In the second the face vectors are differentiated, and this part must be zero. The next lemma says so.

Lemma 4.66 Piola identity (Piolova identiteta)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map on \(D\) whose components have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of the first and second order, continuous at every point of \(D\). Let \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) be the vectors (4.37). Then at every point of \(D\)

\[\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = \vek 0 , \tag{4.39}\]

where the partial derivative of a vector means the vector of the partial derivatives of its components.

Proof

We must show that after differentiation all terms cancel. We differentiate each vector product by the product rule, then use the symmetry of mixed derivatives and the exchange of the order in the vector product. For short we write \(\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial\Phi/\partial x\), \(\vek f_{\mathrm{y}} = \partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} = \partial\Phi/\partial z\) for the columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\).

  1. Derivative of a vector product. Let the components of the vectors \(\vek p\) and \(\vek q\), which depend on the point, have a partial derivative with respect to \(x\) at the point \(P\). The \(x\) component of the vector \(\vek p\times\vek q\) is \(p_{\mathrm{y}} q_{\mathrm{z}} - p_{\mathrm{z}} q_{\mathrm{y}}\) (definition 2.30). With \(y\) and \(z\) held fixed this is a sum of products of functions of the one variable \(x\), and by the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81, items 1 and 3) its derivative is
    \[\Big(\frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,q_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\,q_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) + \Big(p_{\mathrm{y}}\,\frac{\partial q_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} - p_{\mathrm{z}}\,\frac{\partial q_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    the \(x\) component of the vector \(\partial\vek p/\partial x\times\vek q + \vek p\times\partial\vek q/\partial x\). The same holds for the other two components and for the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\). Hence
    \[\frac{\partial(\vek p\times\vek q)}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek p}{\partial x}\times\vek q + \vek p\times\frac{\partial\vek q}{\partial x} .\]
  2. By step 1
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} , \\ \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{z}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} , \\ \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{y}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{x}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} . \end{aligned}\]
    The components of the vector \(\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\) are the mixed derivatives \(\partial^2\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x\,\partial y\), first with respect to \(y\) and then with respect to \(x\) (definition 1.124).
  3. Let \(P\) be a point of \(D\). All points closer to \(P\) than some number \(r > 0\) are in \(D\), because \(D\) is open. The first and second partial derivatives of the components exist at them, and the mixed derivatives are continuous at \(P\). By the theorem 1.125 on the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives, at \(P\)
    \[\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} .\]
    We denote these three vectors by \(\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\vek g_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\).
  4. We insert them into step 2 and group the terms into three pairs:
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = {} & \big(\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\big) + \big(\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{xz}} + \vek g_{\mathrm{xz}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\big) \\ & + \big(\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\big) . \end{aligned}\]
  5. By item 1 of lemma 2.31 \(\vek q\times\vek p = -(\vek p\times\vek q)\), so each bracket is the zero vector. The sum is \(\vek 0\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. We have not found the identity in the sources of the library. Writing it with the columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) and the connection with Nanson's formula (CM (3.3.25), PDF p. 127) are ours.

What does the identity say? By theorem 2.54 the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\), divided by \(J_\Phi\), are the rows of the inverse matrix \(\mat F_\Phi^{-1}\). The lemma therefore says that the sum of the derivatives of the rows of the matrix \(J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-1}\), each with respect to its own coordinate, is zero. We see the geometric meaning on a very small curved box with the sides \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\). On the faces \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) the face vectors, multiplied by the area \(\Delta y\,\Delta z\) of the face of the box, are about \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(x)\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(x + \Delta x)\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\), and their sum is about \(\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\). The same holds for the other two pairs of faces. The lemma therefore says that the face vectors, multiplied by the areas, add up to the zero vector, just as the sides of a closed polygon add up to the zero vector (figure 4.50). We will show this exactly after the theorem.

Theorem 4.67 Divergence theorem for a curved box (izrek o divergenci za ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(V = \Phi(K)\) be a curved box with the surface \(S\) and the outward unit normal \(\vek n\) (definition 4.65), \(E\) an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(E\) (definition 1.90). Then \(V\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), and

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.40}\]

where the left side is the integral over a set with volume (definition 4.30) and the right side the flux through the six faces of the curved box.

Proof

We must show that the integral of the divergence over \(V\) is the sum of the fluxes through the six faces. The change of variables theorem carries the integral to the box \(K\), there we write the integrand as the divergence of a new field and use the divergence theorem for a box. For short we write \(J = J_\Phi\) and \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) for the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) (definition 4.13). The partial derivatives of the field \(\vek v\) are derivatives with respect to the coordinates of a point of the body, those of the map \(\Phi\) with respect to the coordinates of a point of the box.

1. An open set around the box.

  1. Let \(D'\) be the set of the points \(P\) of \(D\) for which \(\Phi(P)\) lies in \(E\). The points \(\Phi(P)\) with \(P \in K\) make up \(V\), which lies in \(E\), so \(D'\) contains \(K\).
  2. \(D'\) is open. Let \(P \in D'\). The set \(E\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that every point closer to \(\Phi(P)\) than \(r\) lies in \(E\). The components of the map \(\Phi\) are continuously differentiable, hence continuous (lemma 1.91), and there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for points \(Q \in D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) each component of the point \(\Phi(Q)\) differs from the same component of the point \(\Phi(P)\) by less than \(r/2\). By (1.10) the square of the distance between \(\Phi(P)\) and \(\Phi(Q)\) is then less than \(3r^2/4 < r^2\), the distance by lemma 1.28 less than \(r\), and \(\Phi(Q)\) lies in \(E\). Since \(D\) is open, there is also a \(\rho > 0\) such that the points closer to \(P\) than \(\rho\) are in \(D\). All points closer to \(P\) than the smaller of the numbers \(\delta\) and \(\rho\) are therefore in \(D'\).
  3. On \(D'\) let \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = v_{\mathrm{i}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\) for \(i = x, y, z\) be the components of the vector \(\tilde{\vek v}(P) = \vek v\big(\Phi(P)\big)\). The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable on the open set \(D'\) with values in the open set \(E\), and the \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(E\). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}\) are therefore continuously differentiable on \(D'\), and
    \[\frac{\partial\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}(P) ,\]
    where \(k\) runs over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and likewise for the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\).

2. A new field on the box.

  1. On \(D'\) let \(\vek G = (G_{\mathrm{x}}, G_{\mathrm{y}}, G_{\mathrm{z}})\) be the field with the components
    \[G_{\mathrm{x}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{y}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{z}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} .\]
  2. The field \(\vek G\) is continuously differentiable on \(D'\). The components of the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) are differences of products of the first partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\Phi\) (definition 2.30), and these have continuous partial derivatives on \(D\) (definition 4.65, item 1). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81, items 1 and 3) the components of the face vectors therefore have partial derivatives that are sums of products of continuous functions and so continuous (corollary 1.69, item 1). The same holds for \(G_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\), which are sums of products of the functions \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}\) with components of the face vectors.
  3. By the product rule, applied to each term of the scalar product, \(\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = (\partial\tilde{\vek v}/\partial x)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} + \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), and likewise for \(G_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\). The sum is
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = {} & \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial x}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial y}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial z}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} \\ & + \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\Big(\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
  4. By the Piola identity (lemma 4.66) the bracket is the zero vector, and the last term is zero.
  5. Into the other three terms we insert the chain rule of step 3 of the first part. The component \(i\) of the vector \(\partial\tilde{\vek v}/\partial x\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(\Phi)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}\). Writing \((\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the component \(i\) of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), we get
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(\Phi)\,\Big( & \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{i}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial y}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}})_{\mathrm{i}} \\ & + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial z}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}})_{\mathrm{i}} \Big) . \end{aligned}\]
  6. Let \(\mat M\) be the matrix with the rows \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\). By the theorem 2.54 on the inverse via the determinant \(\mat M/J\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), whose columns are \(\partial\Phi/\partial x\), \(\partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\). The bracket of step 5 is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F_\Phi)_{\mathrm{kj}}\,M_{\mathrm{ji}}\), that is, the element \(ki\) of the product \(\mat F_\Phi\mat M\) (definition 1.98). By definition 1.107 \(\mat F_\Phi\,(\mat M/J) = \mat I\), so \(\mat F_\Phi\mat M = J\,\mat I\), and the bracket is \(J\) for \(k = i\) and \(0\) for \(k \neq i\).
  7. Of the double sum only the terms with \(k = i\) remain:
    \[\frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = J(P)\,\Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\big(\Phi(P)\big)\]
    at every point \(P\) of \(D'\).

3. Carrying the integral to the box.

  1. The box \(K\) is a set with volume, and the integral over it is the integral over a box of definition 4.8 (lemma 4.32, item 6). The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on the open set \(D'\), and \(J > 0\). The divergence \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) is continuous on \(V\), because the partial derivatives of the components of the field are continuous on \(E\). By the change of variables theorem 4.59 \(V = \Phi(K)\) is therefore a set with volume, and since \(|J| = J\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \mathrm{div}\,\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} (\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,J(P)\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  2. By step 7 of the second part the integrand on the right equals the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) at every point of \(K\).
  3. The field \(\vek G\) is continuously differentiable on the open set \(D'\), which contains \(K\). By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, applied to the box \(K\) as a body made of boxes with a single cell, the integral of the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) over \(K\) equals the sum of the integrals of the function \(G_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + G_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + G_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) over the six faces of the box, with the outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

4. The faces.

  1. On the face \(z = b_3\) of the box \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the integrand is \(G_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3) = \vek v\big(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\big)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\). The integral over the rectangle is the iterated integral of definition 4.8, that is, (4.38), the flux through the face \(z = b_3\) of the curved box.
  2. On the face \(z = a_3\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the integrand \(-G_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}})\) gives the flux through the face \(z = a_3\).
  3. On the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) the integrands are \(\pm G_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(\pm\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})\), on the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) they are \(\pm G_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(\pm\vek N_{\mathrm{y}})\), with the face vectors of definition 4.65.
  4. The sum of the six integrals is the flux \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). Together with the third part this gives (4.40).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1 (PDF p. 479) states the theorem for closed bounded regions bounded by a surface made of smooth pieces, and proves it for regions that lie between graphs in the direction of all three axes (PDF pp. 480-481). The change of variables is stated in LEBL2 Thm. 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134). The proof by carrying the integral to the box and by the Piola identity is not from the sources.

The proof has shown why the theorem holds for a curved body too. The change of variables carried the integral to the box, where the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) was replaced by the divergence of the field \(\vek G\), whose components are the fluxes of the field \(\vek v\) through the faces per unit area of the faces of the box. Two moves did the work. The chain rule and the inverse matrix turned the derivatives of the field \(\vek v(\Phi)\) with respect to the coordinates of the box into the derivatives of the field \(\vek v\) with respect to the coordinates of the body, multiplied by \(J\), exactly the factor that the change of variables demands. The Piola identity made sure that the derivatives of the face vectors gave no term. The fundamental theorem of calculus worked inside the theorem for a box, once in each direction.

The theorem also says what exactly figure 4.50 means. A constant field \(\vek v = \vek c\) has divergence zero, so the flux of a constant field through the surface of every curved box is zero. By the linearity of the iterated integral (lemma 3.39, item 1) the flux through a face is the scalar product of the vector \(\vek c\) with the vector whose components are the integrals of the components of the face vector. Taking \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) for \(\vek c\), we find that the integrals of the face vectors over the six faces add up to the zero vector.

We will cut the ball into a cube, which is a body between two graphs, and into curved boxes. A body made of such pieces is treated by the next corollary, which extends corollary 4.40.

Corollary 4.68 Divergence theorem for a body cut into curved boxes (izrek o divergenci za telo iz ukrivljenih kvadrov)

Let \(V\) be the union of sets \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\), each of which is a body between two graphs (definition 4.15) or a curved box (definition 4.65), and let no interior point of any of them lie in another.

  1. \(V\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(V\)
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  2. Let the pieces of the surfaces of these sets (definitions 4.36 and 4.65) be divided into outer and inner ones, and the inner ones into pairs, so that each pair consists of pieces of the surfaces of two different sets and the flux of every continuous field through one piece is the negative of the flux through the other. Let \(S\) be the union of the outer pieces, the surface of the body \(V\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces. If the field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable on an open set \(E\) that contains \(V\), then
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.41}\]

The integrals over \(V\) and over the pieces are integrals over sets with volume (definition 4.30).

Proof

We must show both items. The first follows from the additivity of the integral over sets with volume, for the second we add the divergence theorems for the pieces.

1. Volume and integral.

  1. Each piece is a set with volume. A body between two graphs by theorem 4.33, a curved box by theorem 4.67.
  2. By assumption no interior point of any piece lies in another. By the additivity of the integral over sets with volume (lemma 4.32, item 4) \(V\) is therefore a set with volume, and the integral of a continuous function over \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

2. The divergence theorem.

  1. Each piece \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(V\), hence in \(E\). If it is a body between two graphs, then by theorem 4.39 the integral of the divergence over it equals the flux through its six pieces of surface, and the integral of definition 4.20 is by theorem 4.33 the integral over a set with volume. If it is a curved box, theorem 4.67 gives the same.
  2. We add the equalities over \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\). The divergence is continuous on \(V\), so by the first part the sum of the left sides is the integral of the divergence over \(V\).
  3. The sum of the right sides is the sum of the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces. The inner pieces come in pairs with opposite fluxes, which cancel. What remains is the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces, which is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482): for a body that auxiliary surfaces cut into finitely many pieces, the integrals over the auxiliary surfaces cancel in pairs. The proof follows the source.

The proof is the same argument as for corollary 4.40, only with two kinds of pieces. The first item came from the additivity of the integral, which knows neither the order of integration nor the shape of the pieces, only that the pieces do not overlap. The condition on the pairs must be checked for every cut, as for the round bar. When two descriptions of the same surface are related by a map with a negative Jacobian, corollary 4.64 gives it.

Let us test all this on a ball. A steel ball of radius \(R = 10\) mm, for instance a ball of a larger rolling bearing, is the set of the points \(P\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\), where \(O\) is its centre and the origin of the coordinate system. We cut it into the cube \(V_0 = [-a, a] \times [-a, a] \times [-a, a]\) with the half edge \(a = 4\) mm in the middle and six pieces, one over each face of the cube (figure 4.51). The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) over the top face is made of the segments from the face \(z = a\) of the cube to the surface of the ball that lie on rays from \(O\). We describe a point on the ray through the point \((s, t, 1)\) by its height \(z\). Since it is a multiple of the vector \((s, t, 1)\), it has the coordinates \((s\,z, t\,z, z)\). The numbers \(s = x/z\) and \(t = y/z\) are ratios of coordinates and say in which direction the ray goes. The ray meets the face \(z = a\) at the point of height \(a\) and the surface of the ball at the point of height \(R/|(s, t, 1)|\), where \(|(s, t, 1)| = \sqrt{1 + s^2 + t^2}\) is the length of the vector \((s, t, 1)\), since the point \(R\,(s, t, 1)/|(s, t, 1)|\) is at the distance \(R\) from \(O\). We divide the height between the two evenly by a number \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\):

\[\begin{aligned} \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda) &= (1 - \lambda)\,a + \lambda\,\frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} , \\ \Phi(s, t, \lambda) &= \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda)\,(s, t, 1) , \end{aligned} \tag{4.42}\]

on the box \(K = [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\). Here we write the coordinates of a point of the box as \(s\), \(t\), \(\lambda\) instead of the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) of definition 4.65, so as not to confuse them with the coordinates of points of the ball. The face vectors are therefore \(\vek N_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial\Phi/\partial t\times\partial\Phi/\partial\lambda\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{t}} = \partial\Phi/\partial\lambda\times\partial\Phi/\partial s\) and \(\vek N_\lambda = \partial\Phi/\partial s\times\partial\Phi/\partial t\). The face \(\lambda = 0\) is the top face of the cube, the face \(\lambda = 1\) a part of the surface of the ball, and the faces \(s = \pm 1\) and \(t = \pm 1\) are flat, in the planes \(x = \pm z\) and \(y = \pm z\) through \(O\) (figure 4.52).

Is \(V_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi(K)\) a curved box? We must check the three conditions of definition 4.65 on an open set that contains \(K\). The first condition needs the derivatives of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), which has a root in the denominator. We do not yet have the derivative of a root for functions of several variables in the book. Let us derive it with the same trick of a difference of squares as in lemma 4.16.

Lemma 4.69 Derivative of the reciprocal of a square root (odvod obratne vrednosti korena)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(p\) a function that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90) and positive at every point of \(D\). Then the function \(f\) whose value at the point \(P\) is \(1/\sqrt{p(P)}\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), and

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -\frac12\,f^3\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} , \tag{4.43}\]

and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the difference quotient of the function \(f\) converges to the right side of (4.43) and that this is continuous. We remove the root as in lemma 4.16, with a difference of squares.

  1. Difference of roots. For positive numbers \(A\) and \(B\) the roots \(\sqrt A\) and \(\sqrt B\) are positive, because the square of the number \(0\) is \(0\) (theorem 1.36). From \((\sqrt B - \sqrt A)(\sqrt B + \sqrt A) = B - A\) we get
    \[\sqrt B - \sqrt A = \frac{B - A}{\sqrt A + \sqrt B} , \qquad |\sqrt B - \sqrt A| \le \frac{|B - A|}{\sqrt A} .\]
  2. Let \(P \in D\). The function \(p\) is continuous (lemma 1.91), so there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|p(Q) - p(P)| < p(P)/2\) for points \(Q \in D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_1\). For such points \(p(Q) > p(P)/2\), and by lemma 1.28 \(\sqrt{p(Q)} > \sqrt{p(P)/2}\).
  3. Continuity of the function \(f\) at \(P\). For a point \(Q\) of step 2, by step 1
    \[\begin{aligned} |f(Q) - f(P)| &= \frac{\big|\sqrt{p(P)} - \sqrt{p(Q)}\big|}{\sqrt{p(P)}\,\sqrt{p(Q)}} \le \frac{|p(Q) - p(P)|}{p(P)\,\sqrt{p(Q)}} \\ &< \frac{\sqrt 2\,|p(Q) - p(P)|}{p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}} . \end{aligned}\]
    For \(\eta > 0\) we take the band that the continuity of the function \(p\) at \(P\) gives for the error \(\eta\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}/\sqrt 2\) and that is not larger than \(\delta_1\). For points \(Q\) closer to \(P\) than this band \(|f(Q) - f(P)| < \eta\), so \(f\) is continuous at \(P\) (definition 1.67).
  4. The difference quotient. The set \(D\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that the points \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(|h| < r\) are in \(D\). Let \(k(h) = \sqrt{p(Q_{\mathrm{h}})}\). By step 1 with \(A = p(P)\) and \(B = p(Q_{\mathrm{h}})\), for \(0 < |h| < r\)
    \[\frac{f(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - f(P)}{h} = \frac{k(0) - k(h)}{h\,k(0)\,k(h)} = -\frac{p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P)}{h} \cdot \frac{1}{d(h)} ,\]
    where \(d(h) = k(0)\,k(h)\,\big(k(0) + k(h)\big)\).
  5. The function \(k\) is continuous at \(0\). By step 1 \(|k(h) - k(0)| \le |p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P)|/\sqrt{p(P)}\), the distance \(|Q_{\mathrm{h}} P|\) is \(|h|\), and \(p\) is continuous at \(P\). By the corollary 1.64 on the sum and product of continuous functions the function \(d\) is therefore also continuous at \(0\), with the value \(d(0) = 2\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)} > 0\).
  6. The function \(1/d\) is continuous at \(0\). There is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|d(h) - d(0)| < d(0)/2\), hence \(d(h) > d(0)/2\), for \(|h| < \delta_2\). For such \(h\)
    \[\Big| \frac{1}{d(h)} - \frac{1}{d(0)} \Big| = \frac{|d(0) - d(h)|}{d(h)\,d(0)} \le \frac{2\,|d(h) - d(0)|}{d(0)^2} ,\]
