    which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|d(h) - d(0)| < \eta\,d(0)^2/2\).
  7. By the definition of the partial derivative 1.25 the quotient \((p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P))/h\) converges to \(\partial p/\partial x\,(P)\). By the lemma 1.80 on limit and continuity, item 1, the function that has the value of this quotient for \(h \neq 0\) and the value \(\partial p/\partial x\,(P)\) at \(h = 0\) is continuous at \(0\). Its product with the function \(-1/d\) is continuous at \(0\) by corollary 1.64, and by step 4 it equals the quotient of the function \(f\) for \(h \neq 0\). By item 1 of lemma 1.80, used in the other direction,
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P) = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}(P) \cdot \frac{1}{2\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}} = -\frac12\,f(P)^3\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}(P) .\]
  8. Continuity of the derivative. The functions \(f\) (step 3) and \(\partial p/\partial x\) are continuous at every point of \(D\), so by corollary 1.69, item 1, the product \(-\tfrac12\,f\,f\,f\,\partial p/\partial x\) is continuous too. For \(y\) and \(z\) we repeat steps 4 to 8 with the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 4.1.4 (PDF p. 156) computes the derivative of the function \(\sqrt x\) with the same trick of a difference of squares. The proof is not from the sources.

We apply the lemma to the function \(p = 1 + s^2 + t^2\) of the point \((s, t, \lambda)\), which is a polynomial, positive everywhere, with the continuous partial derivatives \(2s\), \(2t\) and \(0\). The function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\) is therefore continuously differentiable in all of space, with the derivatives

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\,\frac{1}{|(s, t, 1)|} = -\frac{s}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} , \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\frac{1}{|(s, t, 1)|} = -\frac{t}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} .\]

The derivatives are products of a polynomial with the third power of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), so by the product rule (lemma 1.81, item 3) and by the lemma they again have continuous partial derivatives. The derivative of the first with respect to \(s\) is, for instance, \(-1/|(s, t, 1)|^3 + 3s^2/|(s, t, 1)|^5\). The components of the map (4.42) are sums of products of polynomials in \(s\), \(t\), \(\lambda\) and the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), so they have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order at every point of space. The first condition holds.

The Jacobian. The derivatives of the map are \(\partial\Phi/\partial\lambda = \big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big)\,(s, t, 1)\), \(\partial\Phi/\partial s = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial s}\,(s, t, 1)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial t = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial t}\,(s, t, 1)\). The determinant is linear in each column and is zero when two columns are multiples of the same vector (lemma 2.51, items 2 and 3). The terms with the vector \((s, t, 1)\) in the first two columns therefore contribute nothing, and

\[J_\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\Big( \frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} - a \Big)\,\det\big(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, (s, t, 1)\big) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\Big( \frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} - a \Big) ,\]

which SymPy has confirmed too. The determinant is positive where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} > 0\) and \(|(s, t, 1)| < R/a\). On the box \(K\) we have \(|(s, t, 1)| \le \sqrt 3\), so \(a < R/\sqrt 3 = 5{,}774\) mm suffices, which holds for \(a = 4\) mm. For the open set we take \(D = (-\tfrac54, \tfrac54) \times (-\tfrac54, \tfrac54) \times (-\tfrac14, \tfrac54)\), which contains \(K\). On it \(|(s, t, 1)|^2 < 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac{25}{16} = 4{,}125\), so \(R/|(s, t, 1)| > 4{,}92\) mm \(> a\). Since \(R/|(s, t, 1)| \le R\), also \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} > a - \tfrac14\,(R - a) = 2{,}5\) mm. The third condition holds. The smallest value of the Jacobian on \(K\) is \(28{,}38\ \text{mm}^3\) (NumPy).

The second condition. Let \(\Phi(s, t, \lambda) = \Phi(s', t', \lambda')\) for two points of \(D\). The \(z\) component gives \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s', t', \lambda')\), a positive number, and the \(x\) and \(y\) components, divided by this number, give \(s = s'\) and \(t = t'\). Then \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a linear function of the variable \(\lambda\) with the positive coefficient \(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\), so the equality gives \(\lambda = \lambda'\). The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi(K)\) is therefore a curved box.

We get the other five pieces by rotations. The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis is the image of the same box \(K\) under the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}} = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{x}})\), where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}} = s\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = t\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components of the map (4.42). This is \(\Phi\) followed by the map \((x, y, z) \mapsto (z, y, -x)\), a quarter turn about the \(y\) axis, with the matrix with the rows \((0, 0, 1)\), \((0, 1, 0)\), \((-1, 0, 0)\) and the determinant \(1\). The components of the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are components of the map \(\Phi\), one of them with the opposite sign, so they have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order. By corollary 4.44 the Jacobian of the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}\) is \(1 \cdot J_\Phi > 0\), and different points again go to different points, because a rotation does not map two different points to the same point. In the same way we get the pieces \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\) and \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\) with the maps \((-\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{x}})\), \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}})\), \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), all of whose matrices have the determinant \(1\).

The pieces fill the ball and do not overlap. The points of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) are exactly the points \((x, y, z)\) with \(|x| \le z\), \(|y| \le z\), \(z \ge a\) and \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\). Indeed, a point \(\Phi(s, t, \lambda)\) with \((s, t, \lambda) \in K\) has \(z = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) between \(a\) and \(R/|(s, t, 1)|\), \(x = s\,z\) and \(y = t\,z\) with \(|s|, |t| \le 1\), and \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| = z\,|(s, t, 1)| \le R\). Conversely such a point has \(s = x/z\) and \(t = y/z\) in \([-1, 1]\) and \(z \le R/|(s, t, 1)|\), so \(\lambda = (z - a)/\big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big)\) is in \([0, 1]\). Every point of the ball that is not in the cube has a coordinate whose absolute value is larger than \(a\), and it lies in the piece in the direction of the coordinate with the largest absolute value. All pieces lie in the ball, and so does the cube, because by (1.10) each of its points is at most \(\sqrt3\,a = 6{,}93\) mm from \(O\), less than \(R\). The union of the seven pieces is therefore the ball. An interior point of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) has \(|x| < z\), \(|y| < z\) and \(z > a\). If, for instance, \(x = z\) held, the points \((x + h, y, z)\) with a small \(h > 0\) would not be in \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\). It therefore does not lie in the cube, where \(z \le a\), nor in the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), where \(z \le x\), nor in \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), where \(z \le -x\), nor in \(V_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\), where \(z \le \pm y\), nor in \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), where \(z < 0\). The same holds for the other pieces. An interior point of the cube has all coordinates smaller than \(a\) in absolute value and lies in no piece. The cube is the body between the graphs of the constant functions \(-a\) and \(a\). The ball is therefore made of seven sets that satisfy the condition of corollary 4.68.

Volume. By the change of variables theorem 4.59 with the function \(1\) the volume of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) is the integral of the Jacobian over \(K\). We compute the inner integral over \(\lambda\) with the fundamental theorem of calculus. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^3/3\) has the derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial\lambda = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big) = J_\Phi\) with respect to \(\lambda\), its value at \(\lambda = 1\) is \(R^3/\big(3\,|(s, t, 1)|^3\big)\) and at \(\lambda = 0\) it is \(a^3/3\), so

\[\int_0^1 J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = \frac{1}{3}\,\Big( \frac{R^3}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} - a^3 \Big) .\]

The integral of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|^3\) over the square \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\) is \(2\pi/3\), which SymPy has computed, because it needs the arctangent function, which we have not defined. So by the theorem 4.9 on the order of integration the volume of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) is

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}V = \frac{R^3}{3} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} - \frac{4a^3}{3} = \frac{2\pi R^3}{9} - \frac{4a^3}{3} = 612{,}80\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

By corollary 4.68, item 1, with the function \(1\) the volume of the ball is the sum of the volumes of the pieces, \(8a^3 + 6 \cdot \big(2\pi R^3/9 - 4a^3/3\big) = 4\pi R^3/3 = 4188{,}79\ \text{mm}^3\), the volume of a ball from school geometry. The terms with \(a^3\) cancel. The cube in the middle does not change the volume, because for every small enough \(a\) the six pieces complete it exactly to the ball.

Face vectors. We computed the integrals of the components of the face vectors of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) over its six faces with SymPy and NumPy. In square millimetres they are \((0, 0, 174{,}08)\) for the face \(\lambda = 1\) on the ball, \((0, 0, -64)\) for the face \(\lambda = 0\) on the cube, \((\pm 27{,}52, 0, -27{,}52)\) for the faces \(s = \pm 1\) and \((0, \pm 27{,}52, -27{,}52)\) for the faces \(t = \pm 1\). The sum is the zero vector, \(174{,}08 - 64 - 4 \cdot 27{,}52 = 0\), as the theorem for a constant field demands. On a flat face this integral is the outward normal times the area. The face on the cube is a square with the side \(8\) mm and the area \(64\ \text{mm}^2\), the face \(s = 1\) has the normal \((1, 0, -1)/\sqrt 2\) and the area \(\sqrt 2 \cdot 27{,}52 = 38{,}92\ \text{mm}^2\).

Fluxes. The field \(\vek v = (x, 0, 0)\), with the coordinate \(x\) in millimetres, has divergence \(1\), so the integral of the divergence over each piece is its volume. The fluxes through the faces of the pieces \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) in cubic millimetres, computed with SymPy and NumPy, are:

face \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\)
\(\lambda = 1\), on the ball \(313{,}23\) \(1467{,}93\)
\(\lambda = 0\), on the cube \(0\) \(-256{,}00\)
\(s = 1\) \(149{,}78\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(s = -1\) \(149{,}78\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(t = 1\) \(0\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(t = -1\) \(0\) \(-149{,}78\)
sum of fluxes \(612{,}80\) \(612{,}80\)
volume \(612{,}80\) \(612{,}80\)

For each piece the last two rows are equal, as theorem 4.67 says. The faces \(t = \pm 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) lie in the planes \(y = \pm z\), whose normals have no \(x\) component, so \(\vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) there. The face \(s = 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and the face \(s = -1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are the same set of points with opposite fluxes, \(149{,}78\) and \(-149{,}78\). The face \(\lambda = 0\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) is the face \(x = a\) of the cube, through which the cube has the flux \(a \cdot (2a)^2 = 256\ \text{mm}^3\).

That the two fluxes through a shared face are opposite for every field we see as follows. The face \(s = 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and the face \(s = -1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are described by the same function of the variables \(t\) and \(\lambda\), because \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-1, t, \lambda) = \Phi(1, t, \lambda)\), since \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) depends on \(s\) only through \(s^2\). The vector of the first face is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{s}}\) of this function, the vector of the second \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{s}}\) of the same function, so the fluxes are opposite for every continuous field, as for the cut of the round bar in section 4.2.12.

Neighbouring pieces have twelve shared side faces, one along each edge of the cube. The following table covers them all. In it \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi\), and \(u\) is the parameter of the face that is not \(\lambda\). In each row the maps of the two pieces give the same point.

piece and face neighbouring piece and face equality
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(-1, u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(u, -1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(u, 1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = 1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(1, -u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(-1, -u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(-u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(u, -1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(u, 1, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)

We check each equality by inserting the components. In the fifth row, for instance, \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda) = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -u\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(1, -u, \lambda) = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -u\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), the first with \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((1, u, \lambda)\), the second at the point \((1, -u, \lambda)\). The values are equal, because \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) depends on \(s\) and \(t\) only through \(s^2 + t^2\). SymPy has also checked all twelve equalities, for every map that is the product of a function of the variables \(s^2 + t^2\) and \(\lambda\) with the vector \((s, t, 1)\). We describe each face by its parameters in the order that gives its vector of definition 4.65, as in the paragraph after figure 4.49: on the faces \(s = 1\) and \(t = -1\) the parameter \(u\) comes first and \(\lambda\) second, on the faces \(s = -1\) and \(t = 1\) \(\lambda\) comes first. When \(u\) stands in different places for the two faces of a row, as in the first row, we get the description of the face of the neighbouring piece from the description of the face of the first piece by a map \(\tau\) that exchanges the parameters. When it stands in the same place, as in the fifth row, the equality has \(-u\), and \(\tau\) changes the sign of the parameter \(u\). In both cases \(\tau\) is linear, maps the rectangle and the open set of the parameters of one face onto the rectangle and the open set of the parameters of the other, and has the Jacobian \(-1\). By item 3 of corollary 4.64 the fluxes through the two faces of each row are therefore opposite for every continuous field.

The face \(\lambda = 0\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), however, is the top lid of the cube, described differently. The cube describes it by the coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) on \([-a, a] \times [-a, a]\) and the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) by the parameters \(s\) and \(t\) on \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\), with the point \((a s, a t, a)\) and the face vector \(-\vek N_\lambda = -a^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). By the change of variables theorem 4.59 in the plane, with the map \((s, t) \mapsto (a s, a t)\), whose Jacobian is \(a^2\),

\[\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a}\int_{-\mathrm{a}}^{a} v_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, a)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = a^2 \int_{-1}^{1}\int_{-1}^{1} v_{\mathrm{z}}(a s, a t, a)\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s ,\]

so the two fluxes are opposite for every continuous field. In general corollary 4.64 says the same. The same holds for the other five faces of the cube. The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), for instance, describes the face \(x = a\) by the points \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(s, t, 0) = (a, a t, -a s)\) and the face vector \(-\vek N_\lambda = -a^2\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), the cube by the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) and the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The change of variables with the map \((s, t) \mapsto (a t, -a s)\), whose Jacobian is \(a^2\), gives opposite fluxes. For the other four faces the computation is the same (SymPy). For the whole ball the sum of the fluxes through the six faces on the ball is \(4 \cdot 313{,}23 + 2 \cdot 1467{,}93 = 4188{,}79\ \text{mm}^3\), the volume of the ball, as corollary 4.68 demands. The pieces \(V_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\) and \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\) have, by the symmetry of the field, the same fluxes as \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), and the piece \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\) the same as \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\).

What does this mean for mechanics? We immerse the steel ball in oil under the pressure \(p = 100\) MPa. The displacement field \(\vek u = \varepsilon\,(x, y, z)\) with \(\varepsilon = -p/(3K)\), where \(K = 163{,}3\) GPa is the bulk modulus of steel, has at every point the strains \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon = -2{,}041 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and no shear strains, exactly those that by section 3.2.4 a small piece under the uniform pressure \(p\) has. The stress \(-p\) at every point is in equilibrium, because it is constant and we neglect the weight, and on the surface it gives the pressure \(p\). The divergence of the field is \(3\varepsilon\). For small displacements the flux of the displacements through the surface is approximately the change of volume (section 4.2.5), so by corollary 4.68 the volume of the ball changes by approximately \(3\varepsilon \cdot 4188{,}79\ \text{mm}^3 = -2{,}565\ \text{mm}^3\). The exact change is by corollary 4.60 \(\big((1 + \varepsilon)^3 - 1\big) \cdot 4188{,}79\ \text{mm}^3\), which differs from this by \(0{,}0005\ \text{mm}^3\). For the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) the face on the ball contributes \(-0{,}4275\ \text{mm}^3\), the face on the cube \(0{,}0523\ \text{mm}^3\), and the side faces nothing, because the displacement points along the rays from \(O\), which lie in the planes of the side faces. The sum \(-0{,}3753\ \text{mm}^3\) is \(3\varepsilon\) times the volume of the piece. The faces of the cube move inward, and each contributes \(\varepsilon a \cdot 64\ \text{mm}^2 = -0{,}0523\ \text{mm}^3\) to the flux of the cube, the opposite of the neighbouring piece.

A thick spherical shell with the inner radius \(R_1 = 40\) mm and the outer radius \(R_2 = 60\) mm, such as we will load by pressure in chapter 11, has no cube in the middle. We cut it into six pieces (figure 4.53). The piece in the direction of the \(z\) axis is the image of the box \(K\) under the map

\[\Phi(s, t, \lambda) = \big((1 - \lambda)\,R_1 + \lambda R_2\big)\,\frac{(s, t, 1)}{|(s, t, 1)|} ,\]

which puts the point on the ray through \((s, t, 1)\) at the distance \((1 - \lambda)\,R_1 + \lambda R_2\) from \(O\). The components have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order for the same reason as for the ball, and by the same computation \(J_\Phi = \big((1 - \lambda)\,R_1 + \lambda R_2\big)^2\,(R_2 - R_1)/|(s, t, 1)|^3\), which SymPy has confirmed. The determinant is positive where the distance is positive, for instance on the open set \(D = (-2, 2) \times (-2, 2) \times (-\tfrac12, \tfrac32)\), where the distance is larger than \(30\) mm. Different points go to different points, because the ray fixes \(s\) and \(t\) and the distance fixes \(\lambda\). The volume of a piece is \(\tfrac13\,(R_2^3 - R_1^3) \cdot 2\pi/3 = 106\,116\ \text{mm}^3\), the volume of the shell \(4\pi\,(R_2^3 - R_1^3)/3 = 636\,696\ \text{mm}^3\) (SymPy). We get the other five pieces by the same rotations as for the ball. The points of the piece in the direction of the \(z\) axis are exactly the points \(P\) with \(|x| \le z\), \(|y| \le z\) and \(R_1 \le |\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R_2\). We show this as for the ball, only with \(\lambda = (|\overrightarrow{OP}| - R_1)/(R_2 - R_1)\). Every point of the shell is at least \(R_1\) from \(O\), so it has a coordinate that is not zero, and it lies in the piece in the direction of the coordinate with the largest absolute value. That an interior point of a piece lies in no other piece we show as for the ball. The pieces meet in twelve side faces that lie in the planes \(x = \pm z\), \(y = \pm z\) and \(x = \pm y\). Here too the map is the product of a function of the variables \(s^2 + t^2\) and \(\lambda\) with the vector \((s, t, 1)\), so all equalities of the table hold, and the fluxes through the two faces of each pair are opposite. The faces \(\lambda = 0\) on the inner sphere and \(\lambda = 1\) on the outer one are outer pieces of the surface.

A tube, the body between two cylinders with a common axis, we cut in the same way, only by planes through the axis. As an example we take the ring of section 1.18.5, a short steel tube with the axis \(z\). We measure lengths in millimetres. The ring together with its surface is the set of the points \(P\) with \(40 \le \rho_{\mathrm{P}} \le 60\) and \(|z_{\mathrm{P}}| \le c\), where \(\rho_{\mathrm{P}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{P}}^2}\) is the distance of the point from the \(z\) axis and \(c > 0\) half the height of the ring. The planes \(y = x\) and \(y = -x\) cut it into four pieces. Seen from above it looks like the annulus of figure 4.53, only with the \(y\) axis in place of the \(z\) axis. The piece in the direction of the \(x\) axis is the image of the box \(K = [0, 1] \times [-1, 1] \times [-c, c]\) under the map

\[\Phi(\lambda, s, \zeta) = \Big( \frac{40 + 20\,\lambda}{|(1, s)|},\ \frac{(40 + 20\,\lambda)\,s}{|(1, s)|},\ \zeta \Big) ,\]

where \(|(1, s)| = \sqrt{1 + s^2}\). It puts the point at the height \(\zeta\), on the ray from the \(z\) axis in the direction of the vector \((1, s, 0)\), at the distance \(40 + 20\,\lambda\) from the axis. The components have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order for the same reason as for the ball, by lemma 4.69 with \(p = 1 + s^2\). The Jacobian is \(J_\Phi = 20\,(40 + 20\,\lambda)/(1 + s^2)\) (SymPy), positive on the open set \(D = (-\tfrac12, \tfrac32) \times (-2, 2) \times (-2c, 2c)\), which contains \(K\) and on which \(40 + 20\,\lambda > 30\). Different points go to different points, because the height fixes \(\zeta\), the ray fixes \(s\) and the distance from the axis fixes \(\lambda\). The volume of the piece is

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}V = 2c \cdot \frac{60^2 - 40^2}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = 1000\,\pi\,c\ \text{mm}^3 ,\]

where \(\int_0^1 20\,(40 + 20\,\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = (60^2 - 40^2)/2\), and the integral \(\int_{-1}^{1} \mathrm{d}s/(1 + s^2) = \pi/2\) was computed by SymPy. The four pieces give \(4000\,\pi\,c\ \text{mm}^3\), the area of the annulus \(\pi\,(60^2 - 40^2)\) times the height \(2c\). We get the other pieces by quarter turns about the \(z\) axis. The piece in the direction of the \(y\) axis is the image of the box \(K\) under the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}} = (-\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components of the map \(\Phi\), and we get each next piece from the previous one by the same quarter turn \((x, y, z) \mapsto (-y, x, z)\), whose determinant is \(1\). So we check the conditions of definition 4.65 as for the ball, and likewise that the pieces fill the ring and do not overlap, only with the two coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) in place of three. The face \(s = 1\) of the piece in the direction of the \(x\) axis and the face \(s = -1\) of the piece in the direction of the \(y\) axis are described by the same function of the variables \(\lambda\) and \(\zeta\), because \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(\lambda, -1, \zeta) = \Phi(\lambda, 1, \zeta)\). The first face has the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial\Phi/\partial\zeta\times\partial\Phi/\partial\lambda\) of this function, the second \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{s}}\), so the fluxes are opposite, as in the first row of the table. For each next pair of neighbouring pieces we get the same equality by turning both sides by a quarter turn.

With this we have proved the divergence theorem for all bodies that we cut into finitely many bodies between graphs and curved boxes so that the inner pieces of the surfaces pair up with opposite fluxes. Such are the box, the body made of boxes, the round bar, the ball, the thick spherical shell and the tube, for instance the ring, that is, all the bodies of our examples. Such are also the bodies that a mesh of the finite element method cuts into six-faced elements (chapter 15), when each element is the image of a cube under a map with the conditions of definition 4.65 and two neighbouring elements describe their shared face by descriptions related by a map with a negative Jacobian, as for the pieces of the ball. COOK describes such elements as images of a cube whose faces are the images of the faces of the cube (§6.5, PDF p. 231), and FELIPPA demands for elements in the plane that the Jacobian be positive everywhere (§19.4.2, PDF p. 289). For bodies that we cannot cut in this way we have not proved the theorem. KREYSZIG states it for bodies bounded by an arbitrary surface made of smooth pieces (§10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479) and says that a proof for them would need a further limit process (PDF p. 482). When a later chapter needs such a body, it will say that it relies on this stated theorem. The cuts of the ball and of the ring into curved boxes are not from the sources.

With this we have what we need for a body in space: the integral over a body and over its surface, the change of variables and the divergence theorem, which connects the integral over a body with the integral over its surface, for all the bodies of our examples. The next section writes equilibrium in a new form, which does not speak of the forces on single small pieces but of the work of the forces on the small displacements the supports allow, first for a rigid body, then for a bar and a truss. For a body in space we will derive this form in section 4.5, and there the divergence theorem will play the role that integration by parts plays for a bar.
